The following article Is reprinted from the Railway Sape Journal (London, April 2nd, 1887) In the course of our visit, as interesting as it was instrue. live, in August last. to the Lancaster Agricultural Show, we were particularly impressed with the essentially healthy and vigorous physique of the calves shown, and were informed that this excellence arose from the animals having been fattened OD. the Lancaster Calf Food," which we subsequently learned is manufactured by Messrs. Carruthers and Co., of Lancaster, who for a century have maintained a deservedly good reputa- tion for the excellence of their productions, and who for upwards of 25 years have devoted special atten- tion to the manufacture of food for cattle and calves. Their feeding principle from the first has been to provide for all the wants of the animal, economy in rearing young stock with sound and well-developed frames, and after- wards maintaining the system in a state of health and vigour, and many who have used Messrs. Carruthers and Co.'s manu- factures through all these years testify that this subject has been fully realised, their stock having been wonderfully ex- empt from disease or loss. The Lancaster Calf Fcod, as its name imports, is prima facie intended for the rearing of calves, and as a milk substitute is unsurpassed. It is a veritable molter/a in parvo, eznbracing,as it does, all the contltnents for a highly nourishing food. It contains oil and fatty sr, and albumenoids, starch, sugar, and mucilage. This will suffi- ciently account for the ease with which it can be digested after having been formed Into a suitable gruel. Calves can be reared with it from three days old to twelve months without the ad- dition of milk, although for young calves it is usual to add skim milk for the first few weeks. Not only is the Calf Food suitably for calves, but it is especially , valuable for all animals that may be aifing. Its nourishing qualities are suited admirably for rearing young pigs, and improving the condition of horses, whilst in dairy cows it produces the richest milk. Mixed with oatmeal in the proportion of two to one, it is unsurpassed for its fattening powers, both in increase of weight and quality of meat. The price elm by Meisrs. Carruthers is very small, for it is only 13s. per cwt., carriage paid to any railway station, so that taking into account its many undeniable virtues, it would surely be a waste of time to look tor a cheaper or. more nutritious provender for stock. Peal* is not rest—not inactivilly. t it cometh to true hearts as unto deep, ' ...Far-flowing, mighty rivers. Little souls • r Will always babble, surge' and struggle on, As do the little streams; but natures large, 'Though sometimes ruffled, in their depths are Great natures will have peace., It will be born ~ Of their right spirits. Harmony with them Shall be indeed a god-begotten son— Sign of good will and love to all things good.

GRANNY'S COMFORTER. "Where is your father, now, my child ? God only knows. 'T was a day like this, and just as wild-- Flow the wind blow S ! He sailed away across the bay. So brave and true; And never a word has since been heard Of ship or crew. Vr"l "And now my other boy, they say, psr

Has gone from me, Dying a thousand leagues away Across the sea I I Alas! of both my sans bereft! Yet God knows bast! And, little one, you still are left, So I am blest !"
The child beside her granny stands—

The most pushing man is the man who gives momen- tum to a wheelbarrow. Monsieur Goussaut. President of the Chamber of Accompts, was celebrated for stupidity. One day standing behind a player at piquet. who did not know him, the player throwing a foolish card, exclaimed, "I am a mere Goussant!" The President enraged at finding his name used as a proverb, said, "You are a fool." "True," said the other, without even looking back, "that is just what I meant to say." , The late Lord Kelly, who was remarkable for his rubi- cundity of nose, having spoken rather disrespectfully of a gentleman in the army, an Irishman present observed that if any man that had lived, or ever had lived, or ever could live, had said the same of him, he would have pulled him by the nose. "Yes," replied Foote, "I dare say you would; but in the present case that would not do; there are ways enough of revenzing an insult with- out running oneN hand into the fire." A Scotchman and an Irishman were sleeping at an inn together. The weather being rather warm, the Scotch- man, in his sleep, put his leg out of bed. A triti-eller, in passing the room door, saw him in this situation, and having a mind for a frolic, gently fixed a spur upon Sawney's heel, who, drawing his leg into bed, so dis- turbed his companion that he exclaimed, " Anal) ! my dear honey, have a care of your great toe, for you have forgot to cut your nails I belave." The Scotchman being sound asleep, and sometim•s, perhaps, not a little dis- turbed by other companions, still kept scratching poor Teague, till his patience being quite spent, he succeeded in rousing Sawney, who, not a little surprised at finding the spur on his heel, loudly exclaimed, " Deil take the daft dile of an ossler ; he's ta'en my boots off last night, and left on the spur!" ; IRISH TYPES AND TRAITS.—It is one of the contradic- tions in the Celtic race that, amongst a people eminently .pootical, marriage is almost entirely a matter of business. A father having a marriageable son looks among his neighbcurs for a girl whose portion will about match what he is prepared to give his boy. Then, the girl being found, there is a consultation with her father, and a meeting takes place at the house of either, at which, the bargain being satisfactorily concluded, the match is made. The girl's father beOns by offering a smaller sum than he means to give, which offer is treated with scorn; then he advances bit by bit, throwing in now five pounds, now a cow, till he has reached the limit of his intentions. Then hands are clapped into each other with tremendous emphasis, the girl and boy, who have been wait ng while their fate hangs in the balance, are called in and informed of the happy result, and the even- ing winds up with festivities to commemorate the match- . making.—Katheriae Tynan, in the Magazine of Art. WOMAN'S Waite its ewe Furtrae..—Man as well as woman has suffered by civilisation. Her gifts have often turned to destrnctiod in his hand; and though he may look with an anxious eye upon the changes that ' have come so thickly and so swiftly upon woman, he may find his own advancement is hidden in hers and dependent upon it. May not the time be come when the strength of • woman is imperative to make man stronger?—when it is necessary for him that she should be his fitting companion—loyal but not servile? May ' not the hour have struck when her own elevation is abso- lutely necessary to prevent his deterioration? And out of the present may not that future be already preparing which will increase, and not decrease, the physical and mental distance between man and woman ?—when she will fully taste the satisfaction, not of her inferiority, but of his superiority, of which every fresh development in her favour now makes her the jmilcler and preserver? —The Countess of Portsmouth, in The Woman's World. Of all the Ministers employed by Catherine IL, Count Stackleberg had the most wit and the most pride, and this he displayed particularly in Poland. M. von Thugut, being sent to that country by the Emperor Leopold, when he was to have his audience of Poniatowski, was Introduced into a saloon, when, seeing a man gravely seated, and surrounded by Polish lords respectfully standing before him, he took him for the king, and began his complimentary speech. It was Stackleberg, who was in no hurry to set him right. Thugut, in- formed of his mistake, was vexed and ashamed. In the evening being at cards with istacklebera and the king, he played a card, saying, "The king of clubs .!" "You are wrone !" said the king; it is the knave ! " The Austrian Ambassador, pretending to have been mis- taken, answered, slapping his:forehead, " Ah, sire, pardon me, this is the second time to day I have taken a knave for a king !" No Toxe ON HER.—A woman, living on Columbia' street East. came down town the other day with a " yearling" in a baby carriage, and when she reached a certain dry goods store she left the cab at the door and went in to trade. The youngster was good-natured over being left alone, and one of the clerks in the store, who knew the mother well, thought to play a joke on her. While she was busy trading he slirped out and wheeled the carriage into an adjoining store. A rush of customers prevented him from seeing the woman as she went out. She stood at the door for a moment, as if wondering if she had forgotten something, and then started off and went straight home. By that time "hub" had become uneasy and was raising a row, and , they sent in for the clerk to come and get him. The mother having departed for home, he was obliged to follow her with cart and baby, the latter howling at the top of his voice and attracting general attention. The clerk had reached the gate, when the woman came out, and as she saw baby and cart she threw up both hands and exclaimed—" Dear me, but I thought it was a spool of twist that I had forgotten !" THE INVENTOR OF THE JACQUARD Loom.—lt is a fact strange enough, but true, that most inventors of things which have made this and other countries prosperous have had humble birth, have experienced arduous youth- ful toil, have met with constant and disheartening rebuff, and have too frequently disappeared from the world—if not in poverty, at least without sufficient to bequeath to descendants to keep them aloof from the acceptance of the charity of others. M. Jacquard, of Lyons, was no exception to this rule. Born in 1752 of humble weaver parents, his childhood was unromantic. Without educa- tion, his inclinations were pretty much left to their own development. He betrayed a taste for mechanics, which was to some extent encouraged in his occupations as typefounder and in a cutlery manufactory. His father's death led him to set up as a figure-fabric weaver, but he failed, and subsequently endured many vicissitudes. He applied all his energy to the consummation of the inven- tion which had originated in his mind so early as 1790. He succeeded somewhat, but his invention fell into the hands of the Prefect at Lyons, and both he and the machine were "arrested" and taken to Paris. It VMS on , this occasion that he had an interview with Napoleon. The Emperor ridiculed Jacquard's mechanism, but Jac- , guard demonstrated his success, and eventually brought , Set the invention which bears his name, and is known ever the civilised world. THE OLD MAN WAS TOo HASTY.—A staid old Hub- bardstown farmer came to the Hub yesterday to do "a leetle tradin'," and as he meandered Clown Washington- street "headed for the Fitchburg depat," as he said, he suddenly halted, gazed excitedly at a sign in front Of a clothing-house, and then darted into the store, exclaim-' lag, " Well, I vum' that is good !" After due delibera- tion, he selected alO dollar suit of clothes, tendering in payment just 7 dollars. "That's the right change," said he to the astonished clerk. "But I don't understand it; I told you that suit would be 10 dollars," argued the clerk. "Yes, I know, but don't your old sign out on the door say, 'All we want is 70 cents, on the dollar?" and, picking up his new purchase, the honest old Hubbards- town farmer hastily left. Ile trotted along, congratu- lating himself on his wonderful smartness, and was heard to mutter, "I guess I'm lively enough for these 'ere city folks." But a sudden change came "o'er the spirit of his dream," after he had walked a short distance. A look of utter disgust overspread his face, the bundle fell from hisarms, and in a mournful tone he said, "Why didn't I look round a little before I bought these clothes ?" • The consternation was due to another clothing sign that read, "Goods sold here at half-price." After studying the situation for several minutes, he resumed his journey dep6twescd, saying, "I might have saved 5 dollars just as well as not if I hadn't been in such a pesky hurry." YEAD WARTCH. By BROTHER WHIMS. Aw wur one day welly crazed wi this complaint. in seem' a mate o',moine aw axed him th' best cure for yead wartch. He sed us aw must her a good walk of abeawt three moile before aw bed any din- ner that day, becose, he said, th' blood geet aw in a rook on th' top o' mi brain, un that causcd mi furt hey th' yead wartch. So off aw seet beawt de- lay—aw walked fro' eaur heause to Slopper-street, Chowbent ; three toimes theere un back, un then aw seet mi deawn eawr Sale easy cheer, un after lap- pin' a new blanket abeawt mi bumps aw noicely went sleep. Bur, hrawever, aw wur wakkent in abeawt hauf an heansr bi eawr Bill comin' bowtin' ith heause wi hauf a cae's yead craddlet up in his arms. Eawr Sal ses, " Whar hasta getten, Bill?' He says, "Aw've ony getten a cae's yead us butcher Gustus gen mi; he's given a cae's yead to every one oth' lads Chowbent us'll tell him th' biggest, fie, un aw towd him a whopper. Aw sed us wey'd bed a pig In 1822 us eat nowt else bur gonder shavin's un gal- vanised sawdust fur three months un two days, un fur this lie aw geet a cae's yead. Wheere mun aw stick it eawt oth' cat's road?" Hoo ses, "Hang it ith' parlour theere, just o'er thi fayther's yead, un moind un dunnowakken him, neaw. becase he's get- ten th' yead wartch, un aw don't want him disturbed at present." "Aw reet," he said; un he coome clomperin' in with his treasure under hit arm, pulled th' sofa be- heend mi cheer, jumpet on th' top on it wi' his clogs ' on, un suddenly thinkin' abeawt string furt hang it up wi' he bawls eawt—"Eh, mother, fotch us a lump o' coord, so as aw con hang it up." Eawr Sal ' coome bowfin' in welly eawt o' puff, sheawtin',' "Shur up thi meawth, wilto? Didn't aw tell thi not furt make a din becose thi fayther's getten yead wartch? It's no mostal use o' tellin' tin nowt, un corn off that sofa wi' thi clogs. If thi fayther seed thi he'd welly go crazy." Bur, heawever. Bill wudnt be satisfied. Flev a piece o' string he would, un after lookin abeawt fur hauf an beaus un foindin noane, he suddenly be- thowt bissel o' th' cloothes loine, so off he bowts ith' kitchen wi' th' bread knoife, slashes a piece off it, an coome bangin' to wheere he'd left th' cae's yed again. He stuck th' yed on th' floor un pun- ched a hole through it wi' his clog un then fastened th' coord firmly, us he thowt, on a knot, un slingin' o'er his shouder' jumps upo' th' sofa agen. He'd just getten it noicely on th' hook when th' knot coome undone, un th' cae's yed coome aw ov a rook on th' top o' my yed, makkin mi sheawt eawt, fur aw wur welly crazy wi' pain. Whoile aw this wur gooin on, eawr Bill ud run 1 eawt o' th' heawse, knockin' a can o' swillin's o'er I wi' bein' sich a hurry furt ger eawt o' mi road, un hid hissel th' pig cote Aw seet mi deawn agen un in a bit eawr Sal comes in wantin' t' know what wur up. "Why," aw see, "that young brat Bill has setten mi yed agate wartchin agen wi' that con- founded cae's yed. Aw dunno what tha towd him fart come messin abeawt me wi' it fur when tha knows weel enough whar a mischievous young vamp lie is." Hoo naer sed nowt, bur went away agen till hoogetten to wheere th' swillin's wur, un boo sheawts eawt "hang hi! well aw'll be bleat iv he hasn't purred th' ssvillin' can o'er, wi' three pen- orth o' swillin's us aw geet froth' Teawn Hall yes- terday in it. Aw'll very neer break his yed when he comes in. Aw reckon th' pigs ull her furt goo beawt meat to-dsv neaw through his meyther." Just at this tonne who should pop in bur owd mother Owdham froth' next door. " Hello,Jemmy," hoo ses, " heaw's thi yed this mornin' ?" " Why,' aw ses, "it's a lot was nor it wus yesterday. Iv it goes no better awst hey t' hey th' doctor." Hoo ses " aw'll tell thi what curet eawr Ben when he wur bad. Aw geet a washin' mug full o' mustard un black puddin' broth, un he stuck his feet in it, un aw geet another mug full o' tay leaves un sawt be- beend him un gen him a good shower bath. Tha knows whar I meean ; aw laded th' tay leesves an sawt on th' top o' his yed wi' a can, un it curet rhim i' ten minnits. In fact, he sed he cud see th' pain comin' eawt o' th' eend uy his toes into th' mustard un wayter. It must o' curet him becose he's /vier hed th' yed wartch sin." Aw wur determint furt try this cure, so aw went ,to th' dur un sheawted o' eawr Bill, but he wur a good whoile afore he'd come, frikkent lest aw wan- ted furt lay on him ; bur aw ticed him in at last, so aw ses " Fotch thi mother's sling can; aw want thi fart goo reawdd to th' nayburs un get th' can full o' tay leeaves, becose owd mother Owdham'a recommended a tay leeave shower bath firt tak th' pain eawt o' mi yet'." "Aw reet," he ses, un off he seet, bangin' th' yard dur after him, un whistlin' th' tune o' "Sally Crabstick sells fish." Bill wurnt lung th' lone afore he met little Neddy Johnson un he see "Bill, whar arto dooin wi' that tin churn i' tin hond. Arto gooin a hawkin' lemon squash?" Bill ses "Thad awns. nod; awm gooin a getherin tay leeaves fur mi feyther ; he's bad wi' yed wartch." Neddy halt un sea "Whar iv wi' play a bit or a trick o' thi feyther, Bill? Wirt agree wi mi?" Bill ses "It depends what soart ov a trick it is. Tell Tai what tha wants furt do." "Well," Neddy ses, "aw thowt awd gooto owd Ike Skinflint's druggist shop un buy a penorth o' caus- tic soda, un weyd mix it among th' tay leeaves un naer let on to nobody, un it ud fotch awth yure off his yed same us iv he'd bin shaved wi' a brickbat." Bill ses "Oh, iv that's thi joke awll agree wi' thi," un wi' this Neddy went on his errand whoile Bill wur gerrin th' tay leeaves. He svurnt lung i' col- lectin' a can full, un thinkin' Neddy wur a lung toime wi' th' caustic, he thowt h'd goo un meet him bur he hadn't far to goo afore he met him wi' th' stuff on his arm. "Bill." he see," weyst want a jug fart melt this in? its aw lumps." "Oh nay," Bill ses, " vsp it o' th' floor; awll break it wi' nn clog." So after they'd brokken it i' bits they mixed it wi' th' tay leeaves tin Bill went whom. (To be concluded next week.)

div.head: BIG NUGGETS OF GOLD.
div.p: BIG NUGGETS OF GOLD.

The luckiest "find" ever made in California 'RV made by a man named Finney, who "turned up" a solid lump of gold near Downieville, in 1866, that weighed five thou- sand ounces, worth 1800 das. per ounce, which would make the nugget worth £lB,OOO. This was the largest nugget of pure gold ever discovered. Heretofore the Australian nugget found in the Ballarat gold fields has been considered the largest. It was valued at £15,000.1 This man Finney, or "Old Virginia," as he was called, went to Washoe, California, and there he made the great , silver discoveries, where the " Comstock " lode was located, and where Virginia City, which was named after him, stands. He died in great poverty. He was cele- brated for his wonderful head of hair, which was of a rich, dark brown in colour, full of golden tints, and which fell in heavy curls over his stalwart shoulders. He was very proud of his head covering, and always carried in his "outfit" a brush, comb, and small hand mirror, and whenever he made his "camp," while prospecting, would comb and dress his hair with great care. When misfortune overtook him, and he continued "playing ,in bad luck "—as he termed it—he began to neglect his hair, and it became frowsy, began to turn gray, and fall out, so that a few years before he died he was nearly bald, and his few remaining hairs were quite white. Had he added to his " outfit" Mrs. S. A. Allen's World's Hair Restorer, he might have retained his hair as long as he lived, for it never fails to strengthen and invigorate the hair, restore its colour, and render it soft, glossy and strong. It can be found at any chemist's or perfumer's in the world. It is the best and most agreeable hair dress- ing known. Try it.

that Mr. Stambridge, who WWI pist about to marry the deceased, declares upon oath .that she told him the evening before her death, she had had a -violent quarrel with her brother, Mr, Derrick; this is denied by the latter, and a counter-charge is brought.by the sister of the deceased against Mr. Stambridge, Who also denies on his Part that he had eny disagreement with the deceased. I leave you, gentlemen of thg jury, to,carefully consider the be'armu of these con! dieting statements:" " Then," went on the Coroner, " we come to the important evidence given .by Eliza Richards-Levi- donee all the more important I:cc:Luse it was given unwillingly, and because efforts had been made to' tamper with it by one who ought to have set her a better example," and here the Coroner gave a wither- ing .glance in the direction of Richards, who looked, as some of thelaudience said afterwards, like a har- dened old reprobate. "'The deceased was heard to call loudly on her brothes name, arid then imuk- (Reidy followed the report of the ,-pistol which caused her death. • Richards, moreover, owns he thought be heard, hiS Master's footsteps hurrying across ilie•farroyard." "I didn't, I tell ye," shouted Richards, to the .horror of everybody. ”Re were miles away 'upon the moor 1" • "Remove that man," said the coroner .in an awful voice, looking at 'Watkins. "I'll go without any removing from that young chap," and Richards stalked across the room to the door. Here Watkins gave the old Man a, gentle push, not officially, sfi much as with a friendly con- sideration for his welfare, and the door was shut upen him. • Lastly," resumed the Coroner, after Making a Solemn pause to mark his sense of the enormity of Richarthi conduct—"Lastly,and this is a very serious matter, as I need hardly point out to you, gentlemen of the jarv—Mri 'Derrick acknowledges that the revolver with Which the crime was undoubtedly com- mitted—was his own. Mr. Derrick states, moreover, that he was miles away on the moor the evening his sister was shot,. but be is unable to bring forward as a witness any irrson who saw. him there. - It is undoubtedly is terrible thing to imagine that a man, of education and respectable position should be guilty 'of the death of • hia own sister, and we .can hardly conceive any adequate motive for such a crime." Then, with a few words of solemn appeal to the jumthe Coroner dismissed them to their delibera- tions and they retired to Martin's little smoking-mein across the entrance-hall, to consider their verdict. And now that Martin was publicly accused be. fore them all, and the crowd of neighbours regarded him with indignant horror-stricken looks, and there was a more or less involuntary shrinking away from that very part of the room where he sat, with his face still calm and steadfast, though full of sadness, then Anne no longer feared to draw attention to him by anything she might do or say. They were sitting side by side as before; and with an air which would have been defiant if it had not been for the sweetness of the loyal affection which prompted her, and which beamed from her eyes Anne put Out her hand, took her brother's, and held it in her own. " laiiids of a feather," whispered one farmer to another. . "She knows all about it, bless You." The time seemed an etonity to Anne, but it was barely hall-an-hour before the jury came solemnly trooping back to their places. The moment was come which to the accused and to those who love them must be more like the agony of death than anything else we COAI suffer.' And all I —unhappy soul—it was the second time in her troubled • life that Anne had lone through this torture. She clasped her brother's hand tightly, she could hardly breathe, she could hardly see—but she could hear; and these Were the weeds she heard: "Wilful murder against Martin Derrick." • (To be continued)
LIBERAL 3LEETINGS AT LYMIL
SPEECHES BY MR.' H. GLADSTONE, M.P. AND
MR. P. 3. POWER, M.P.

On Monday evening two meetings were held at Lymm—one in the Assembly room of the Plough Hotel, and the other, an overflow meeting, in the Congregational School-room—to hear addresses from Mr. Herbert Gladstone, M.P., and Mr. P. J. Power, M.P. The principal meeting was that held at the Plough, where the chair was occupied by Mr. W. president of Altrincham Division Liberal Association. There was a crowded attendance, and amongst those present were the Rev. Hugh Davies, the Rev. W. Evans. Dr. °mull, (Warrington), Messrs. Swanwick, T. Morris (Warrington), Dodds, 11. Cameron, E.-Pord, Paterson, E. Brown, Stephens, and others. The Chairman having spoken Mr. J. A. SwANwics, chairman of the Lymm Liberal Asscciation, proposed a resolution declaring abhorrence of the unconstitutional manner in which the Government are carrying out their odious coercion policy in Ireland calling on the Government to give power to Ireland to deal with Irish affairs, and recording confidence with Mr Gladstone, with the hope that he may be spared to bring • about the consummation of his desire for a true union between the English and Irishpeoples, thereby clearing the way for the prosecution of many urgently required re- forms (cheers.) • Mr. T. W. KILLICK seconded the resolution.

Mr. H. GLADSTOICE, M.P., on rising to support the reso- lution, was greeted with loud and continued ' cheering. The Irish question was, he said,. the one upon which the next election would be fought, and the one to wiech people's minds were constantly turned. What was the method of the Tory Government in Ireland ? It was not to govern Ireland by the people, with the people, and for the people, but to govern it against the people and in spite of the people (" shame.") Their methods were two- fold, they were the methods of repression and coercion ("shame.") it did not require men of very great ability, given a certain amount of force, to govern a country by re- pression and coercion. Any individuaLif he had the strength could knock a man down and trample upon him when he was down. The government in Ireland had at their back the whole of the military forces of the British Em- pire, and it was no hard task for them to lock up Irish- men and keep them in prison. CA Voice: "And steal their trousers," and laughter.l Yes, and steal their trousers. He was glad to see in that day's newspapers that Mr. William O'Brien had got them back again. (Laughter and cheers.) When the Government put Mr. O'Brien in prison they, got a Tartar who would be in the end too much fer them. (Cheers.) What was their task ? It was to fight the coercion policy of the Government until they destroyed it. The Government had deliber- ately placed themselves upon the steep and dangerous slope of coercion. Ascent for them was now impossible, and it should be the endeavour of the Liberals that there should be no delay half-way; to use a forcible expres- sion, they should at lance, or as soon as possible, knock them to the bottom of the slope of coercion. (Cheers.) The longer this process of coercion lasted ih Ireland the worse it would be in the interests of peace and order, and the more difficult would it be to adjust all the conflicting interests of the various sections in, Ireland when they were in a position to take in hand the settlement of the question. We had from the present Government no hope of reform of the system of government which pre- vailed in Ireland. The Government had distinctly said that they did not. mean to take up the Irish question next Parliament. They were going to make an English and a Scotch session, and, if that proved so, both the Conser- vatives and the Liberal Unionists would have falsified the pledges which they made at the last election, and which they had repeatedly made since. They had de- clared that there were serious grievances in Ireland, that the system of Government in Ireland was bad, they had pledged themselves to take up that system at the earliest , possible moment, and now that moment had come they turned their backs upon their pledges, which they had now falsified. The Liberal policy was one of concilia- tion, but that was not the case of their opponents. The policy of the Government was producing separation be- tween the English and the Scotch on the one hand, and the Irish on the other, wherever they may be found'. The coercive policy was in itself a separatist policy, whereas the Liberal policy would have the effect of strengthen- ing the \ power and resources of , the great country of which we are all so proud. (Cheers.) The country was fast becoming sick of the Liberal Unionists. English people liked to deal with a downright Conservative or a downright Liberal, but they did not like to have anything to do , with dishonest middlemen. (Cheers). The chief tactics of their op- ponents consisted in trying to throw dust in the eyes of their friends, and trying to divert them from the. main question' a the day—to persuade them.' to leave the straight path, and to go off into the byways that lead nowhere. The time had come to, sweep away alien powers of foreign officials and to 'substitute a genuine Irish adminstration ,pf purely Irish, business. The leaders of the Liberal Unionist party had forfeited all the right they at one time had to be called the leaders of the Liberal party. If they tried to trample out nationality, wherever it might be, the more they endeav- oured to trample it out the stronger it would grow, and the more they resisted and thwarted it the more certain in the end it was to be irresistible, and so long as one Irishman was to be found in Ireland so long would the idea of natidnality exist and Lord Hartington and all the troop oLLiberal Unionists would be powerless to weaken it. (Cheers.) The Irish Government, in the Crimes Act, had taken armour thatwas two heavy for'them to carry, and the British people were beginning to have a pretty shrewd idea of what was going on in Ireland, and to what it was tending. The British people would best be convinced of the error of the Government in Ireland by the working of Coercion. The Government could not stop half-way. There were only two alternatives, either the Irish people must be governed according to their own ideas, or they must be dragooned into submission. (Cheers.) I Between these two alternatives people must choose for themselves. He rejoiced to think that at the next election the result would not be doubtful. (Re- newed Cheers.) The resolution having been supported by other speak-

CHAPTER XL THE VERDICT. Captait Stimbridge, was next called Upon, and he tame forward with a sullen, half subdued fury, which boded /le good to the Derrick family. " ou were engaged to ,hi married to the de- ceased young lady, I understand," began the ,Coroner. " I was, sir. I am proud to own 'it; the thought alit is the only consolation and comfort left rae in my desolation and bereavement." " Aud you wish to deny upon oath that there was any disagreement between you and the deceased?" "I do, sir. I call Heaven and earth, and all 'those honourable gentlemen here present to witness that there never was anything between me and the late Miss Susan Derrick, but the most perfect love, affectioq, and harmony. And. whips° says otherwise ought to be prosecuted for wilful and corrupt per- jury—whosoever they may be, relatives of the de- ceased orwhat not—" and he turned a threatening face towards Anne, who was just then too much absorbed in her Own gloomy and terrifying thoughts to be aware of his presence in the room. "When did you last see the deceased ?" "On Thursdnv night, Sir. We had been te- gether all the afternoon at Tavistook, buying articles to ornament and beautify the happy home we hoped to have had together. We parted, sir; at the door of this very house with the mutual respect and affection for each other, becom- ing those who are just about to enter the nuptial state. I can say no more, sir," and Stambridge hid his face in his handkerchief. "We all feel deep sympathy with you, Ma Stambridge--" and the Coroner's words were rer echoed by a pitying murmur round the room. " I much regret being obliged to ask another question or two. Considering your relations with the de- ceased, no doubt the most perfect confidence existed between you. Did she ever tell you of any person who had any ill-feeling against her, any person whcr had ever quarrelled with her, or was likely to do hos any injury ? " "Yes, she did." Stambridge's handkerchief wen' down from his eyes, and there was a. fierce trines!. in them as he answered. "She told me that yes, Thursday night, and they were almost the very last words as she ever spoke to me: 'Martin and I have just had a regular flareup, and you know what a nasty temper he has.' Those were her ver words. I shall remember them as long as I live." , Martin sprang to his fee as Stambridge spoke. ' Then he recollected himsel f,and with one quick glance at Anne, he resumed his seat and kept his e 3 es fixed on the ground, as before. In 'another minute the climax of the scene ap- proached. Everyone's heart beat a little quicker, as in a stern,sig,nificant tone, which, in the ears of every- one present meant—" Prisoner at the bar l" the Coroner sununoned Martin Derrick. ' He was a dignified and manly figure, as he rose and walked to the table with firm steps. Tall, square- shouldered, his head hold erect, there was about him a look of reserved and silent power. But around this strong, self-possesed man there was weaving a net of circumstances which presently would make him as helpless as a child. The one or two people in the room who believed in Martin Derrick felt a cold shudder rum through them at the deadly meaning of- the 'Coroner's words, which he uttered as soon as Wan had taken the oath. • "It is my duty to warn you, Mr. Derrick, that what you say may be taken as evidence against you. Will you tell me where you were on the afternoon and evening of last Friday?" "I was on the moor." "How long were you away from home?" "From noon or thereabouts till half-past nine at night." "Did you meet any one during that time ? " "Not a living soul since three o'clock in' ft,. afternoon." "Can you describe to the jury on what part of the moor you were?" Martin thereupon gave a minute description of the direction he had taken during the earlier part of the day, when the atmosphere was fairly clear, and then he Old them how in the thick- fog which had come on during the afternoon he bad lost his way entirely, and had found it again only After great difficulty. "How do You account fbr the fact that your ser- vant, Eliza Richards, heard the deceased call loudly upon your name, if, as you say, you were at that time miles distant from the house f" Martin's lips quivered under his moustache, there was a slight falter in his voice, as he replied after a moment's pause, "I can only suppose that my poor sister hoped I was somewhere within hearing,ancl flats she called upon me to protect her from the man, 'who- ever he was,who was-threatening her life." "A likely story," Stambridge was heard to mutter, and there was an incredulous sneer upon many of the faces of the men present. "Will you state what was the causeof the quarrel between yourself and your deceased sister?" , Martin's eyes flashed, and he lifted up his head haughtily. "I deny, sir, in the strongest words I can use, that there was any quarrel between us. Captain Stapbridge knows quite well—," and Martin gave him a swift, stern glance, "that as lately as last Wednesday evening I gave my sister Susan thirty pounds as a wedding present, and they went together to Tavistock to buy those things he has been talking of, with the money." Stambridge,here questioned by the Coroner, owned to the fact of the money having been given, but added —" Susan told me her brother was very angry with her about the way she had spent it." "I deny it, on my oath I deny it !" cried Marti- shewin,c, some excitement as the charge was persisto, in. "there is not a word of truth in what Captain Stambridge has been saying." The Coroner took no further notice of Martin's de- nial—it seemed a matter of small importance to him —but went swiftly on. And then the last,the most dreadful question of all, was put to Martin. 'Mr. Derrick, I warn you, you need not reply un- less you choose. Is this revolver yours?" "Yes,that revolver is mine," was Martin's firm and clearly-spoken answer. "Where do you generally keep it ?" "In my bedroom. But last Friday morning I had been cleaning it, and 1 left it on the top of the book- shelf in my little room downstairs." "Do you generally keep it loaded ?" "Yes, always." "And you loaded it again after you had cleaned it last Friday morning ? " 64 yes.

_ "Loaded each chamber ? " • " Certainly." "One of the chambers had been discharged when the policeman found, the revolver on Friday night. What do you know about it ? " "I know nothing except what has been stated here to-day." "I haveno further question to ask you, Mr. Derrick." Martin went backto his seat, and as he did so, there passed between himself and Anne, a 100k— such as two soldiers might give each other who were cut off from all help, surrounded and over- whelmed by the superior force of the enemy: There was little left to hope for, but they would stand by each other, and support each other to the last. The Coroner then summed up the evidence. It had rarely been his task, he said, to hold a more painful, and a more mysterious inquiry. Here was a young lady of considerable personal attractions, -- parently, not an. enemy in the world, with an mediate prospect of a happy and highly respecto-- marria,,e, suddenly struck down by a cruel an. violent death. The apparent absence of motive for the crime, was one of the most puzzling features of the case. "Of course," said the Coroner, "the idea of self-destruction cannot be entertained for s moment, because the revolver was found at son* distance from the deceased, and the medical evv. ience proves that death was instantaneous. We know flora Miss Anne Derrick's evidence that some man was concealed in this house when she returned home last Friday evening, and as far as her testimony on that point '',roes, he was a man respectably dressed. As not a single article in the house was missing' it is reasonable to suppose that the crime was not committed by any person who had entered for the purpose of robbery. There remain then, two suppositions The death might pos- sibly have been accidental, from that criminal care- lessness in the use of firearms, of which we unfor- tunately hear nearly every day; and the culprit might have fled in terror. But a more likely sup- ' position is that some person may have had a violent luarrel with the deceased, and have taken her life in II MCCAW of- passion. We have the remarkable fact

ers, was, on being put to the meeting, carried with loud applause. At a second meeting, which also was well attended, the ehair was occupied by Mr. Join' RYLANDS, who said that in his experience of political life he had found that whenever the Liberals had taken anything up, they had succeeded in carrying it through. As it had been in the past, so, he prophesied, it would be in the future. He believed that Ireland would have home Rule within the lifetime of nlany of those present. (Cheers.)—A pro- position in similar terms to the one carried at the other meeting having been proposed by Mr. T. H. EvAsfs, and seconded by Mr. H. MILNE, . .

Mr. P. J. POWER, M.P., rose to support it, and was re- ceived with loud cheering. He said that those who were familiar with English life were aware that the English working-classes required many reforms in the existing laws. The Irish question, however, blocked the way, and there were those who for selfish purposes—for the purpose of preventing legislation which would affect their own class privileges—desired that it should continue so to block the way. Wit, thanks to the extension of the franchise, the working-classes were now better repre- Sented in Parliament than they Were before. Sad as were many of the deeds which laad been done in Ireland in the name of the English Government, the Irish people had viever cherished any ill-will against the English people; and they had full confidence that' the working people of England would not any longer allow their Irish fellow- subjects to be trampled under foot. (Cheers.) From every Tory platform and every,Tory newspaper we were told that the country gave at the last election an irrevocable mandate against Home Rule, but that he was not pfepared to admit. (Hear, hear.) The question came upon the people by surprise at a time when the Liberal party wasso rent that the members of it did not know to whom to look for guidance. But the past few months had dissipated many clouds. Men had gone over to the other side who ought to have gone over long ago, and the Liberal party were led by William Ewalt Glad- stone. (Cheers,) But even admitting that the country gave a mandate against Home Rule, did it give a man- date in favour of coercion and oppression? Hitherto Coercion Acts had only been passed to meet an increase of crime. The reports of the judges' charges at the last assizes in Ireland showed that at present Ireland was singularly free from crime, yet the present Tory Govern- ment nad asked for and received drastic powers of coer- cion in perpetuity. The Irish people were saddled with an Act which would not be tolerated in England for 24 hours, and that Act was being adminis- tered by stipendiary magistrates who knew, noth- ing ' about the law and were perfectly incom- petent to discharge the duties entrusted to them. In the presence of such an Act the English people might wish to know how the poor' weak, unarmed, decimated Irish Nationalists proposed to act. As an Irishman he I said they would be unworthy of the confidence of the English people if they lay down like craven cowards be- fore the Coercion Act. (Cheers.) No, poor though they were,they would fight this Coercion Act inch by inch ,foot by foot. (Loud cheers.) If one was put into prison another would take his place, and when they had all gone, there were Englishmen with hearts in their breasts who would be ready to stand between the Irish people and their oppressors. (Cheers.) The question was whether the English people were prepared to tolerate the present state, of things by propping up a gang of rack-renters in Ireland. There were only two ways out of the difficulty. There was the Cromwellian method, which was out of the question, and there was the happier, the holier way of conciliation. He had little doubt as to which of those two policies the English people would prefer. On the part of the Irish people, he could promise that they would repay ten-fold everything that was given to them. (Cheers.) Mr. I. S. LEADAR, the Liberal candidate for the divi:

sion, spoke in suppOrt of the resolution. He criticised 1 the conduct of the Government with regard to the pro- ceedings in Trafalgar-square. The object of the Govern- ment, he said, was to persuade the country that there was anarchy in London which had spread from Ireland to England, and which, both in Ireland and England, needed a strong hand to put it down. Mr. Matthews, the Home Secretary, was posing as Napoleon the Third used to pose, as the saviour of society. He sometimes wondered whether Mr. Matthews was a designing or merely an incapable man, Certainly if he had designed it he could not have taken more effective steps than he did on Sunday to throw London into a conflagration. Mr. Leadam pro- cecded to ridicule the • idea of drawing an analogy between the London riots and the proceedings in Ireland, pointing out that in London the question was only the right of meeting in a special place, whereas in Ireland the question was the momentous one of whether the people were to be allowed to hold any meet- ings at all. The resolution was also supported by Mr. IlEnniner GLADSTONE and Mr. A. La B (Oldham), and on being put to the meeting it was unanimously carried.

Mr. Herbert Gladstone, who was the guest of Mr. Jas. Dodds, Crooklands, arrived in Lymm about five o'clock on Monday. On driving into the village he was much cheered by a crowd of enthusiastic admirers, numbering from 250 to 300 persons who had assembled at Newfield. The following gentlemen, all of whom were present, were invited by Mr. Dodds to meet Mr. Glad- stone at dinner at Crooklands :—Mr. Power, M.P., Mr. John Rylands, Mr. W. Milne' Mr. Le,adam, Mr. A. Lee, Mr. Swanwick, Mr. R. Dutton, Mr. G. L. Welford, Mr. Skilling, and Mr. T. W. Killick.

div.head: OUR LONDON LETTER.
div.p: OUR LONDON LETTER.
LONDON. THURSDAY NIGHT.

Lord Salisbury's appearance at Oxford yesterday was looked forward to with a measure of interest not bounded by the political subjects upon which he might touch. There have been for some weeks past persistent rumours alleging failing powers on the part of the Marquis, which might any moment have critical results upon the constitution of the Ministry. Lord Salisbury came back from Royat and Chateau Cecil somewhat refreshed from the labours of the session, but with plain warning (so it. wes said) that further close devotion to State affaifs would be attended with certain risk. I be- lieve there is no doubt that within the last month overtures of the most direct and precise character have been made to Lord Hartington with the object of inducing him to relieye Lord Salisbury of the principal burden of the Prerniership. Lord Har- tington, personally, might have been won over, but it ia a necessity, of the situation that if he marches into the allies camp it must be with drums-beating, colours flying, and the full muster of his personal following. It would be easy enough to find a place for Lord Hartiington. Lord Salisbury would be only too glad to divide his own postessicms. But when it comes to Sir Henry James, Mr. Ileneage, Mr. Finlay, and half-a-dozen others who believe they have established a claim upon Conservative patron- age by their desertion of the Liberal banner, it is a very different thing. That means the displacement of some estimable men whose personal influence is perhaps not overwhelming in weight, but who in the aggregate are able to withstand the tendencies in this direction. Accordingly Lord Hartington has remained outside, and Lord Salisbury has staggered along. Lord Salisbury turned up to time at Oxford last night, and I hear from one present that there was in his manner no discernible failure of his usual force and spirits. He has evidently determined to keep his hand on the plough, following it up to the last furrow. This is good news for the Conserva- tive party, for it is difficult to see where they are to find a leader when they lose Lord Salisbury. Mr. Balfour would probalfly be ready to suggest a sub- stitute, but the time has not yet come for the final advancement which this young gentleman has al- ready begun to look upon as his own. One of the incidents which most amuses the on-looker of the little game now being played out is the prospect of Mr. Balfour outstripping luid outshining his former irregular chief. But a year ago this dilettante sprawling youth seemed to have no chance against Lord Randolph Churchill— He did not even pre- sume to enter the running against him. Now he is steadily coming to the front, whilst Lord Ran- dolph is, with quite surprising monotony, lagging behind. If Mr. Balfour were to be promoted to the leadership of the House of Commons there would be a prospect of some interesting rencontres between I him and his former henchman.
One thing which Lord Saliabury's speech finally settles is the tirst order of affairs in Parliament next

session. Once more the old question of Procedure is to come to the front:and engross the attention of Parliament till it is settled. Having their hand in with the work of coercion in Ireland, and having made a few essays in London, the Government have determined to coerce the House of Commons. Their policy, admirably conceived as a piece of tactics, is to prepare for next session a respectable and attrac- tive programme, including a long series of social measures desired by Great Britain, to announce their desire and intention of carrying them, to ad- mit the impossibility of 'doing so under existing procedure, and thereupon to put in the forefront of their programme a, drastic measure of Reform of Parliamentary procedhre. This will include Closure by a bare majority, the principle for which Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal party fought through a - winter session five years itgo this very month, and which Was then opposed and obstructed by some of the gentlemen who now sit on the Treasury bench I and form the Cabinet of Lard Salisbury. This would- be an awkward position for some politicians; but it is no new experience for the present Govern- ment, and Lord Salisbury, with an uneasy look a-head, Prepares to meet it with an assumption of a light heart and the adoption of the terribly old il- lustration of the open and shut umbrella. Poor M. Grevy has at last made up his mind to go, and ;here is a vacant chair among ,the,Republi- can Presidencies. Perhaps it is more correct to say that M. Grevy's mind was made up for him. He was most loth to go, having arrived at the comfor- table conviction that it was for the interest of the nation that he should remain at the Elyse. It, was Clemenceau who forced his hand, and the still young advocate, inheritor of Gambetta's opportuni- ties, may now be expected to take a front place. M. Grevy was, in some respects, a moder President of the French Republic. lie was certainly a re- markable contrast from any one of his predecessors. from the First Consul to M. Thiers. He wasin some respects like the bourgeois King Louis the Eigh- teenth. Under his reign, the Elyse, which, in its time, has seen what Pip called " larks.",was an ex- ceedingly hum-drum establishment. The President was accustomed to rise at eight o'clock, take his chocolate and unwholesome hot roll, after which, seated in a fat arm chair in a vast room on the ground floor of the palace, he received visitors, offi- cial and otherwise. At noon there was the simple defeuner, answering to our luncheon. Here the too- famous " family " assembled, M. Wilson leaving his multiform affairs to talk with his father-in-law. After dejeuner the President used to play a game of billiards, or, if it were flue, walk in the garden, feed the -ducks, and fondle his grand-children. Later in the afternoon he was fond of playing• chess. There were seldom visit:lin at dinner, and at ten o'clock all the lights were put out, and the Pre- sident of the French Republic put on his night-cap and went to bed. It was a hum-drum home life, gilded for M. Grevy with many opportunities of saving money. Like a distinguished person, head of another state, he kepi; his expenditure far within the limits of a generous sum allotted, and quits office, possibly a wiser, certainly a richer man.

Your readers will not be startled by the news proclaimed by a Dublin paper-that in the forth- coming trial of the libel case against the " Times " Mr. Parnell and other Irish members are to appear in the witness box. It was added in the original statement which appeared in this column three or four weeks ago, that Mr. Gladstore will be sub- pcened. Mr. W. H. Smith will also be called,into , the witness box, and have his placid feathers ruffled , by rude inquiries as to the sale at the bookstalls of the pataphlet containing the alleged' libel. Mr, 0 Donnell is daily and all day engaged upon the preparation of the case, which he :is pursuing with an obstinacy reminiscent of his manner when he had a speech to make in the House of Commons and the House showed indisposition to bear him. It remains to be seen how far the presiding judge will allow him to go. At present his intention is to throw light on many dark passages in recent Irish History, to which end he will exercise the right of subposnmg witnesses till the list includes most of the men who have taken active part in Irish affairs in the past seven years. Mr. O'Donnell incidentally proposes to himself the pleasant task of using the witnesa box to pay off some old scores against for- mer colleagues, whose devious ,polilical history be hopes to draw from their own lips. - The death .of Valentine Baker has drawn forth from various quarters united testimony to his worth as a soldier and his attractiveness as a friend. In recent times we have, unhappily, a parallel case where a promising career has been fatally over- clouded by discovered sin. (Of course, Ido not allude to Colonel Hughes-Hallett, who seems to be getting along comfortably enough and still enjoys the confidence of the Licensed Victuallers of Roches- ter.' Why his name should ba retained on the roll of the British Army and the more distinguished one+ of Valentine Baker's was struck off is one of those things that are hard of understanding.) Valentine Baker was very little In London since he left it in disgrace. But his relations with London society were always very intimate, since Egypt is a pretty- well frequented social highway. The last time I saw him was at a memorable dinner party given, by Colonel Fred Burnaby at the Junior Carlton on the . eve of his departure on the fatal journey that ended at Abu Ilea. It was a particularly, lively party, for Lord Randolph Churchill was there, as yet unfet- tered by official responsibilities. Lord Wolseley, to the last a firm friend of Baker's, was also present.

Tan DYNAMITARDS.—Two men, named respectively Cal- lan and Harkins, alleged tobe American Fenians, were on Monday, charged at Bow-strept Police Court, with con- spiring together to cause an explosion likely to endanger I life. Superintendent Williamson stated that he had dis- covered a substance in Callan's lodgings which Colonel Majendle and Dr. Dupre had declared to be dynamite. It was upon Harkins that was found a few days ago a cut- ting from a newspaper referring to a projected meeting at Birmingham at which Mr. Balfour was expected to be present. The prisoners were remanded for :a week.

FOREIGN NEWS.
THE CRISIS IN FRANCE.-DEMANDS FOR THE PRESIDENTS RESIGNATION.

- -- PANTS, MONDAY NIGHT.—M. Grgvv is about at his wit's end to find a premier. He has in vain appealed for assistance in his dilemma from MM. Clernenceau, Prey- cindt, Floquet, and Goblet, and now he has made up his mind to summon M. Brisson to the Elys&r. but there is no reason to think that this politician will be a whit more inclined than the others to saddle himself with the unenviable burden involved in the premiership. A meet- ing. organised by the Antonomilit and Socialist section of the Municipal Council of Paris. was held this evening, which was attended by all the Radical Members of the department. About 300 persons were present. among them being M. Longcnn, a member oi the Senate, and four deputies, MM. Milliard, Achare. Planterau, Basfy. Laissant, Camelinat. Brialoc. Milleraud. and Calvinhac. At the commencement. of the proceedings, M. Besson, a member of the Council, read the following proposal ••-" The deputies for the Department of the Seine are r-quested to de- mand the resignation of the 'President of the Republic, and only to support a Government which will devote it- self to the introduction of reforms, and which will pro- mise to demand the resignation of M. Griivy:' A corn- mitteeof vig,ilance,,consisting of 35 members, was 'con- stituted for the denartmertt, including eight deputies, eight members of the Municipal Council, 'two members of the District Council. and "15 members of The Com- mittee of Federation of the Seine. The Committee of Vigilance will constitute 'itself permanently, and will appeal to the non-federated•committees, and will prepare to organise the forces of the Republican patty in 'readi- ness for all eventualities. .

Paws, TITESDA'Y AFTERNOON—M. Grevy conferred, to- day, with M. Brisson, who informed the President that he felt constrained to declare that the crisis was not of a Ministerial bat ef a Presidential character. It would be too painful to express this -reasons for holding that view. RESIGNATION OF PRESIDENT GREVY. PARTS, WEDNESDAY, 2 P.M.—President Grevy conferred with MM. Jules Ferry and Raynal for two hours this morning. 6 rat.—A. Grevy has -resolved to resign. In inter- view this afternoon with M. Maret, the Radical Deputy, the President announced this decision, -which he aid he had taken since the morning. M.Waret said that since M. Grevv had resolved to resign, it would be better that he should not delay the-execution of his determination. M. Gre-vy answered that he intended to asi M. Ribot to- morrow to form a Ministry which could summon a con- gress to elect-a new President. If 'M.Ribot refused,then-he wouldapply to M. Goblet,and should the latterdecline also, the duty:of constituting a Cabinet would devolve upon M. Ronvier. In any case he would not have recourse to a dissolution of Parliament. But he would mit relin- quish his office without first addressing the country in-a Message, In which he would repudiate all responsibility for the -consequences, and would declare that his resig- nation -was not voluntary, but was necessitated by the impossibility of governing. In departing he would offer sincere wishes for the future of the Re- public.

AMENTCA.--13ARNII1STS RHOWMEEPPROYED. Nsw YORK, MONDAY MORNING.—A fire broke out late Isst night at the headquarters of the show and mena- gerie of 'P. T. Barnum, which is now located at Bridge- port. In spite of the efforts made to check the Barnes, they spread -rapidly, the large quantities of -straw and numerous wooden structures 'forming only too ready fuel for the devouring fire. The alarm occasioned to the vast turniber of animals of all kinds gathered together In the dhow was horrible to see, and the cries of terror were still more horrible to hear. Many poor animals, blinded by flame and -smoke, became stupefied, and made no effort to escape. Others, however, rushed madly into the fire, only-to perish more quickly. Hun- dreds of animals were thus destroyed, amorist them being large numbers of elephants, tigers, and lions.; whilst the loss of life amongst the smaller creatures is 'incalculable. Thirty, elephants and one lion have suc- ceeded in escaping into the open country, causing the greatest alarm amongstthe inhabitants. A second lion, whilst rushing from the burning sheds, was shot six times, but nevertheless made good his escape for the time. He was found a-few hours later in a stdble,calally fealting upon a cow he had slain. The loss in money to the proprietor cannot be put at less than 600,000 dollars. One of the watchmen is missing, and as he was struck down and stunned as he rushed from the building to give the alarm, it is supposed the 'five was the work of an incendiary. NEw YORK. MONDAY.—"Nearly -all the elephants which escqned after the fire have been captured. Among-those burnt is Alice,'lrnown se Jumbo's wife. Mr. P. T. Barnum has lust vurchased an enormous amount of real estate in Bridgeport, Connecticut, on which five churches, the old court-house, six livery stables, three bank buildings, and more than 100 private residences and dwellings are located. The property is worth over 6,000,000 dollars.

div.head: FISHERIES 'COMMISSION.
div.p: THE FISHERIES 'COMMISSION.

- - WASHINGTON. 'MONDAY Morrr.—The Fisheries Com- missioners held an informal meeting to-day, at which they discussed questions of procedure. The first formal meeting will takuplace to-mo Trow. It was agreed that Mr. Moore, Third Assistant Secretary of State, and Mr. Bergne should be secretaries. There will be no short- hand writer, and no record will be kept except when de- cisions are reached, neither will there be a chairman. Each day there will be discussions, and the decisions will be written and signed. Everything will be kept per- fectly secret until the final result.. CONCENTRATION OF lIITSSIA.N TROOPS.

- VIENNA. SUNDAY NU:DiT.—The concentration of troops along the western frontier of 'Russia is being closely watched by Russia's two western neighboUrs, and is being met by movements of a similar character. R is, however, strictly forbidden to a newspaper correspon- dent to indicate the nature and extent of these counter movements on the part of the German allies.
Ma. GLADSTONE AND .COL. DOPPING.

Messrs. Robins, Cameron, and Kelm, solicitors to Cot Dopping, having written on behalf ,of Col. Dopping to Ms. Gladstone, demanding a withdrawal of the state- ments made in his speech at Nottingbam, together with an apology, or else to be furnished with the pame of the right hon. gentlernari'e solicitors, have received from Mr. Gladstone in rtply a copy of the following letter, which was addressed to Col. Dopping " Hawarden Castle, Chester, Nov. 20.—Sir,—The cor- respondence between yourself and Professor Stuart on the particulars of the occurrences at Gweedore having concluded. I had my speech at Nottingham of the 18th of October put into type for revision. 'lt reached me on Tuesday last, and since that time I have considered in what manner I ought to act, so as to fulfil the assurance I gave you—l cite it from memory—that I would do -what might appear to be fair and just. I may here mention that some of the citations made by you from newspaper reports do not corresnond with what I said. In particular, I I am firmly persuaded that I did not say the rifle was loaded, nor does any such word appear in a memorandum which I took down from Professor Stuart's mouth for use in my speech. But, on the other hand, although Ido not think the auditory understood me to be imputing to you the use of a loaded rifle, justice obliges me to admit that some impartial readers of a report sent to me for eorrec• tion bait thought, that, apart from the particular word, the narrative might be assumed to mean that the rifle was loaded. I proceed from these preliminaries to the substance. On Friday last I sent to London instructione to strike off the speech, omitting the paragraph which related to Gweedore, and inserting an explanation in parenthesis, which I will forward to you immediately on receiving the speech in print. Considering, however, that my words, as reported, did carry--,-and, as I spoke hem, have been deemed cai)able of carrying—a construc- tion of which you might justly complain. I think the correction of the speech does not wholly meet your just claim upon me. I wish, therefore, to make the following explicit statement in addition:— , 1. The idea ;lever crossed my mind of imputinee you the use of a loaded rifle, or what is possibly implied in such use. 2. I regret, also, that I Aid not by expreas words ex- clude -that imputation, and explain that niy meaning was one altogether different 3. I should wish the fullest publicity to be given to these declarations, and consider that it falls to me to g ive this publicity. Haviog now endeavoured to redeem the assufance which I gave you. I have the honour to be, sir, your faithful servant, W. E. Guannum. Lieut.-Colonel. Dopping, &c., &c.

The Countess of Mardi died on Monday evening in Lon. don from typhoid fever. Her ladyship was the daughter •if Mr. W. G. Craven, and was married to the Earl of March in 1882. Two boys, sons a Mr. Charles Swain, organist at thf Parish Church, Stockport. were sitating on Monday on the ducicpond in Woodbank Park, with a young lady named Price, when the ice gave way. Miss Price and Harry Swain seized a scarf which a lad called Collier threw to their aid, but Jas. Alfred Swain was drowned. '

SHOCKING SUICIDE.—On Thursday morning Isabella Kennedy, aged 27, factory operative, wi found to have committed suicide at Leigh. The deceased had suffered from dropsy for some time, and having said there was no hope of her getting better she became very despon- dent. She went to bed on Wednesday night with her mother, but got up during the night and cut her throat, with a razor. She was found lying in a pool of blood next morning. div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVENLIIER 26, 1887. s
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVENLIIER 26, 1887. s
DESTRUCTIVE FIRES.

A fire broke out onSunday in the new premises erected by the London, Brighton and South Coast Railway Com- pany for their large Continental traffic at Newhaven Wharf, and was not got under control until damage had been done to the extent of about £15,000. On Saturday morning the stables and outhouses at the reaidence of Mr. James Talbot Power, at Leopardstoym Park, County Dublin, were burnt down. Mr. Power and his steward inspected the stables on Friday night, and the fire broke out an hour or two later. Nine horses which were in the stab'es were saved. The damage is estimated at about £5,000. The cause of the fire is not known.

Early on Sunday morning a 'fire broke out on the ex- tensive premises in F.astgate-strect. Chester, occupied by Messrs. Lemont and Sons, household furnishers and decorators. The premises, together with their contents, and-the offices in front, occupied by the Cheshire Conser- vative Registration Association and Mr. Williams, Chethire County Auditor, were completely gutted. The total damage is estimated at £15,000. A little before three o'clock on saturday morning a 'fire 'broke out in the shop of Messrs. Todd Brothers, drapers and milliners, lgorthgate, Darlington. There was no chance of saving Messrs.' Todd's premises, the fire haring got such a stronghold. Within an hour or so most of the interior fell in. The firemen chiefly directed their attention then to the preservation of the adjoining property,: but Messrs. Wallis and Greenwood's premises, the next to Mesirs. Todd's, got on fire at the top, and the roof was burnt, with Clothing in the top storey, which was the workrocm. The constant stream of water, how- ever, got the fire under, and it did not penetrate below. The cause,of the "fire is unknown. The total damage may be put , down•at 16,000 or 0,000. About 1 a.m. on Saturday. a fire broke out in the store-honse of thoextensive bleaching works of Messrs. Watson and Shield. 'situate on the river Dighty, six miles from Dundee, bywhich in two hours goods valued at upwards of 26,000 were destroyed, owing to the scarcity of water. The buildings in which the fire origi- nated fell in ruins, but the arrival of the Dundee Fire Brigade at three o'clook rendered valuable assistance in confining the fireto these. Incendiarism is suggested. The goods destroyed consisted of flax, tow, and jute yarns, which had'been sent in by different Dundee ship- pers. Danhill Church.Fletcbing, Sussex, caught fire from the overheating. of a stove on Monday, and before the arriyal of the Uckfield and Sheffield Park fire brigade the flames had obtained such a strong hold that all endeavours to extinguish the fire were not successful until thereof and tower harl fallen in.

A fire ;occurred, early on Tuesday, at North Shields at the offices of Mr. Henry B. Thompson, borough rate collector, an on subsequent examination being made, the charred body of Mr. Thompson was found. Late on Monday, a fire, which did a large amount of damage, occurred at the well-known Ship Hotel, Green- wich. A boy who was passing at half-past ten, saw a glare in the windows and gave the alarm, but though therfire brigade was soon on the spot sand there was a plentiful supply of water, it was over two hours before the flames were subdued. The two top floors, used as stores and dormitories, *ere burned out, and the rest of the building was seriously damaged.

div.head: IRELAND.
div.p: IRELAND.

-Viscount Lifford died on Sunday, at his count+ Donegal residence, after a long illness, aged 76. Prince Edward of Saxe-Weimar, commander of the forces in Ireland, has left Dublin, on *tour of inspection.
Mr. Cox, M.P., was chased early on Saturday morning into Dangan Castle, but not captured. He slept on Fri- day night at a house at Ballylean, which was lately oc- cupied by a boycotted landlady. -

The Government, in view of the recent disturbances at 'Hilrush, county Clare, have decided upon permanently 'increasing the police force stationed there, and also upon quartering military in that town. - - -- - --

The out-offices of the residence of Mr. James Talbot Power, Di., a Roman Catholic Unionist, who is to en- tertain Lord Hartington during his forthcoming visit to Dublin, were maliciously burnt on Friday night, the damage amounting to several thousand pounds. Mr. Power has received many threatening letters since the announcement that he was to be Lord Hartington's host appeared. Mr. John Dillon, speaking at Galashiels on Saturday evening, said that a few hours before leaving Ireland he was secretly informed that a warrant had been signed for his apprehension. He intended after addressing meetings in Scotland and England to return to Ireland. The democracy was with the Nationalists of Ireland, and there was no large town in England or Scotland where the Unionists could hold an open meeting.

On Saturday a farmer named M'lnery, near Carrahan, five miles from Ennis, fired at a sheriff's bailiff who had seized some of his sheep under a civil bill decree. Ser- geant Joyce followed him, and Winery turned and fired on the sergeant, who returned the fire, but none of the shotstook effect. Later in the day M'lnery was arrested, and a revolver, fully charged, was found upon him. He was remanded for eight days.

Nine persons, of whom three were girls and one an old woman of 70, were sentenced at Ballyhaunis on Saturday to terms of imprisonment varying from ten days to three weeks for intimidation and obstruction on the occasion of seizures for rent. They were conveyed under an escort of 100 police to the railway station for Castlebar gaol, followed by a large crowd.

In the Queen's Bench, Dublin, on Monday, counsel, on behalf of Dr. Cross, who stands committed for trial at the Cork Assizes for the murder of his wife by poisoning her with arsenic, applied for a conditional order to changethe venue of trial to whatever other assize dis- trict the Court might approve of. The grounds of the application were that public opinion in Cork had been seriously prejudiced againsr him by reports of the case in the newspapers. The conditional order was granted, and on Tuesday, after hearing arturnenis, an order was made for the accused to be tried before a special jury.

div.head: MR. 'O'BRIEN IN GAOL.
div.p: MR. 'O'BRIEN IN GAOL.

On Saturday gaolers at Tulle- more were amazed to find their prisoner standing in his cell clothed in a suit of ordinary garments. Since the clothes in which he entered the prison were taken from him by a warder, Mr. O'Brien had been lying in bed in the infirmarycell without any clothes to wear. When the fact became known there was consternation amongst the officials. The governor was engaged at the time in consultation with Dr. Maccabe,of the Prisons Board, and the visiting justices, Messrs. Goodbody, Otway, Toler, Fox, and Tarleton as to the arranements to be made for the forthcoming investigation into the prison treatment of Mr. O'Bkien and others. He at once pro- ceeded to the cell and found that the report conveyed to him was only too true. How the clothes got into the cell is of course a mystery.; When the news reached Dublin it caused much amusement and much gratifica- tion, h,ut the strange part of the matter is that it caused very little surprise; in fact, it was an open secret for some days that a project was on loot to provide Mr. O'Brien with a snit of clothes. It is amazing, therefore, that no word reached the authorities of the plot in pre- paration. It only shows how difficult it is for a few officers in Dubin Castle to deal with a whqle nation. INTERVIEW WITH MR. PARNELL. A reporter had an interview with Mr. Parnell on Mon- day. In the course of conversation, the hon. member's attention was directed to Mr. Dayitt's speech at Stepaside county Dublin, on Sunday, in wtfich the latter seemed to criticise the action of some of the" Plan of Campaigners" in avoiding arrest. I do not think, said Mr. Parnell, that it would become me either to criticise or to approve the management of the movement called the "Plan of Campaign." I was not consulted about the initiation, and since then I have been unable, owing to the state of my health, to take any part in active political matters outside the House of Commons. Those on the spot, and who are actively engaged, are the best judges as to what their own honour and the interests of their country require. Mr. Devitt is in a different position, and his opinion is entitled to respect, coming from one who is in Ireland, and who is a man of singular and remarkable courage, who has never shrunk frean the consequences of his words and acts. I do not gather, Ithough, that Mr. Devitt did criticise. He seemed rather to be apprehensive that some things might be misunderstood in America, "but," continued Mr. Parnell, "on the general situation I may say that in my judgment more feeble or inept Government never lield the reins in Ireland. They are teaching Irishmen a most disAstrous lesson. By their bungling incapacity they are teaching them that the law may be success- fully defied, for the law, as recently constructed by the Unionist majority of the House of Commons. is daily defied, and with impunity, by thousands of members of suppressed branches of the National League, and by every National newspaper editor in Ireland. In fact, ono of the results of the- Coercion Act and of firm and resolute government is that for every offence against the law committed before the Act, there are hundreds committed now. I leave it for you to say;' con- cluded Mr. Parnell, "erhether the respect of Ireland l'or the Imperial Parliament, the possibility of her continued 'government by die same agency, or the solidity of the Union will be increased, or whether, on the contrary, this administrative Inca- picky does not render much nearer the concession of such reasonable powers of self-government as shall make our people law-abiding, prosperous and happyil tteplying to questions respecting his health, Mr. Paran said there was absolutely no foundation for the state. tcents - published recently on-the authority of the Lon- don correspondent of an Irish newspaper. So far from it being true that he is in better physical condition than he was reported last week, Mr. Parnell's physician, Sir Floury Thompson, under whose care he has been for 12 , months past, is imperative in his directions that the honourable gentleman shall keep as quiet as possible during the winter. He must avoid all exposure and f4tigue, so that the interval may be employed ij. re- niplqating as much as possible in anticipation of the labour of the next session. Mr. Parnell has not been staying at Eltham for a long time past, neither is it true that he keeps horses there, or that he has been seen rid- or drivinr, in the locality. The interviewer adds that Mr. Parnell is looking very thin.
The death is announced of Colonel tikroyd, formerly AP. for Halifax.
