div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.

The Northampton shoe manufacturers have resolved on a lock-out of all the riveters and finishers in their employment. This insure affects orer 5,000 workmen. Mrs. Goodson, the wife of a fisherman, of Austin-street, King's Lynn, has just been delivered of four children, all boys. Three of them were born alive, but one of the three died shortly afterwards. The mother and the two surviving children are doing well. -

On Monday morning a young woman named Agnes °lilies committed suicide by throwing herself into the Clyde at Rutherglen. Three years ago yeeterday the mother of the girl deprived herself of life in the same way. A factory worker in the east ead of Glasgow also committed suicide oa Sunday night in the Clyde.

For cutting hair off cows' tails, a man, named William 361mstone, has been sentenced by the magistrates of Shap, near Penrith, to three months imprisonment in each of two cases. Prisoner had gone to vazious farms, and mutilated the tails of cows, no less than twenty-one 'beasts having been operated upon. The hair was after- wards offered for sale.

A singular fatality has been reported to the New- castle police. William Quinn, a fish curer, and a .woman named Gleeson lived on different storeys of a tenement house in Dog Bank. New castle. On Saturday night they qoavrelled on the stairhead, and in the struggle both fell out of a 'window, a distance of Mt. They were both seriously injured, and the man died on Sunday night.

Lord No-rthwick died on Sunday morning at Upper Norwood, after a lingering illness. The deceased' was born in 1811. He served in the lit Life Guards, of which he was captain, In 1842. Prom February, 1837, to August, 1841, he sat for Evesham in the House of Com- mons; and from 3anusry, 1847, to January, 1859, repre- sented East Worcester in the Lower House, be then suc- ceeding to the peerage on the death of his uncle.

THH Ruts:ass OF toe Rev. J. Batt-Cox. —ln the Court of Appeal, on Monday, the Master of the Rolls and Justices Bowen and Fry, concurred in allowing the appeal of Mr. Hakes from the order of Lord Chief Justice Smith, for the discharge of the Rev. James Bell-Ccx from custody. Mr. Cox was imprisoned for a breach of the Public Worship Regulation Act, at Liver- pool. The effect of the decision of the Court of Appeal is to declare him 'wrongly released from gaol. Sir Henry Peek, Bart., having brought an action to recover loss sustained through an Untrue statementin the prospectus of the Plymouth and Deyonport Tramways Company, the Court of Appeal, on Saturday, held that the directors of the company must make good such loss. In 1883 Sir Henry took £4,000 worth of shares in the company, in the prospectus of which it was stated that the Board of Trade had authorised the use of steam on the tramway, which was untrue. The company has since been wound up. SENTENCE ON MRS. JEFFERIES..--At the adjourned Middlesex Sessions, on Monday, Mary Francis Jefferies, 72 years of age, described as a hotel keeper, and who was convicted last sessions of keeping a disorderly house at Brompton, was brought up for sentence. The prisoner's counsel handed in a medical certificate stating that she was suffering from diabetes and could not un- dergo hard labour.—The Assistant Judge sentenced her to six months"' imprisonment as a second-class mis- demeanant and to pay the £4OO she forfeited over the last trial

SKOCIT}TO• 'NAME LW-DIM' AT BOLTON.—On Monday aftlfrnoon; as three performers (Zelleto, Onreto, and Zelvardeo) were giving a trapeze entertainment at .the 'Victoria Variety Theatre, Bolton, one of the acrobats took s flying leap, and was canght by a corn- panion,banging bead downwards from a trapeze in the roof. The apparatus gave way, and both were pre- cipitated amid great excitement into the net, which fortunately proved strong enough to hold them; but one was so injured as to be unable to appear at the evening performance. FUNERAL OF SLR WITLIAnt MC.ARTITIIR. The funeral of the late Sir William Mc.Arthur took place on Monday. at Norwood Cemetery, a short preliminary service having been held previously at Bayswater. There was a large number of mourners, including relatives of the family, and Sir Robert Fowler, Sir George Chubb, Canon Fleming, and Dr. Allon. Amongst those present were representatives of the English and Irish Wesleyan Conferences, Wesleyan Missionaryßociety, and numerous other organisations with which the deceased was more or less intimately connected.

THE MINERS' PARLIAMENTARY REPRESENTATIVES.—The principal question discussed at the annual delegate meet- ing of the Northumberland Miners' Association, at New- castle, on Saturday, was the recent ballot with regard to the payment of the salaries of Messrs. Burt and Fenvrick, the labour representatives of the county. Resolutions were sent in from a number of miners° lodrtes calling for a rescinding of the decision, and expressing the opinion that to dispense with the labour representatives would be disastrous. Information was refused to the press as to the result of Saturday's deliberations, but the feeling prevails that a fresh ballot on the subject will be taken forthwith. THE CRIMINAL LAW AMENDMENT Ac.—Two serious cases under the Criminal Law Amendment Act were tried at the Liverpool Assizes on Saturday. In one, two women were sentenced to imprisonment—one for 21 and the other for six months—for procuring a girl of 15 for unlawful purposes; and in the other case John Moore, a chemist, was sentenced to two years' imprisonment with hard labour for assaulting a number of children. Mr. Justice Day expressed his regret that Moore had from the deficiency of evidence escaped the hands of justice, and said that had the jury been iible to convict him of the full offence he would never have seen the outside of a gaol again. DEATH OF MR. TITUS SALT.—Mr. Titus Salt, chief of the well known Saltaire Mills firm, died suddenly at his residence, at Saltaire, on Saturday. Deceased had been in an ailing condition for some days, but no serious con- sequences were anticipated until Saturday forenoon, when he became worse, and died about four o'clock. Be was the fifth and youngest surviving son of the late Sir Titus Salt, Bart., and was in his 45th year. He has left a widow (a daughter of the late Mr. Joseph Crossley, of Halifax), three sons, and one daughter. In May last the deceased entertained the Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg, on the occasion of opening the Saltaire Exhi- bition, of which he was thn chief promoter. By his death the Liberal party has lost a zealous advocate and gener- ous supporter.

FRAUDULENT TRADE STAINPS--A Glasgow firm has re- ceived the following letter from Dusseldorf, Geririan.y. It is of such a remarkable character that they think Its contents ought to be made public. although it is marked " stricriy private :"—" Dusseldorf, November 14, 1887. Dear Sirs,—Will you kindly inform me whether you are buyers of Swedish steel bars for the India or China mar- kets? There is now made in Germany a quality of steel hars, stamped and all with Swedish brands, winch to all practical purpose is equal to the real article. If you like to try the quality I can send you some samples, and if you decided to buy some afterwards you need not get the works to stamp any brand which you may decide upon putting on. This you can get done after the bars haveleft the works, or the works will do this for you. This is strictly private, and I shall be glad if you will kindly treat it as such. Only some people I know are making these days enormous profits out of this."

EXTRAORDINARY CONCEALMENT CASE.— On Monday, Mr. Yatei, the Cheshire county coroner, held an in- quest at Leftwich Workhouse, on the body of the infant child of Fanny Broomfield, until a few days back cook at The Brockhurst, Northwich. Evidence was given by Alice Mills, laundry maid, 'Janet Wilson, housemaid, and other servants,sthat the cook, who had been at The Brockhurst three months, was taken seriously ill in her bedroom, that subsequently they heard the cry of a child, and after listening heard a box shut when something heavy had been thrown into it. The cook then dressed and went downstairs. The other servants searched the box, and found the dead body of a baby. Dr. Joynson, who was called in, said he believed the child had breathed, and that the cause of death was suffocation. He would not swear, however, that it had had a separate existence. The jury then returned a verdict that death was due to suffocation during birth. One juryman declined to sign the depositions. REMARKABLE CASE.—A remarkable trial for murder was concluded on Saturday at the Stafford Assizes. The accused was a young farmer named Kynaston, f Bas - church, in Shropshire, and the deceased was his wife. The woman met her death from a gunshot wound; and while the prosecution sought to show that this was caused by her husband, the latter alleged that the woman had committed suicide. The two were on very had terms, and they Occupied separate rooms. The pri- soner awoke two of his servants at two o'clock on the morning a the Ist August, telling them that he had heard a gun go off, and all three proceeding to Mrs. Kynaston's bedroom, they found the Woman lying dead, with a discharged gun by her side. A surgeon who was examined for the prosecution allowed that the deceased might have done it herself, and in defence the prisoner's ,on, a child of seven, was called, and he stated that he heard the gun discharged, and that his father was then in bed with him.—The jury returned a verdict of acquittal. THE ESSEX TRAGEDY.—EXECITTION OF A YOUTH. —Jos. Morley, aged 17, blacksmith, was executed, en Monday, at Chelmsford Prison, for the murder of his landlady, Mrs. Bodger, at Dagenham, near Romford. After the conviction, Morley confessed that he entered the woman's bedroom early in the morning, and cut her throat with a razor four times, hut he denind that Ahad nay intention of criminally assaulting her. He said he owed her money for lodgings, and so killed her, thinking to be undiscovered, and that the debt would be for- gotten. He had been very penitent in prison. In sombre, foggy weather he was led, pinioned, to the scaffold, preceded by the chaplain, reciting the 51st Psalm. Morley had been crying. but he walked firmly to the gallows, \ repeating, in a quivering voice, after the chaplain, the words, "Lord have mercy upon me." Berry wos tho hangman, and gave a drop of seven feet, the ' •-ueed youth only weighing eight stone. When i fac •;,,I been covered with the white cap, Berry drew e,b and the culprit dropped into eternity. . Death v ..stantaneous, but there was a slight quivering of the iiiebs. The fatal rope had been used once before, at Oxford last week, the man then hanged being the heaviest (17 stone) Berry has yet executed. Morley was the youngest and lightest of the large number of unfortunate persons who have passed through Berry's hands.

EMIGRANT SHIP RUN DOWN.-
TERRIBLE SCENES.-LOSS OF 130 LIVES.

The dense fog which had hung about the south coast during last week led, on Saturday night, to a ter- rible catastrophe off Dover. At daybreak, on Sunday morning, boats came ashore at Dover from the screw steamer Ebro, of Sunderland, bringing a portion of the passengers of the screw steamer W. A. Scholten, of and from Rotterdam, with a general cargo, for New York. Amongst these was the second mate of the Scholten who reported a terrible lose of life from bis vessel, which was run into and sunk about ten o'clock on Saturday night, some ten miles south-east by south of Sand Head, by an unknown steamer. This, it is presumed, was the Rosa Mary, screw steamer, of and from Hartlepool, with coal, for St. Nazaire, which was seen in the roads with bows stove in. The captain of the latter vessel, however, reports that she herself was run into whilst at anchor by an unknown steamer. The first boat which came ashore from the Ebro brought thirty-one persons, and the second twenty-six. A coastguard crew then put off, and landed ten more; whilst a boatman named Ball brought seven ashore in his own craft One of the Ebro's boats made another trip, and landed 13, making a total of 87. When the persons landed had been counted, the terrible extent of the disaster became ap- parent It was known that the Scfholten had on board about 210 souls, of Which those landed at Dover were the only survivors. These were all taken to the Sailors' Home In the town, where the scene was an reopening one. Many of those saved have been separated for ever from their relatives by the disaster. One lady lost her husband and three children. She herself was picked up from the sea with one of her children clasped in her arms, but when she was safely got into the boat, it was found that her child was dead. Five of the inmates of the Home were injured by cuts and bruises, and two women who were slightly injured have lost their hus- bands, one of them having been married only a few weeks. Mr. Fox, the Mayor of the borough, and two town councillors attended at the Home, and gave directions for the relief in every way of the survivors, who are nearly all of German extraction. An interpreter was necessary, and (he post having been undertaken by Mr. Grossman. the wants of the sufferers were more readily attended to. They lest the whole of their possessions, and most were landed with the scantiest possible cloth- ing; indeed, many of them wore nothing but night gar- ments, having already retired to rest when the disaster occurred.

When the shock occurred passengers rushed up from be- low, most of them being in their berths for the night. It was found that the Scholten had been struck on the port bow, and in a few minutes the order was given to lower the boats. In doing this there appears to have been some difficulty, two only being made use of. whilst three were not launched. This caused a dreadful scene of terror, for the alarm spread like a lightning flash amongst the passengers, a rush being made to the sides of the vessel by the terror-stricken people, where the boats were being lowered, and many were with difficulty restrained from leaping down from the bulwarks. Terri- fied mothers clasped their children in their arms. The shouts of the officers to the crew were hardly audible in the midst of the shrieks of terror as the ill-fated ves- sel rapidly filled. The water rushed in with great force, driving the people towards the stern to escape, if it might be, their impending fate; but there was no hope of res- cue. The boats which were available were already full, and the others useless. In a short time scores of per- sons of both sexes and all ages were struggling in the water, and their cries for help were pitiful. Within twenty minutes of the time when the shock occurred the Scholten had disappeared, engulfing as it sank a great proportion of the passengers and crew. There were only nine or ten English people on board. At low water the mast of the sunker steamer is visible from Dover, about three miles south-east of the Admiralty pier. A young man, about 25 years of age who was a pas- senger from Newcastle to New York by way of Rotter- dam, and who was amongst those rescued, gave the following account of his experiences in connection with the catastrophe:—" There were only nine or ten English on board the Scholten„ one being a young lady named Sarah Louisa Gold, and who belongs to Tunbridge Wells. I became friendly with a young men named Stepney, who, like myself, belongs to Newcastle, and with a man named Thomas Robson. We also became acquainted with Miss Gold. We left Rotterdam on Saturday morn- ing at about ten o'clock (deck time). When we were about ten miles, I suppose, south-east of Dover—we were all in our bunks—when we heard a tremendous crash. I ran on deck amidst a general scramble. I found that a steamer had struck us on the port bow. At first it did not seem as if any damage had been done, but in a few minutes we heard the order to lower the boats. The sailors managed to lower two boats, but the three others could not, it seemed, be lowered; at any rate they were not lowered. One of them, I believe, would have held nearly a hundred persons. I and Miss Gold did not get a chance to get into either of the boats. The fog had just left the water it seemed, and the sea was fairly calm. There were numbers of life-belts on our vessel, and placed where all could reach them. • Miss Gold and I each put one on. About 20 minutes after the collision our steamer foundered. We stood on deck until she wr nt down, and then we were in the water together. We could not swim, but we kept together. Several persons had, like ourselves, put life-belts on, and these floated abouttin the sea. All the others, with the exception of those who had got into boats, went down with the vessel. All who were rescued from the sea were wearing life-belts. A steamer, which afterwards proved to be the Ebro, of Sunderland, came close to the sunken vessel, and her boats rescued several of our passengers, and took them to the steamer. They returned to the wreck, and picked up more, taking them also to the steamer. The vessel that had run into us we did not Fee again, for it went during the crossing of the boats. I and Miss Gold had kept together, and got drifted towards the rescuing steamer. A rope was thrown towards us, and we held on until the boat came and picked us up. We wish to state that every praise is due to the captain and officers of the Ebro, for they rendered every assistance that seemed in their power. It is a curious thing with re- gard to the belts, that in the afternoon a number of the passengers were trying them on, and laughing at their strange appearance, little thinking how soon they would want them. None without belts were picked up except one, and this was a stout woman, who clung to a life buoy. We were landed in boats at Dover by daybreak on Sunday morning." The chief engineer of the Scholten was pieken up after floating in the sea for three hours by the English steamer Lutsmore, bound to Bilbao, and brought to Newhaven. The engineer of the sunken vessel, named Edphovel, was in the engine-room at the time of the collision, and has no knowledee of its cause. It appears that all the Eng- lish passengers were saved. During Sunday the har- bour tugs and vessels made several journeys to the sunken steamer, whose mast was plainly visible at low tide. Bodies and floating goods have been brought ashore, as many as 18 corpses being landed in one jour- ney. These comprised seamen, women, and children. In the afternoon the screw-steamer Rosa Mary, 1,129 gross tonnage, came into the harbour. The twenty bodies which were recovered on Sunday from the neighbourhood of the wreck were ex- amined with a view to identification before the Mayor and Coroner. Those identified were tho chief mate of 'the Scholten named Steilberg; the second steward, Duvitt; chief stewardess Halt; cabin passenger Henry Blaine, of Gallipoli; steerage passenger Solomon Goldschmidt, of London; and several others. Among the survivors was a lady who had received a black eye. She was amongst the foremost to examine the dead bodies. She stated that her husband and sons had been drowned Her husband had sold his business to go out to America, and had two thousand pounds with him, but this sum had gone down with the ship, and she is left penniless. It is stated that the crew of a mackerel boat, from Hastings, the master of which goes by the name of "Duster," saw the colli ion. A steamer ran into her nets, and the boat chased the steamer which, while running away, collided with the Scholten. It is further alleged that fragments of nets were found on Sunday morning on the bows of the Rosa Mary. CONFLICTING STATEMENTS.

As to which was the defaulting vetisei, and whether the Dutch vessel and the Rosa Mary ever were in collision, are points which it will remain for the official in- quiry that is ,to take place to solve. It is, however, impossible to disguise that amongst the seafaring class in Dover, the almost universal feeling prevails that the English vessel was at fault, and that with her rests the responsibility for the calamity. According to the story told by the crew and passengers of the W. A. Scholten, that vessel WAS struck amidships shortly after half-past ten, by another vessel going apparently at full speed; and thia is significant judged by the nature of the injuries sustained by the Rosa Mary herself. The stern of the vessel had been carried com- pletely away, while the bows were cut down even below the water's edge. The iron plates, some five-eighths of an inch in thickness. were twisted and torn in terrible fashion, leaving a wide aperture, through which the water after the collision must have rushed in in an irresistible volume but for the water-tight compartment forward, which probably saved the vessel from immediately sinking. As it was, the Rasa Mary gradually made water in her hold, and a donkey-engine had to be constantly employed to keep her afloat. Of the 21 bodies brought ashore in the course of Sunday at Dover, the majority had died from exposure and were floating lifeless in the water. Fdrty-eight bodies, six pockets of hops, three bales of tobacco, twelve life-belts, and sundry oars, spars, dm., have been picked up and landed at Dover. The first mate and fourth engineer have been recognised among the dead. The ill-fated vessel is lying in from twelve to fifteen fathoms of water. IN'QUEST. - - - - - - •

The inquest on the bodies of the unfortunate passen- vers and seamen of the W. A. Soholden, recovered after the sinking of the vessel, was opened 'at the Hotel de Paris, Dover, on Monday, before the Borough Coroner, Sydenhain Payn. The progress of the jury through the docks on the way to inspect the, bodies of the 21 victims at the dead house was watched by, a large crowd of spectatots. They were accompanied by second Lieut, Moritz, Dr. Ayme, medical officer, and the Purser Helstnga, for the !purpose of identification. In the majority of cases decomposition had oomtnenced to set in, and this was specially noticeable with regard to the female victims. Amongst those identified were the first mate of the emigrant ship, and the stewardess. On returning to.thelotel the Coroner proceeded with evi-

div.p: deuce as to the Went.lootG,oo. It lIHS um yet been de- cided when divers will be sent down to examine the nature of the injuries sustained by the sunken vesseL Messrs. J. Coverdale and Son, West Hartlepool, the owners of the steamship, Rosa and Mary,have received a telegram from Capt. Webster, commanding the vessel, with reference to the disaster off Dover. In this telegram, Capt. Webster states that his vessel was lying at anchor at the time of the collision, and the anchor light was burning brightly, the anchor watch was kept, and he himself was on deck at the moment of disaster.

The inquest was resumed, at Dover, on Tuesday after- noon, on the bodies recovered from the wreck of the W. A. Scholter. The first witness examined was the purser of the sunken vessel, which, he said, carried 161 passen- gers. He described the terrible scenes which ensued after the collision. and spoke highly of the conduct of the crew of the Ebro in saving lite. The second officer then deposed that he was on the bridge when lights, apparently stationary, were discovered. Other evidence ''been given, the inquiry was adjourned.
WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of this Board was held at the Workhouse. Warrington, on Wednesday morn- ing. There were present the Rev. G. F. Roberts (chairman), Messrs. Greening, J. Houghton, KU- shall, Jolley. Isherwood, Derbyshire, Bonnell, Clarke, Hibbert, W. Houghton, Humphries, Rat- cliffe, Harrison, Eckersley, J. C. Sutton (clerk), and Ward (workhouse master).

div.head: 'REOINT APPOINTMENT OF A MEDICAL OFFICER,
div.p: THE 'REOINT APPOINTMENT OF A MEDICAL OFFICER,

Referring to the appointment of medical officer for No. 1 district made at the previous meeting, Mr. DARBY- SHIRR said he just wished to remark that he thought it was unfortunate the Board was not permitted to see the applicants for the post of medical officer before the ap- pointment was made. When Dr. Jack and Dr. Fox were the candidates they both appeared before the Board, but in the case of the last appointment neither of the appli- cants attended. He simply wished to say that that was unfortunate.—The CHAIRXAN : I think it was an accident that they were not seen; I don't think there was any in- tention.—Mr. DARRYSHIRR : I am glad to hear that.—The Cmix said the usual practise was that when a situation was vacant, and they had received applications and tes- timonials, they either proceeded to the appointment or they made a selection. If they made a selection they asked the clerk to request the selected candidates to ap- pear before the Board. It would have been quite com- petent for them to have requested the two candidates for the post referred to to appear before the Board.—Af- ter a little further discussion the mattes dropped.

div.head: WOHEHOUSE FULL.
div.p: THE WOHEHOUSE FULL.

In their minutes, the Rouse Committee recommended that 100 pairs of blankets be obtained to meet emergen- cies.—The CHAIRMAN was sorry to say that the Work- house was full. There were about 400 inmates in the house.—Mr. WARD, the Workhouse master, said there were then 397 in the house, but they had had 400 in dur- ing the week. The body of the house was full, and he was making further provision in the room that had been used as a day-room. As yet it had not been necessary for two to sleep in a bed.—Mr. DAREYSHIRE : We are not so badly off, then.—ln answer to Mr. Ratcliffe, Ir. Wuna said there was about the same number in the house that there was this time last year.—The minutes of the committee were confirmed.

SCEGOL FEES. The School Fees Committee reported that fees had been allowed in 88 cases, 74 of which were old, and 14 new cases.—On the motion of Mr. GREENING, seconded by Mr. Jottzy, the minutes were confirmed.

div.head: DISTRESSED aILINMAKERS.
div.p: THE DISTRESSED aILINMAKERS.

Mr. ISHERWOOD asked if there were any of the Stafford- shire chainmakers, who were on strike, in the workhouse, because he understood that there were some children belonging to a chainmaker at Padgate Schools.—Mr. MiNns' the superintendent of Padgate Schools, having been called into the room, said that there were two chil- dren of a chaiiamaker at the schools. From what they said their father was in the workhouse. He had been on tramp six or seven months seeking for work, and hacl not been able to find any, and at last he broke down in Warrington.—Mr. ISHERWOOD said there were a number of chainmakers who began singing in the streets on Satur- day night, and he believed this was one of them .—Mr. DAREYSHIRE thought they should endeavour to get the man to repay the cost of his maintenance after he got into work. He did not belong to this Union, and that was a condition on which he should leave the work- house.—The CtEnx thought that when a man had been six months out of work, and had broken down with sickness, and in the last stage of destitution, there was not much chance of charging him for his maintenance hereafter.—Mr. JOLLEY said the -question of the chain- makers' strike was one they could not interfere with, but these poor people were almost starved to death be- fore they left their homes. To ask them to pay anything in the state they were in was like trying to get blood out or a stone.—Mr. HARHYSHIRE said he did not propose that the man should be asked to pay anything while in the miserable condition he was then in. They all knew that it won/$:1 be nonsense to do so. What he said was that when the man got into work again he ought to repay the ratepayers the money he had cost them. He did not be- long to this Union; and if he did not pay himself the Union he belonged to should pay.—Mr. JOLLEY said he did not mean anything personal to Mr. Darbyshire, but to show that it was impossible to ask this man to pay anything. Farm labourers with Us. or 12s. per week were princes compared with these poor chainmakers.— Mr. HORNELL asked if the chainmakers were not in re- ceipt of a werkly allowance ?—Mr. JOLLEY : Are you pre- pared to say what the allowance is ?—Mr. BovnErs. said he was not.—Mr. JOLLEY said he thought it would be found to be HARRISON asked what was the I reason for calling it the chainmakers' strike ?—Mr JOLLEY said that the chainmakers went on strike simply because I they were starved on the wages they got.—Mr. GREEN- I IRO said it was quite true, as Mr. Jolley said, that the wages were very low, but still the chammakers made themselves worse by coming out on strike. He did not think they were justified in coming out on strike, because they were getting wages that kept them in a fashion at all events.—The CHAIRMAN said they could not usefully go into that matter at that time.—Mr. HARRISON sug- gested that the cost of the man's maintenance should be regarded as a loan, but the CLERK replied that this was not practicable.—The CHAIRMAN said if they thought the game was worth the candle they might light it. (Laugh- ter.)—Mr. ISHERWOOD was of opinion that a great many of the people who represented themselves as being on strike were simply loafers.—The matter then dropped.
THE WORKHOUSE HOSPITAL CONDEMNED.

Dr. SPINKS, the medical officer for the workhouse, wrote in his report book that the workhouse hospital was badly constructed and ought to be taken down and re- built on a modem Plan. Within the last 30 years it had been enlarged three times but not improved. They were now very short of room, particularly for skin and other infectious diseases.—The matter was referred to the House Committee, Mr. RATCLINE remarking that the report might lie on the table for six months. The relief cases were then proceeded with.

div.head: IiAZAAR AT LATCHFORD.
div.p: IiAZAAR AT LATCHFORD.

On Tuesday and Wednesday a sale of work was held in St. James' Schoolroom, Latchford, in aid of the parish mission fund. It was opened on Tues- day afternoon by Lady Greenall, and amongst those present at the ceremony were the vicar (the Rev. F. Slater) and Mrs Mater, the • Misses Greenall, Mrs Dun, Mrs Beamont, Mrs Peter Stubs, the Rev. E. C. E. and Mrs Carleton, Mrs and Miss Dodd, Mrs Dar- wall, Mr. and,Mrs John White, Mrs Wilkinson, Mrs Willcocks. Mr. and Mrs H. N. Houghton, Mr. and Mrs C. S. Burgess. Mrs Gibson Smith, Mrs Venn, Mrs Chorley, Mrs Chandley, and many others. In the course of a, statement explaining the object of the bazaar, the Vicar said there was a debt of £2O remaining en the old mission house, which they wanted to pay off. They wanted £2O in aid of the churchwardens' funds, and £2O for parochial missions, which made £6O mall. Parochial missions always ran away with a great deal of money, and they were now anxious to employ a man to work amongst the men in the parish. If they could get a layman who would devote the whole of his time to such work, a great deal of good might result. Any", amount above £6O that might be realised would: be devoted to the funds of the school. Lady Greenall then declared the bazaar open, and said that she trusted it would be a successful one. The several stalls that comprised the bazaar were in charge of members of the congregation, and were stocked with goods of various descriptions, useful and miscellaneous. A flower stall in the centre of the room contained.a num- ber of orchids, there was also a refreshment stall, and an art stall that had been prepared by the Vicar. There was also a "fine art" gallery, and at intervals there were exhibitions of "Jarley's Royal Living Waxworks," which were under the charge of Mr. Whalley. The room, which had been decorated by Mrs. O'Brien, had a very attractive appearance. The following ladies assisted at the stalls :—Mesdames Slater, Fairhurst, Warburton, Taylor, H. Houghton, Ictott, Hall, P,adnall, Wignall, B. brown, and Brazier; and the Misses Taylor, Hutchin- son, .t. Taylor, White, E. White, and A. Dooley.

And so terrible Is the icy rigour of the climate amidst the lofty heights of the mountains, especially of the icy plateaux of Lipes, that the muleteers find the chewing of these leaves alone enables therm to withstand the icy rarefied air, and to support the long night'. watches to prevent the mules they are transporting to Peru from straying. THE Fair Traders had a night of it, at Warring- ton, last week, but, although they doubtless en- joyed themselves, after a fashion, it cannot be said that their proceedings were edifying. Some of the supporters of the movement seem to think that Fair Trade is the modern Philosopher's Stone that will transmute all things into gold, and they have about as much reason for their faith as hid the alchemists of old. Protection, for that is what Fif:ir Trade means, is an exploded economic fallacy, but it is just possible that by reconsidering it, by exploding it again_ancl again, discoveries may be made which will lead to legislation on the land laws—even as the search for the Philosopher's Stone led ROGER BACON to the discovery of gun- powder and GEBEE to a knowledge of the proper- ties of acids. So far, the agitation for Fair Trade has been a case of "great cry and little wool." . The fact is, leading politicians can perceive that it is hopeless to expect to revive the Corn Laws, on however small a scale; and they can see, too, that the Fair Traders are as to numbers in inverse ratio to their noise. It sounds like a grim joke when one learns that Mr. JOHN WHITE is "the only enrolled member of the National Fair Trade League in Warrington;" but we know that Mr. WHITE is not given to jokes, grim or otherwise— he is as grave as a graveyard. It was the proper thing, of course, to put him in the chair; indeed, so far as the Warrington branch is concerned, he must be looked upon as chairman, secretary, treasurer, and committee— all in one. Let us at once admit that the League might be in a much worse position as to its branch; for instance, if there were another enrolled mem- ber in it, there would almost of a certainty be a difference of opinion, for wherever two or three. ' Fair Traders are gathered together there are two or three opinions in the midst of them. Mr. WHITE, is at least consistent with himself; his speech, as chairman, was clear, if it was not con- vincing. He doesn't beat about the bush after the manner generally of Fair Traders; he goes straight to the point, and declares himself in favour of a duty on corn; the country is to be saved by increasing the price of the four-pound loaf. This is not Mr. WHITE'S way of putting it; but this is what his doctrine means. He quoted ADAM SMITH for the statement that "no equal capital puts into motion a greater quantity of pro- ductive labour than that of the farmerr but he did not state, as he might have done, by way of con- trast, that more recent political economists have discovered that no equal capital puts into motion a less quantity of productive labour than that of the .brewer; nor did he state either that ADAM SMITH was an out-and-out Free Trader, whose mission it was in his time to rout such vulgar fallacies as those which the Fair Traders are trying to palm upon the country to-day. Mr. WHITE foresees that the mass of the people will not care to have money taken out of their pockets even if they are assured that it is to be applied to relieving the long-suffering farmer; and he offers what—if the proposal came from Mr. CrtAnsroxs--would be called a gigantic bribe ; he suggests that, under certain conditions, the money received from the tax on corn should be applied "towards the free education of the people." This is, to be sure, tempting; our Tory friends are getting on; they are certainly beginning to realise that Free Education is a present-day prob- lem, and, if the Liberals do not mind what they are about in this matter, they may find; to quote Mr. DISRAELI'S famous illustration, that their clothes have been stolen whilst they were bathing. But, seriously, we have no fear that Mr. WHITE'S proposal will be parried into effect; the electors are not unaware of the fact that two-thirds of the cost of the aucation of the children in our ele- mentary schools are already paid by the State; and they know that it will be an easier matter to induce .he Legislature to pay the other third than to persuade Parliament to step in and put a tax upon the food of the people. We quite admit the force of the statement that education "must tax some- one," and that in that sense it is not free. It will tax everyone--,just as our two-thirds Free Educe?.

THE Visit Of Mr. HERBERT GLADSTONE to Lyllllll, and of Mr. JOSEPH HOWES to Warrington, has put , new life into the Liberalism of the district. Great enthusiasm has been displayed at each meeting in favour of Home Rule for Ireland. The more the principle of Home Rule is discussed, the more it is found to command the sympathy and support of the masses. The people are always ready to be led; the difficulty is to find leaders who are ready to "move on." Mr. GLADSTONE has never been lacking in political activity since he became leader of the Liberal party; but he has been hampered in his. movements by slow-footed creatures of the Gosoitcs and HARTINGTON type. He is now get- ting rid of 'these clogs, and is ready to go forward at a pace whicir surprises and delights all true Liberals. Mr. HERBERT GLADSTONE is in this respect a. chip of the old block. He is young, and strong, and aggressive as a man should be who would storm. strongholds and rout the enemy. A few of the "curled darlings" of the Tory party at- tended the meeting, at Lymm, on Monday, with a view to disturbing the proceedings generally, and Mr. HERBERT GLADSTONE particularly. But they met their match, and more than their match, for he promised them that if they would come upon tho platform he would argue the question with them until they had not half a leg to stand on. It is hardly necessary to say that they did not accept the invitation; they might have a faculty for noisy objection; but, anything in the shape of argument was beyond them. Mr. H. GLADSTONE made one strong point against Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S attitude in backing up a Coercionist Government which Liberal Unionists—if there are any left—would do well to. take seriously into consideration. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, he said, in April,. 1886, affirmed that there was no caselor coercion when, in the previous three months, there had been 256 outrages and three murders.; but, after that, he voted in favour of the Tory Cbercion Bill, when the returns showed 166 outrages and no murders. There is no recon- ciling such inconsistency; it "calls virtue hypo- crite, and truth a liar." At the same time it cuts the ground from under the Tories when they try to make. a stand in support of the Government. The fact is, all things considered, Irishmen are be- having with great forbearance under the frightful provocation to which they are being subjected. Mr. H. Gransrosz, at Lymm, and Mr. How ES at Warrington, quoted from judges' charges to show that Ireland was comparatively free from crime. Mr. Wrislios o?Brunic, M.P., advised his fellow- countrymen to shun outrage as they would shun, poison; and the Tories repay him for giving this good advice by putting him in gaol. They have an idea that they can crush Nationalism out of the hearts of' thelrish. But they cannot; the only thing they are capable of is turning the hearts of Irish- men against them, and sowing the seeds of misery wherever they go. But their days of mischief are numbered; there is a gathering of the forces which will sweep them aside; there are signs of accumu- lation on every hand; and when the next elec- tion comes, if Liberals do their duty man- fully, Toryism will be lying on its back, and ;Liberal Unionism will be nowhere.

FRANCE is undergoing another crisis; but a crisis every six months, or so, is a matter of course with France. The peculiar feature, how- ever, of the present crisis is that it is Presidential as well as Ministerial. M. Rouvvex, the head of the latest Cabinet, was defeated on Saturday by a motion sprung upon him by M. CLEmENcr.Au, the leader of the Radical section in the Chamber. It is said that M. CLISMENCEAII was astonished at his own success, and there can be little doubt that he would not have secured so many votes for his motion if it had not been thought that a blow struck at M. ROVVIER would reach the President of the Republic. There is a strong feeling in France against M. WILSON, the son-in-law of M. GREVY. There is good authority for the old say- ing that the sin of the father descends upon the children; but it is something new to see the father suffer for the conduct of the son-in-law. A Parliamentary Commission is inquiring into the conduct of M. WILSON in connection with the trafficking with honours, and so far as it has pro- ceeded it must be admitted that it is damaging to M. Wusox. It is not at all unlikely that it will be proved that he has abused the confidence re- posed in him as permanent Private Secretary of M. Glom and, meantime, public opinion is "dead set" against the President as Well as the Secretary. This, to those who are looking on, seems unreasonable; but public opinion is not always reasonable, though it is rare that it is wrong in the instinct that it displays. M. GREVY sent • for M. CLEMENCEAII, much to the dis- gust of the Tory element in the Chamber; but in taking this course he was acting in a manner strictly constitutional, seeing that it was M. CLEMENCEAVS motion that had overthrown the Ministry. However, the Radical leader was equal to the occasion, for he plainly told the Pres- ident that there was a Presidential as well as a Ministerial crisis, and that until the former wa& got rid of, he could not engage himself to grapple .irith the latter. This meant that M. GREVT must pave the way by himself resigning; but the President had no ear for this disagreeable sugges- tion. He accordingly called in other counsellors— M. M. FREYCINET, FLOQUET, GOBLET, and Baissox ; but they all told pretty much the same tale, and that was that it was no use any of them trying to form a Cabinet so long as M. GREVY held office. M. GREVY, conscious of his own innocence, dislikes to be made the scapegoat for the offences of his son- in-law. He holds, and there is great force in his contention, that it was intended that the office of President should constitute a solid point of gov- ernment removed from party strife. It would, in his judgment, be a bad precedent if he were to re- tire at the bidding of a faction'; for it would be an encouragement to every unprincipled political ad- venturer. There is no gainsaying the strenkth of this theory, but theory is one thing and actual facts in this case are another. Yielding to the pressure which is put upon him on all sides, M. GREVY has at last announced that he will resign rather than prolong the crisis. He will not insist 'on a dissolution of Parliament, but intends to ad- dress a message to the country. We cannot but wish that the old man who has served his country so well could have been allowed to 'conclude his second term of office with dignity and honour, and it may be that Frenchmen will have the same feel- ing for him before many months are over.

Mr. Gladstone, writing to a correspondent in Hull, with reference to coercion, says:—" Mr. Bal- four has yet to lOarn—first, that. the Duke of Wel- lington could not attain the end he had in view; secondly, that he is notthe Duke of Wellington." This is a neat and ep,iguanunatic way of putting the case. Mr. Balfour. is. not without literary taste, and he will, of course; appreciate it.

Here is a good story:of an Irishman, which is so good that it must be; true.. He was negotiating with the mother for. the younger of two daughters. "Will you have the younger with two cows, or the otherr with three ?" said the mother. "Faith,?' repliedlthe wooer, "rui. have the ouldest. Shure there isn't the difference of a cow between any two women in the wurreld." That Irishman must .have ha& Scotch blood in him —oh?

There has been a meeting, of. the guarantors of the Liverpool Exhibition, .at which some'strong re- marks were made auto the extsavag,ance and mis- management of the EihibitionCouncil. One guaran- tor, smarting underta_ recollection of the 22 per cent. he would have •to pay, spoke, of the Council as a "pack of idiots.' How, if the Council should retort—" you're another. " Fools guarantee money, and wise (or wasteful). men spend it. ,

Three Sutton boys have been fined at Runcorn for ill-treating what Shakespeare calls "the harm- less necessary cat." Their defence was that "they were only playing with itc by striking it with the stick and throwing the brick-bat at it." As the cat died, it would perhaps have been of service if the lads had been given a lesson in playfulness with the stick—to say nothing, of a taste of the brick-bat. '

Judging from the number of pipes that were in full blast, at the Public• Hall, on Monday night, there would seem to have been a iitsposition on the part of a number of the audience to convert the play into a Smoking Entertainment. This would be very pleasant; no doubt,,to)those who like this sort of thing; butthere ampeeple who object to tobacco, especially at second.hand ; and it would be as well therefore to let it be known when smok- ing is allowed.

A tramcar conductor, at St. Helens, has been fined for carrying too many passengers, and at the seine time cruelly lashing his horses. It is bad enough for horses to be oven-taxed, without being whipped in addition. 'lt is some time since there was any complaint about over-loading the 'buses at Warrington'; and; if ,better time be not kept —especially on market dlNys—it is not unlikely that the drivers,will be Wi> often short of a load: Punctuality is the soul of business.

There will be no.diffieultY in the making of the Ship Canal as to labourers. Poor fellows! Some of them find',. after tramping for days to get to Eastham, that they. cannot be employed, and it is pailful to see the look 4 disappointment in their weary eyes. It.must be hard to have to "bog a brother of the 13arth to, give him leave to toil"— and be refused: Those who are not given a job now will, let usliope, have the first turn when the work gets in full swing.

Stockton Heath requires to be looked to, accor- ding to the report of the proceedings of the Run- corn Rural Sanitary Authority. A sad ease was reported of neglect of family and uncleanli- ness on the part of a dmyman employed by Messrs. Greenall, Whitley, and Co., and the relieving offi- cer said "'there were other cases quite as bad." The drayman seems to be pretty well paid for his service.; but it may be that he spends his money in beet instead of beef.

The Rev. W. Edmondson, of St. Peter's Church, Parr, was to have lectured on the Lord's Supper, at Ashton-in.-Makerfield, on Tuesday; but the Rev. H. Siddall, vicar of Ashton, stepped in and forbade his speaking in the parish. The interdict was obeyed; but what should have been a lecture became an indignation meeting. The parishioners of the Ashton vicar are now •up in arms against hint;, they are not afraid of either bell or book. The Rev. H. Siddall has a deal to learn; if he thinks he can suppress opinion by intolerance of this kind he will find he has been living in a fool's paradise.

A vary pretty quarrel amongst Roman Catholic •priests was fought out at the Liverpool Assizes, on Monday. It, related to the possession of furni- ture, &c., which Father Joseph Fagan had left at the house which he had formerly occupied in Wigan. Amongst other things detained was Ouida's Novels; but it transpired that these had been returned. Mr. Mulholland Q.C., remarked that these novels were "hardly religious " ; but why not? Mr. Spurgeon once said he could eat, drink, and smoke to the glo4 of God ; and surely Father Fagan might be permitted to extend the list by adding Ouida's Novels.' They are certainly no worse than the majority of cigars.

Mr. John Bright says :—" The Irish rebel party will not look at mY suggestion because they are rebels." This refers to the proposal for settling the Irish question by referring all Parliamentary business to Grand Committees. But what of people who, in the eyes of Mr. Bright, are the most loyal of men? How is it that neither Mr. Chamberlain, nor Lord Hartington, 'nor Lord Salisbury has had a word to say in favouc of his scheme? Can it be because each Unionist leader has a separate scheme of his own? Or is it because all parties are agreed that, whatever else may be worth trying, Mr. Bright's plan is not in it ?

A correspondent of a Manchester contemporary has been looking up a pamphlet on the Irish ques- tion, written by the poet Shelley, when he was only twenty years of age. Ho wrote, not like a vision- ary, but like an enthusiastic but practical politi- cian. Shelley was always ready to tilt at tyrants. He speaks of the Union, as "the most successful engine that England ever wielded over the misery

of fallen Ireland." This is good, but the following is better—" Tito goodness of a Government consists in the happiness of the governed, If the governed arty wretched and dissatisfied, the Government has faatd in its end." This is the Irish question in a nutshell.

Herriman, landlord' of' the IVlersey Widnes, was out with his gun on the sandbank opposite the Widnes shore, when he shot a. fine specimen of' that rare water bird, the crested Grebe. The beautify' phi- mage of the bird has led to the wholesale destructihn of the species for the purpose of adorning ladies' muff S and bOnnets with the feathers, and the bird now is seldom' to be met with. With a double crest, and a ruff round its neck, the Grebe is rather a pecurfar • looking bird and it is quite a curiosity. Mr. Herrimart intends to have the one he has captured stuffed. He proposed that they reply to the Local Gov- I ernment Board to the effect that the Authority did not consider there was any necessity for the Authority to in- , terfere.—Mr Aaron seconded this proposal, which was ' agreed to.-The only other matter of public interest which came before the Authority is reported in another column. BRUNSWICK WEgLEYAN MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT SOCIETY, HOECORN.=Under the title of an "At Home" the mem- bers of this society held a pleasant and interesting social gathering in the Lecture-room of Brunswick-street School on Wednesday evening. About 150 persons were present, and Mr. fr. Simister, the president, conducted the proceedings, which opened with an appropriate " Indication " written and spoken by Mr. W. Douglas. Mr. T. Fox and Richard Moore rendered the duet "David and Goliath ;"' and Mr. F. Eden recited "The Mariner's dream." Mr. R. Moore contributed the song " Ship- mates " in good style, and Mr. J. Pennington sang "Who will dare the fists with me." A " paperette " entitled "A little talk about talking" was given by Mr. Thomas Leach, junr., and Mr. R, Morris was honoured with th only encore of the evening for his capital singing of "Rocked in the cradle of the deep." "The brave old oak" was sung by Mr. T. Fox, and a quartette consisting of , Messrs. R. Moore, John Howard, T. Fox, and J. Pennington sang "In abscense." An interesting feature of the evening's entertainment was the performanee of the Wolsey scene from Shake- speare's play of Henry VIII. The part of Wolsey was capitally pourtrayed by the Rev. R. G. Hughes, of Widnes, and Henry VIII: had an able representative in Mr. C. Mormon. The other parts were "Crom- well," Mr. J. Molvneux ; Lord, Surrey, Mr. J. Moulton; Duke of Norfolk, *Mr. F. Eden; and Lord Suffolk, Mr. G. Hayes. On the proposition of Mr. Coventry, seconded by Mr. E. Marshall, a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman, and to those who had con- tributed to the entertainment. Mr. Hughes, in reply- ing, said he went to Shakespeare for the beauty and sublimity of the thoughts expressed, and he advised those present to study .aha,kespeare, but not., to go to r theatres.

TIM DOGS' ACT AT WIDNES.-011 Thursday, at Widnes Petty Sessions, William Kay, West Bank ;: Thomas Hall, Mersey-road ; and Thomas. Robinson, Widnes-road • and Thomas Finney, Ball-larc, Dltton, were web., fined s's and costs for disobeying an order of the Bends in allowing their dogs to be at large. THE ALLEG&D WOUNDINa CASE AT. WIDNFX,—At Wid- nes Petty Sessions, on Thursdhy, before Mr. IC Gaskell, junr., Mary Jane Iceeghan a middle-aged nntnan, of Water-street, was again charged with unlawfully woun- ding Ellen Godfrey, an elderly woman of Sankey-etreet The prosecutrix I;ftS unable to appear, and the prisoner was remanded for a week. MARRIAGE OF TIM VICAR OF HEL._ol3T.—OnT2nd IVevem- ber, at Christ Church, Southport, the Rev. W. T. vale, of He/slay, and Mies C. E. Buxton', of Greenfield Pull, Flintshire, were married in the afternoon by the Rev. Edmund Pigott, vicar of Treptham, and cousin of the bride: The tnarriar was of a very qziet character, only the immediate relative& and friends of the several lama- * lies being, present. The bride and bridegroom left in the evening for London. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD. AT WORIC.—ht Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Mr. G. H. Dart', clerk to the Widnes School Board, prosecuted the following parents for not sending their children regularly to schoOl: .Tozeph Davies, -.fames Ilianwood, Edward Lightfoot, John Caffery, John Hayes, William Carter, Thomas Handley, John Grayson, Lawrence Kenny, Matthew Burns, Bernard Kehoe, Catherine Goomley, and Patrick CaDow. The usual penalty of ss, including costs, was imposed in each case. CRUELTY TO A CAT AT RIINCOUN.-OTI nday, at Runcorn Petty Sessions, Williafti Spruee, James Howard, ane James Wrench, youths, pleaded guilty to having on the 13th inst., cruelly illtreated a cat. Evince was given that the Cat belonged to Mr. J. Bate,. farmer, Sut- tofl,. and on the day named, the servant-gal •Mary Hall, saw the defendant; run the animal round the farm yard. Sprite struck the cat with a thick stick, and Howard struck it with a brick. The cat died a feiv days after- wards. The defendants who said they were only play- ing with the cat, were each fined Ls. and costs At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, William Eo- cleston, a collier, of Prescot, was charged with being drunk and disorderly at Rainhill on Tuesday afternoon. He was further charged with ha; ing damaged the cell in which he was placed to the extent of £3.—P.C. Gieen. slade stated that on Tuesday afternoon the prisoner, was drunk, and creating a disturbance at Rainhill, and he locked him up. While he was out of his station for a few minutes the prisoner damaged the cell and the rugs to the extent mentioned.—The prisoner was ordered • to , pay lOs and costs, and the damage, total £4 4s tki, or ,go to gap/ for five weeks. The prisoner, who was only ' married on Tuesday, Went to gaol. STARRED 'WITH A FORE AT WIDNES.—At Widnes Police.tourt on Manday, before Mr. F. H. Gossage,., a Pole named Antony Antaskjesky,. was charged with unJ ,lawfulfy wounding Adam Lanbinskas, also a Pole. 'Ma prosecutor lives at 30, Water-street, and the prisoner lodges with him. About eleven o'clock on Saturday 'night the prisoner was partaking of supper :with the family: and a quarrel took place respecting the victuals. The prisoner was told he must find lodgings elsewhere; whereupon he took up a three pmnged.fork,-and plunged. the weapon into, the prosecutors nose. Subsequently Dt. Mitchinson dressed the wound, which is of a serious character, there beino; danger of blood poisoning or lock jaw: The prisoner Was remanded for a week. An in— terpreter had to be employed. Ftrez RAT, OF MILS. JOHN DRUNDRIT, OF Rl7NCORN.—The- remains of this respected lady were interred at Runcorn. Cemetery on Tuesday. In accordance with the expressed wiAll of Mrs. Brundrit, the funeral was of a strictly pri- vatenature. In the first carriage were Dr. McDougall, 'andthe Rev. W. C. Stafford, Rector of Attenborough• Norfolk. Then came the hearse, containing the coffin, which was hidden from view by the numerous floral' 'offerings from sorrowing relatives and friend.s. In the three mourning coaches following were Mr. John Brun- drit and his three sons, and the Revs. J. J. Bryant and F. lll'hadows. and Messrs. A. F. Brundrit, T. Bankes, Reynolds, Major C. W. Hazlehurst, and Mr. W. H: Wight. Mrs. John Hazlehurst, Mrs. Charles Hazle-• .huist, and Mr. S. R. Chadwick, J.P., sent three carriages to jbin the procession. The funeral service was read by the Rev: W. C. Stafford.

NH. H. Saints-Kinn, M.P.—The Etruria, which arrived from New York on Sunday, broughtamongst her passengers Mr. Henry Seton-Karr, M.P. for St. Helens. Mr. Seton-Karr had been on a visit to the United States, where he stayed for several weeks. SYR GRORGR TREVELYAN ON THE LAST ORNERAL ELEcrrox.—Sir George Trevelyan, in acknowledg- ing receipt of copies of the resolution unanimously pawed at. public meetings recently convened by the Widnes Division Liberal Association, says:—There is no question whatever that at the last general election the country was under the belief that, as a condition of Liberal Unionist support. self-Govern- ment, free from the objections which Lord Harring- ton and Mr. Chamberlain felt towards Mr. Glad- stone's bills, was to be given to Ireland, and that the days of coercion were over. RUNCORN AND THR SHIP CANAL.-- Although Rtmcom will be the scene of most important en* gineering works in connection with the Manchester Ship Canal. the activity shown there is by no means great. Several engineers have taken up their quar- ters in the town, and about 50 labourers have been engaged. It is confidently anticipated, however, that this number will be increased to thousands within a brief period. Two steamers, commonly called yachts, but which are equally available for towing purposes, are berthed in the Old Quay Dock, where also the contractor has stored 30.000 sleepers and 700 tons of deal baulks. A fact that cannot fail to be interesting to the townspeople is that the centre of the proposed canal is indicated at. the Old Quay and for a considerable distance towarcla Warrington by small red flags. LORD CROSS AT Btocrobt.—Lord Cross Was the principal speaker at a Conservative meeting held on• Thursday evening, at Buxton. Responding, to a resolution expressing approval of the home and foreign policy of the Government, he denied that the Crimes Act of last session created new crime, though, he added, if Parliament desired, it had' the right to create new crime. The law, whatever it was, must be obeyed until it was altered. He approved of the imprisonment of Mr. O'Brien and the proceedings against Mr. Wilfrid Blunt, both at whom. he said, had wilfully broken the law and must suffer the consequences. The Government were determined to uphold law and order both at home and in all parts of the Empire. He charged Mr. Gladstone with being in a measure responsible for the recent riots in London, and said that while he approved of the letter he had atitten discoun- tenancing the proceedings-of the mob, he thought he ought to have written it before, because he must have known what would have been the result of his first letter, holding up the Metropolitan police force to the reprobation of the people. THE BRIDGEWATER NAVIGATION COITPA.NY LIMITED.—An application of a somewhat unusual character was made on Friday to Mr. Justice North, in the voluntary liquidation of this company,whose undertaking has been purchased by the Manchester Ship Canal Company. It was stated that the liqui- dators would have to distribute among the preference and ordinary shareholders a sum of over a million of ',money, and as the court would have to determine various questions as to the principle and the; proportion in which the surplus should be divided, meetings had been held for the purpose of appointing a representative for each of the two classes of share- holders in the discussion of those questions which were proposed to be raised by motion before the court. Mr. Thomas H. Birch, of Manchester, had been appointed to represent the ordinary share- holders, and Mr. George Hall Schofield, of Oldham, the preference shareholders, and the present appli- cation was for the sanction of the court to those appointments.—His Lordship had at first some diffi- culty in making the order, because it appeared that Mr. Schofield was the holder of ordinary as well as preference shares, but on being informed that the fact was mentioned in the notices convening the meeting, he sanctioned the appointment, but de- clined to fix a day for the bearing of the motion.

' SCALDED TO DEATH AT RUNCORN. Mr. J. E. Worsley, the coroner for the honor and fee of Halton held an inquest at the Masonic Hotel, Devonshire-square, Runcorn, on Thursday afternoon, touching the death of Thomas Lewis, a young man, who was scalded at the works of the Runcorn Soap and Alkali Company, on the 11th Inst. Mr. John Ashton, solicitor, appeared on be- half of the company, and Mr. C. E. Richmond, H.M. Inspector of Factories for the district was also pre- sent. Mr. J. W. Woodland was foreman of the Jury. Sarah Lewis, 20, Regent-street, said the deceased was her son and was 23 years of age. He was a labourer at the works of the Soap and Alkali Company. The de- ceased was brought home scalded on the 11th inst., and he was attended by Dr. McDougall until death occurred on Wednesday morning. He told her that he fell into a pan of caustic liquor. He saved himself by his arm, and it was a mercy he was not in altogether. D. McDougall deposed that the lower extremities of the deceased were terribly scalded. His limbs were more than scalded, they were corroded.. The tissue was de- stroyed through the action of the strong liquor. He died from lockjaw on Wednesday morning. Invariably the cause of death in such cases was starvation, but in the present instance he (Dr. McDougall) fed the deceased artificially, and death was really caused by the strong spasms he had to undergo. The deceased told him that he lost his balance on the edge of the vat and fell in. Joseph Wakefield, of 7, Granville-street, said he was foreman in the shed where the, accident occurred. He heard the voice of deceased screaming for help, and he ran and stopped the engine. He thett wont to the " pot "

of boiling cauttic liquor, and found the deceased lying on the ground liesides it. Witness pulled the deceased's shoes and stockins and trmsers. off, and then be was foldedin blanket and taken home. Subsequently the deceased told him how the accident occurred. He Maid "the friction wheet did not work so•weil, se he got upon the pot, with one font upon the edge of the pot, and the other upon the revoraing cage, in order to put a bit of handrag in it. Whilst doing this helell into the liquor. If there was anything wrong with the inachinery it was the deceased's place to report the matter, and not to have got upon tee pot. Next morning witnew examined the machinery, and it was then all right. Ile never heard tell of anyone getting. upon the pat in the fashion deceased had done before. " .

James Crank, 60, Nelson-street, 4abottrer at the works, gave corroborative testimony. The Coroner, in summing upi remarked that this was a very lameniable accident, and the jury returned a ver- dict of "Accidental death." RUNCORN BOARD OC GUARDLIaNS. _ _ _

The fortnightly meeting of this Board took place at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday afternoon. There :we present ColonCl Ashton (chatrman), the Revs. J. W. N. Tanner and T. Whitley ;. Messrs. Mclntyre, Aaron, Hewitt, Stokes, Hadtleld, Smith, Taylor, Brandreth, Hamilton, Forster; W. A. Linaker (as- sistant clerk.) THE Woman:oust: NTIRSE.—IL was stated that there had been sixteen applications for the vacant position of nurse at the Workhouse, and a committee was appointed to look over the applications and make a selection'ef can- didates to appear before the Board. VIBRATION AT SCHOOLS.—The Workhouse Mister.(itr. Cunnah) reported that Mr. Mosely, the Local Govern- ment Board inspector, had inspected the schools at the Workhouse and reported that the boys had passed a good and the girls a very good examination. The Inspeg- toes schedules were also submitted to the • Board, and. showed that 99 per dent. of the girls had passed. A COMPLAINT.—The Chairman read a letter whiehthad been received from Mr. D. H. Jones, complaining of the condbct of the Workhouse Master in connection with his (Mr. Jones') contract for clothing.—The Rev. J: W. N. Tanner said the Visiting Committee had gone thoroughly into this matter, and they thought there was •• no blame attaching to the master, and, further, that he-had only done his duty.—The Chairman; It is not necessary for Mr. Jones to come here, then ?—The Rev. J. W. N, Tan- ner: 7 think not.—Mr. Hadfield moved that the report of the Visiting Committee be adopted, anci`Mf. Aaron havingseconded the proposal, it was agreed ten ENTERTA/NING THE INMATES.—The Workhouse IVaster, in his journal, •recommended that a vote of thanks b; given to Mr. James Robinson, of Aston, for a- Magic Lantern entertainment which he gave to the school chil- dren, and also to Mr. Shaw, of the Mersey Mission; Run- corn, for sending a number of books and papers fort dis- tribution in the various wards.—Adopted. CHRISTMAS DINNER.—IL was decided that the •usual Christmas thnner and supper should begiven the inmates. WHO was RESPONSIBLE ?—Mr. Hadfield referred to the case of a. woman named Anne „Shaw, who had been brought from Runcorn to the Workhouse suffering from typhoid' fever. He was of opinion that the case ought to have been dealt with by the Runcorn Com- missioners. The Guardians had no right to look after patients simply because of the neglect of the authorities of Runcorn.—The Assistant Clerk said the case couldhot

be takeir tone Runcorn Hospital without the consent of the Commissioners, 'and the woman could not be waiting whVe negotiations were going on.—Mr. Ward, the relieving officer, said that the doctor told him. that. the woman would die if she were left where she was, but he (Mr. Ward) certainly thought it was a case for the Runcorn CornmissiOners. He also mentioned that the house in which the woman was was in a crowded state: llssarrrto understood that typhoid fever was bkought on by overcrowding amongst other causes.— Mr. TArtork said that was a matter that had been at- tended to.—Mr. HADFIRLD: Yes, the door was lockied after tliediorse was stolen. (Laughter). The matter- then dropped.' ThiS was the chief buspiess.

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

A special meeting was held on Thursday night at the Tbwn Hall. Mr Pi:tchard presided, and there were present Dr. McDougall, Messrs. E. lmison, F. A. Lake, J. R. Frith, S. B. Beckett, and G. Moss (clerk.)
OF THE STAFF.-LIVELY*

DISCUSSION.—A BLOCK. The first business was the appointment of a head stress.to Mill-brow Board School. Only three applie&- tions were considered :—Miss Elizabeth Kennan, of West Bank . Beard School, Widnes; Miss Simkin, assistant mistress&t Greenway-mad Board School, Runcorn; and Miss Sampson, of Doncaster. Mr:BlTlrett moved that Miss Simkin be appointed, for the reason that she had been accustomed to toach infant& the whole of her time, both as a pupil teacher and as an assistant mistress. She had been under the Board for three years, and, he believed, had given every satisfac- tion daring that period. There was not a word said against her. He saw from her testimonial that at Leigh,. where she was for four years, they spoke of her in the highest terms. Under these circumstances he thought it would Be a wise thing for the Board to promote their- [own servant.

Mt. Frith : May I ask if Miss Simkin has been promiSed by the members of the Board, or by .the that she should have the appointment ? The Chairman: No. If so, it must have been without any instructions from the Board. Mr. Frith : Has such been done at an informal meet- _

--- - Dr. McDougall: I object to anything being _discussed at this meeting which is not before us. Mr. Frith: Has Miss Simkin been led to suppose by the clerk in any shape or form that she would kbe ap— pointed ? Mr. Beckett: I don't know anything of WS. There is no seconder to my resolution. MI-. Frith asked the Clerk the question two or • three times, but received no answer from the clerk.. Mr_ Frith then seconded Mr. Beckett's motion, and corro— borated Mr. Beckett's remarks. He said he understood that Miss Simkin had already declined ao situation thronglj the promise that was made to her.- Dr. -McDougall moved an amendment that Miss Kernian be appointed the head mistress -at- Mill Brow school, and in doing so he spoke of 'what he personally knew. Miss Kennan was most exemplary in every sense of the term, but that would not influence him if he thought she was not by far the- most fitted to occupy the post. She had been trained at one of the -finmt Board Schools, and she had remained there for eight years. The result of her first examination was in excess of 93 per cent.; and at her last examination she passed 100 per cent, of those•that were present. She had been trained in teaching all the standards. He only asked them to listen to a single resolution of the Widnes School Board—" At a meeting of the Board held ilthis day, T. S. Timmis in the chair, it,wa.s resolved that la bonus of £5 be paid Miss Elizabeth liennao. assistant mistresss of the senior girls department of West Bank ISchool for her exceptional services during the past year, she having passed the whole of her class at the recent Government examination without a single failure in any subject." Dr. McDougall contended that Miss Keenan was best qualified for the post, and said he did not think Ithat a promise of any description had been made-to Miss ' Simkin, and so far ashe could ascertain no such promise was made.

Mr. Imison seconded the amendment, and he con- firmed and concurred in all that Dr. McDougall had said about Miss Kennan. Mr. Lake said he must confess that of the three candi- dates they had before them he should have been inclined to support Miss Sampson but for her distance from Run- corn. He should support Miss Kennan, who seemed to him to be a most worthy candidate, and an exceptionally good teacher. He did not think that because some busy-- body whether the Clerk a the Board or a member had told a teacher that she might have a certain appointment that that should weigh with the Board. If such a thing had taken place, he would be no party to'it, and, so far as he was concerned, that candidate was out of the field.
---- The Chairman said he had no remarks to offer.

Mr. Beckett said ho thought the chairman was respon- sible for the clerk being instructed to convey to Miss Simkin that she would very likely be recommended to be appointed. Mr. Imison said he was not a party, and so far as his knowledge went no other member was a party to the clerk being authorised to convey an intimation to Miss Simidif. It was never mentioned. The Chairman thought it was out of place to make any allusion to any matter that had taken place in com- mittee. The whole of the matters then contemplated were found not to be workable at all, and they had let the whole thing drop. Mr. Lake: That discussion was entirely informal, and at the end of it it was pointed out that in order to bring the matters forward somemembers would have to give notice. A member did not give notice, it being found that the resolution was impracticable, so that there could not be any instructions from anybody. Mr. Beckett said the other members were quite out of order in interrupting his remarks in that way. He did not now consider it worth while to prolong the discus- sion, considering the strong feeling there, seemed to be on the Board.

The Chairman,after further convemation on the point, put the amendment, for which ibted—the Chairman, Dr. McDougall, Mr. Imison, and Mr. Lake-4. For the original motion only Mr. Beckett and Mr. Frith voted. Miss Kennan was therefore appointed. 4.

div.head: PROTEST.
div.p: A PROTEST.

The next business was the appointment of assistants to Greenway-road school, and Mr. Beckett asked if the other members (meaning Dr. McDougall, and Messrs. Lake and hnison) were willing to co-operate ?—Mr. Lake' said he was so dissatisfied with the manner in which the appointment of headmaster was filled up that he washed his hands of all the appointments connected with it.— Dr. McDougall and Mr. Imison also declined, under the circumstances, to share any responsibility in the matter. Aftetthaving passed a resolution converting Greenway road Mixed School into a Boys' School, the members seoarated without having appointed a staff.
