div.head: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATUILDAY.—Bef ore Alderman Burgess and Alderman Chandley. Lantirrt.—Catherine Corrigan, an old woman, who lives in Cambria Place, was charged with having stolen a pair of boots, value 2s, the property of James Gleave, Mill-street. It seemed that the prisoner was in Mr. Gleave's shop on Thursday night, and surreptitiously carried off the boots. She afterwards sold the boots for 2d to a Mrs. Bradbury. Prisoner was sent to gaol for 14 days and the bench cautioned Mrs. Bradbury for pur- chasing the boots. MONT.—Before the Mayor (Alderman T. H, Sutton), and Councillors Greening, and J. Pierpoint. DRUNKENNESS.—The following persons were dealt with for drunkenness : Bridget Lally, on Town Hill, on Satur- day night, fined 108. and costs; Martin Higgins, in Bew- sex-street, on Sunday morning, fined 5s and costs; Brian Flaherty, at Market Gate, on Saturday, fined 5s and costs; Thomas Curley, in Bridge-street, fined 5s and costs; James Peers, in Tanners-lane, fined 5s and costs; William Lee, in Buttermarket-street, on the 13th inst., fined 5s including costs ; Michael Cavanagh, in Old-road, on the 14th inst, fined 58 and costs; William Bailey, m the Market Place, on the 16th inst, dismissed. ILyrnaaxitio A HORSR.—Hugh Yarclsley, was sum- moned for illtreating a horse by working it whilst it was in an unfit condition, and Henry Barber was summoned for causing it to be SO workbl. Inspector Aplin, of the R.S.P.C.A., deposed that the animal, when he saw it on the 22nd inst, was quite unfit for work, owing to its suf- fering from a cold, and being in a weak condition. Evi- dence was also given by Police Inspector Cox, and Mr. Robinson, VS., after which the Bench fined Barber 5s and costs, and discharged Yardsley. William Patten was summoned for having illtreated two horses, on the 14th inst, by working them whilst in an unfit condition. and John Connor, was summoned for having caused them to be so worked. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the defence. Connor was fined lOs and costs. PRATIDUIANT ENLISTIKENT.—John Kelley, for having fraudulently enlisted in the 3rd Battalion South Lanca- shire Regiment, was sent to prison for 23 days, with

hard lab-our. AN ESCAPED LITNATIC.—IIGHFy Williams, (28,) was brought up on a charge of being a deserter from the Army. He was arrested on Saturday, when he was in possession of military clothing. When he was taken to the police station it was found that he was not in his right mind, although he was quiet in his demeanour. It was afterwards ascertained that he had escaped from Church Stretton Asylum, Shropshire, and he was now re- manded for further enquiries to be made. CHARGE AGAINST A PITELICAN. James Garrity and Mark McGann. were summoned for having been drunk on the licensed premises of John Connaughten,the White Bear Inn, Buttermarket-street, on the 14th inst, and John Connaughten was summoned for permitting drunk- enness. Mr. A. Browne appeared for Connaughten. The case for the prosecution was that on the day in question a constable was called to the White Bear in consequence of a robbery having taken place, and that Garritty and McGann were seen in the public-house in an intoxicated condition. Mr. Browne contended that the evidence did not show that the landlord had wilfully permitted drunk- enness and connived at it. After hearing evidence on both sides, the Magistrates thought there was a doubt in the case, and dismissed +-I w defendants. OssrnucrioNs.—Frank Royston, for causing an ob- struction by allowing a horse and vehicle to remain in the street an unreasonable time on the previous Friday, was dismissed on payment of costs.—John Smith and John Stringer were charged with causing an obstruction by allowing ten beer barrels to remain on the footpath Horsemarket-street, on the 16th inst. Smith was or- dered to pay costs, and Stringer was dismissed. TucsnAv.---Before -Merman Holmth'i. A DESERTER.—John Mainery, al deserter from H.M. Royal 1ri.913 Fusiliers, stationed in Armagh, was remanded to Walton to await escort. WEDNESDAY.—Before Mr. John Fairclough, Mr. R. Garnett, and Mr. R. W. Francomb. BEGGING.—Joseph Rigby (66), Wigan, was brought up on a charge of begging in Buttermarket-street on the day previous. Ile was dismissed'on promising to return to Wigan and go to the workhouse there. IN ESCAPED LIINATIC.—Henry Williams was brought up on remand on a charge of being a deserter from the army. It transpired that prisoner had escaped from a lunatic asylum in Shropshire, and a letter was received from the asylum authorities stating that as he had,been away over a certain period without being re-captured an order of discharge had been made, and he could not be taken back without a fresh certificate. The magistrates discharged the prisoner. TnEv-r OF Boors Daniel Murray, forge labourer, was sent to prison for a month for having stolen a pair of boots, value 6s, the property of Henry Baily, a puddler. The two men lodged at the same house in Dallarrelane, and the boots were taken from underneath a sofa and afterwards were pawned. TIIIIRSDAY.—Before Major Litton, Alderman Webster, and Councillor J., Greening. THEFTS BY A BOY,—Thomas Newhall, a lad, was charged with having stolen two pocket handkerchiefs, the property of Joseph Snaith, outfitter, 134, Bridge-st., and also with having stolen three newspapers from the shop of James Chadwick, newsagent, Scotland-road. He pleaded guilty, and was ordered to receive six strokes with the birch rod. DEGNKENNESS.—John Burns and Thomas Kane were each fined 5& and costs for this offence.

Famex.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Sutton), Dr. Gomall, Alderman Harrison, and Mr. R. Garnett. BEctonso.--Jokn. Towey was sent to prison for seven Idays for begging in Bridge-street on the previous night. DRUNKENNESS .—Richarti Ashton was fined 55., includ- ing costs, for having been drunk in Mersey-street on the previous evening. DISTURBING THE PEACE.—For having committed a breach of the peace by fighting in Bridge-street on the , lath inst., William Richardson and Thomas Garvin were ordered to be bound over to be of good be- \ b Lviour. CattErry.—Owen Toole, Edward Murphy and John Barry were summoned for ill-treating a dog dn the 29th of October. Inspector Aplinykof the R.S.P.C.A.,said that tie defendants had expre*ed their sorrow, and there was no desire to press the case. Defendants pleaded guilty, and, as they consented to pay costs, the case was not gone into. ALLEGED ASSAULT .I—Frank Walkden was summoned for having assaulted Patrick Kelly on the 21st November. The case was dismissed. UNSTAM FED INDENTURES.—Mary Jane Barlow was summoned by James Welsby, master fustian cutter, for absenting herself from work as an apprentice without lawful excuse. It transpired that the indentures were lunstamped, and in consequence the case fell through.

WIDNES POLICE COURT. 4 MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. 11. Dossage. DRUNK AND VAGRANCY.—For the offence of drunken- ness John Tiamey, of MIXIS Bank-road, and Denis Mullin. of no residence, were each fined ss. and costs.—Catherine Sutton, a tramp, was sentenced to seven days' hard labour fcr begging-.
WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. THURSDAY.—Before Mr. 11. Gaskell, jun., and Mr. T. H.

Gossage. DUIINKENNESS.—For the offence of drunkenness the following persons were each fined ss:and costs :—John O'Neil, Major Cross-street; Thomas Moran, Elizabeth- street; William Bell, Appleton; James Wood, Lacey- street; William and Thomas Arnold, 23,Muspratt-street ; and Thomas Tansey, 15, Pitt-street. CHIMNEY ON FlRE—Richard Banner, of Wellington- street, was fined is and costs, 4s 6d, for allowing the chimney of his dwelling-house to be on fire. STREET OasTaucTims.—Wm. Hatton, a carter, of Lugs- dale-road,i was charged with causing an obstruction n the road mentioned, on the 15th instant, by allowing his horse and lurry to remain there an unreasonable time. The case was dismissed on the payment of costs. BREACHES OF THE Pzeos.—James Conroy, Highfield- street ; Patrick Glynn, Water-street; Moses McGuire, IWalmesley-street ; and John Jones, Irwell-street, were each bound over to be of good behaviour, in the usual sureties for committing breaches of the peace.: *Wit THEFT.—William Gandy, aged 14 years, who lives in Moss Bank-road, was charged with having, on the pre- vious day, stolen a trowel and several other articles, value 7s, the property of the Widns Alkali Works.—Mr. Clarke, a foreman, saw the prisoner in an old laboratory in the works, and subsequently ifound the towel and other articles in his posession. He was given into the custody of P.C. Moore, and was now fined 20s and costs, 0K a month in default.

hINCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAY.—Before Mr. Charles Reynolds and Mr. James Handley. LICENSING MATTER.S.— James Howard was granted temporary authority to sell at the Castle Hotel, Halton, recently occupied by Williani Philips. George Ward re- ceived permission to sell at the Cornwall and Devonshire Arms, Church-street, lately occupied by William Doyle. Datnot AND DuaonnEgLy.--:For being drunk and dis- orderly in Bridge-street en the 12th November' John Crogan was fined 10s. Ara costs, Bs. 6d. P.C. Kettle proved the case.—ThoMas Brown, an old man, was charged with being drunk in Canal-street on the 12th of November. P.C. Hulse said the defendant was in charge of a horse and cart, and had 'several narrow escapes of being thrown under the wheel through his drunken state. A fine of ss. and costs, Bs. 6d., was imposed.— John Hough was fined ss. and costs (us 6d.) for being drunk in Spring-street on the 12th November. P.C. Sutherland and Inspector Millington proved the case.— A tramp, named Jacob Williams, was fined ss. and costs, ss. 4d., for being drunk and disorderly in Bridge-street on the previous day.—Alice Johnson, a young woman of bad character, was convicted of using obscene language in Fryer-street on the Bth October, and was fined 103. and costs, 16s. 4d. SCHOOL ATIENDANCE.—WiIIiam Price, of Halton, was summoned by the Union School Attendance Committee for pot sending his child regularly to school, and on the evidence of Mr. Woodier he was fined 6d. and costs, 4s. 6d.

div.head: LORD SALISBURY AT OXFORD.
div.p: LORD SALISBURY AT OXFORD.

The Conference of the National Union a Conservative Associations was continued at Oxford, on Wednesday. Resolutions were passed condemning the National League and the Plan of Campaign; recording a determination to offer strenuous opposition to Disestablishment of the Church in Wales; and affirming the desirableness of pass- ' ing a Tithe Rent Marge Bill as soon as possible after the assembling of Parliament. A resolution was also carried —but only by " a clear majority "—in favour of extend- ing the Parliamentary franchise to women. In the afternoon the Marquis of Salisbury attended a meeting in Oxford Corn Exchange of delegates from many parts of the three kingdoms, who presented ad- dresses eulogising his policy. The Prime Minister, in the course of his reply, thanked the delegates for the proof they had given of unflagging zeal in the Conservative cause. On. all "present "questions—and the noble Mar- quis said he laid enormous emphasis on the word " pre- sent "—the Liberal Unionists and the Conservatives were practically one party, and it was needless to go back or i to look forward n search of questions on which he ad- mitted that grave differences might arise. Lord Salisbury addressed a large Conservative meet- ing in the evening, He thanked them for their enthusiastic reception, which he knew was enhanced by their devotion to the political cause they believed in. He , was not going to talk to them of Home Rule. The measure of Mr. Gladstone was dead; the opponents of the Union were shadowy adversaries who evaded those who would follow them up. It passed the wit of man to frame a bill that would meet at the same time the views of Sir George Trevelyan and Mr. Davitt. The Conser- vatives would not shrink from the Home Rule contest when it was placed before them properly, and until this was done he contended that the Union held the field. It was thought that the patience of the country would be .worn out by a policy of "worry," but such strategy would not answer. The English were not an impulsive but a Teutonic people, and they would not allow themselves to be worn out by obstruction, for which a remedy must be applied. He denounced the " terrible " obstruction of the Irish party, and said that any one of his colleagues in,the Cabinet was worth ,the eighty-six Parnellites together. The Government in- tended to pass a Local Government Bill for England, but hot for disloyal people who would use any extension of local government against the Queen and Parliament. He believed local elective boards ought to be allowed to deal, with the regulation of the liquor traffic, though he was willing to admit that the man who was entrusted with the Parliamentary franchise ought to be allowed to judge how much beer he should drink. There ought to be a Land Purchase Bill for Ireland—not a compulsory measure, but one which would enable the tenants and landlords to terminate dual ownership in land. While he thought there should be reform of the House 'of Commons, he L would not meet any proposal to reform the House of . Lords with a non possumus ; but whatever reform of the , Upper House might come to it would diminish the power of the House of Commons. He would like to see the tithe question settled by redemption and relief afforded i to agriculturists. He deprecated Mr. Gladstone's " shameless " bargain with Wales and Scotland to bring about Home Rule, and said that the Government were resolved to maintain law and order in London as well as , in Ireland.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER, 26, 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, NOVEMBER, 26, 1887.

(laughter and applause). As long as there was only one enrolled member of the Fair Trade League in Warrington there was not much for them to fear. (Hear, hear.) , One speaker had said that their imports exceeded their exports but he would rather their exports exceeded their imports. It was one of the fallacies of fair traders to think that be- cause they got more than they parted with they were on the way to ruin. But between 1876 and 1880 their im- ports exceeded their exports by £822,000,000, that was to say they got that amount more of goods than they parted with. During the same time they imported £147,000,000 worth of bullion and exported £144,000,000 worth, so that they had also £3,000,000 worth a bullion to the good. In all during that period they had got £622,000,000 worth of goods and £3,000,000 worth of bullion more than they had parted with. (Hear, hear.) If they had to pay for the goods they imported with money all the money in the country would scarcely pay for three months imports, and all the jewellery and plate in the country might serve them for another month' but certainly before six months were over they would have parted with every coin in the country. But trade was not carried on as the fair-trader supposed for imported goods were not paid for with money but with English goods that were exported abroad. He mentioned the in- stance of a cargo of coal worth £l,OOO when it left Car- diff for America. After the cargo had been sold the money was reinvested in a cargo of petroleum which when brought to England sold for £2,000, so that in this case double the value of the export cargo had been im- ported, and thereby a good bargain had been made by the English merchant. Yet it was because transactions of this sort were going on that fair traders said the country was going to ruin. (Laughter.) Sup- posing that a cargo had been taken from Cardiff into mid ocean and there sunk, £l,OOO worth of goods would have been exported, and nothing imported, and that ac- cording to the fair traders would have been going to prosperity. (Laughter and applause.) Towards the close of his speech, Mr. Howes forcibly and eloquently urged that reforms in connection with the land, and especially with regard to royalties and ground rents, would do more to remove the depression of trade and promote prosperity than the proposals of the fair traders. After a question or two from Mr. Diggle had been satis- factorily answered, Mr. T. Emmet'. moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Howes. As an instance of the way in which land in- creased in value in the neighbourhood of towns he al- luded to the field whereon the Whitecross works now stand. Some 16 or 17 years ago this field let for its agri- cultural price of £7 or £7 10s, but to-day, if he remem- bered rightly, something like £BO ground rent was paid for it. (Hear, hear.) Councillor numnip seconded, and the vote of thanks was heartily accorded. A similar compliment to the chairman brought the meeting to a close.

MR. HOWES ON "HOME RULE AND THE TORY . GOVERNMENT."

On The -day evening Mr. H owes addressed a crowded meeting in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- street, on "Home Rule and the Tory Government." The chair was occupied by Mr. C. S. Burgess, and amongst those by whom he was supported on the platform were Dr. Goma% Councillor W. Pierpoint, Mr. S. Barlow, Mr. Donhobbin, Mr, W. Stirrup, Mr. E.,Plinston, and others. The CHAIRMAN in introducing the lecturer, said that there was no doubt that very soon Homo Rule would become law, as all the previous measureshad become which had been advocated by the Liberal party. What had been the political history of this country for the last fifty years? One long record of Liberal triumphs. (Cheers.) Home Bele would be, as had other Liberal measures, successfully carried out. The Irish people, by their constitutionally., elected representatives, had asked for Home Rule. They were entitled 'to have it; and they would have it. s(Cheers.) If they did not get it from the Liberal party the time would come when they would get it from the Conservative party, aqd then,, probably, the Tattles would be saying "We are the peo- ple who granted Home Rule to the Irish.", • ThattwoUld be the time when Ireland was a happy, a contented, and a prosperous country. They were not now agitating in fa- vour of the two bills Mr. Gladstone introduced into the House of Commons in the spring of last year. Those bills were dead. One, they hoped, would never rise again, but the 'principle of the other one still lived—a Dublin Parliament and an Irish Executive. (Cheers.) The Tory Govertment had a record of inconsistency and incompetence, and by their blundering they were bringing upon themselves the- condemnation that they deserved. Their record Was one of tyranny and of injus- tice. The duty of the people at this critical time was clear—they must be true to their principles, true to the good old cause, and then that victory which was sure to , come would be clear and decisive. (Cheers.) Mr. HOWES, who was well received, said that since the last election every bye-election had gone in favour of the Liberal party, and there were now many indications of the opinion of the 'people of the country beDig with them in this matter. At the last election the country had not sufficient information before it, but now, when the mate for was becoming so widely ventilated it was evident that the members of the present Unionist party would have to take a dose of Home Rule medicine before their constitutions were in good order. (Laughter and cheers.) The dual party, the combination of Tories and Liberal Unionists, was an apt -illustration of the old adage that "evil communications corrupt good manners." Some of these seceding Liberals, after associating for a time with the Tories, had become more Tory than the Tories them- selves. He wanted to place the blame on the right shoulders, and he did not hold the Tory Government altogether responsible for the presentstato of things. Had It not been for this- seceding Liberals there would have been no-Tory Government and no coercion, and unfor- tunate creatures would not have been murdered in the streets of Mitchelstown. Afterthe last election the pee-' ple were surprised to find that the Goverment, instead of firmly enforcing existing laws, for a long time allowed the law in Ireland to remain in abeyance. Evictions were legal in Ireland, but the Tory Government knew that they could only have order in Ireland when the law was in abeyance, and they tried to keep it in abey- ance for the purpose of keeping the then quiet state of things in existence. The landlords, however, grew furious at this, and commenced to denounce the Government for refusing to enforce the law. Just before this the tenants plan of campaign had been inaugurated, but it • was not in Operation. Sir Michael Hicks-Beach made a speech at Bristol, and said: —" We have been putting pressure on the landlords for the purpose of inducing them to reduce their rents." Mr. Dillon and his friends thought they might help the Government a little in the way of causing pressure, and the tenants' plan of campaign was then renewed with vigour. The Government, however, thereupon became jealous, and turned round upon Mr. Dillon, threa,tening him with a prosecution for carrying on the work which Sir Michael Hicks-Beach had boasted about having in- augurated. Lord Salisbury then appointed his aristo- cratic nephew Mr. Balfour as successor to Sir Michael Hicks-Beach. That was an insult to Ireland, and a de- gradation to the office. Then came the great extreme and the policy of a coercion bill for Ireland was insisted upon. Mr. Gladstone asked for statistics of crime to jus- tify such a measure, but, said Mr. Balfour, "we do not intend to produce statistics of crive." He had not got any, that was the reason, The chArges of no fewer than thirty judges in Ireland at that time proved that there was an exceptional absence of crime. The Liberals also protested against the measure, because of the nature of it. It made the Lord Lieutenant, to all practical purposes, the king of Ireland. These men must be reminded of the lesson that Englishmen had taught others, that, if they dared to oppose the popular will, their political existence was endangered thereby. The Coercion Bill was passed and put in force. As an excuse for this, conduct the Government referred to the terrible system of boycotting springing from the plan of campaign. They contended that it was necessary to introduce a Coercion Bill to pre- vent that system becoming worse. Boycotting, he held, was an English institution, and in the first place it was taken from England to Ireland and planted there. The Coercion Bill was really passed to be used against the organisations of the tenants. Two meetings had recently been held, the recollection of which must be cherished by the voters until the next polling time, and then the voters must drop the expression of their opinion into the ballot box against the present administration, and in favour of the Liberal party. The first meeting was held at Ennis, but as there were no policemen there, there was consequently no disorder. Afterwards there came the meeting at Mitchelstown, which was a repetition of 1819, when, however, the outrage took place in Eng- land. We had succeeded in driving Tory tyranny across the channel; the next election would enable us to drive it from our shores altogether. Havirtg at some length criticised the conduct of the Government in Ireland, Mr.' Howes said that the Government were unable to sup- press the National League, because it was the National League. The people of Ireland were maintained in their struggle by the consciousness that the English demo- cracy was on their side, and because that democracy was lead by Europe's greatest statesman. (Cheers.) They had removed Mr. O'Brien from the jail among his friends to another jail where he was surrounded by enemies, and what happened? The prison walls were too thin to keepsa suit of clothes out. (Laughter.) It would be impossible to perform a feat like that in Eng- land. This showed that the movement was a national one. In Ireland the people had no sympathy with the law, because the law was against the expression of poli- tical opinion, and the delivery of political speeches. While the law went on those line, the people had no right to be in sympathy with it. If rule by the majority was good for England, it was good for Ireland also. Home Rule meant that people should manage their own affairs. That principle was sound. They could not look into the future and tell what Home Rule might lead to, but he could contend that that form of Government, in any country, would lead to wherever the 'people of that country (*sired that it should. He believed in the common sense of the people. Wherever they had been I trusted, SUCCI'M had been the result. Home Rule in the past had always succeeded and he challenged anyone 'to. instance where it had been tried and had failed'. Eng- land refused a modified system 'of Home Rule to the American colonies and lost them. Sensible men should pay attention to these lessons of history. There was never any justification for the cruel policy of the Gov- ernment, and the failure ot that policy made it still more disastrous. They could not, he urged, afford to let the Government ' • g 9 OR tinkering with national affairs

div.head: LIBERAL MEETINGS AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: LIBERAL MEETINGS AT WARRINGTON.

"THE FALLACIES OF PROTECTION." On Monday evening an address was given in Wycliffe Hall, Warrington, by Mr. Joseph Howes, the subject of the address being "The Fallacies of Protection Exposed." The chair was taken by Coun- cillor J. Platt. J.P., and there were also on the plat- form, besides Mr. Howes, Councillor W. Pierpoint, Councillor Fleming, Mr. T. Birchall, and Mr. W. Diggle. There was a large attendance. The CHAIRMAN said they were assembled there that night to hear a lecture from their friend Mr. Howes, who was already very well and favourably known to most of them, on a question which was being made a burning question in Warrington. He was glad that it was, be- cause it was a matter that wanted thrashing out, and if the Tories wished to fight the next election on the plat- form of protection they Liberals would be very much obliged, and very happy to meet them on that ground. (Hear, hear.) At the meeting addressed the other even- ing on behalf of the Fair Trade League the chair 'was taken by a gentleman who certainly had the courage of his opinions. He started at the beginning, and wanted a duty on corn. (Hear, hear.) All fair traders had not the courage of their opinions; they fought round the question, and wished to mislead as to the real issue. He (the chairman) was glad that Mr. John White came at once to the point, the point at which fair traders would have to begin, which was that a duty shottld be placed on food. (Hear, hear.) They all knew that there was not an industry in this country that was suffering worse from the effects of foreign competition than the agricul- tural industry, and that industry would naturally, as Mr. John White very well put it, have to be first con- sidered. He could very well understand why Mr. John White advocated protection for agriculture. As most of them knew, Mr. White had to do with the collecting of rents from farmers, and he (the chairman) had no doubt that just now it was not found to be a very pleasant occupation, for the very shnple reason that far- mers were not able to pay the excessive rents demanded from them. (Hear, hear.) , Not a hundred miles from Warrington—he would not mention names, although he had no doubt that some of them knew to whom allusion

was made—farmers had had to have bailiffs put in pos- session of their farms, and. one of the farmers had had to leave his farm leaving behind stock, crop, implements, and in fact everything on the ground to satisfy the claims of the land- lord. (Hear, hear.) He had no doubt, therefore, that it would be a very nice thing for Mr. John White to have things put upon a more pleasant basis, that was to say, to have farmers protected. But protection all round, was wanted, and consequently those farmers who did not grow much corn, but who fed up cattle, would naturally want a duty on beef, and the food of the people would be taxed in every direction if they once beegan with it. But what would be the effect of it ? Supposing a tax were put upon agricultural produce coming into this country, such as corn beef,' cheese, and so on, the first effect of it would be that the landlords would get their rents very much easier,: because farmers, if protected, ' wottki be wore able to pay. Rents had been coming down of late, and they would still have to come down, because land had been let ' very much ale )ve itf value. I (Hear, hear, and applauseAlßut if this nice little scheme of protection was put into operation there would be no need for rents to come down, and in feet they would go up and the landlords would be the first to get the advan- tage of it. Fame which are now unlet because of the rents demanded, would then be let and the landlords would pocket the benefit, and farms on which 25 or 30 per cent. reduction are allowed on the rents would then pay the full rent. He would ask them at the outset if they were prepared to tax theinselve,s for the benefit of the landlords. ("No.") Well, that was the plaint truth of the matter, if they went to. the bottom of it. (Hear, hear.) If agricultural produce were protected it would mean that throughout the land the British taxpayer would be taxing himself for the benefit of the landlords. He was very sorry for some of the landlords at the present moment, but, looking at the landlords as a whole, they had not all got 'tle worst end of the stick. There was land in Warrington—and they need not go farther than' Sankey-street to look for it—which was let at the the present time for one hundred times more than it was worth twenty years ago. These landlords ought to help their brethren m distress. , (Hear, hear, and laughter.) He thought if anybody was to be taxed for the suffering landlords, it ought to be the landlords who were getting the better part of it. At all events he did not think the British nation would be so foolish as to tax itself for the benefit of landlords either in this country or in Ireland. (Hear, hear' and applause.) He was of opinion that the landlords ought to be left to defend their own in- terests. Those whose rents had increased in value had got the benefit of it, while those whose rents were going down through the operation of the law of supply and de- mand ought to stand by it. (Applause.) There were other interests besides the landlord interest in this coun- try, and the nation could not afford to tax itself for the benefit of any one class. (Applause.) Mr. John White, however, said he wanted protection all round. But it would not be practicable. There were trailes in this ',country which did not need protection; there were trades that protection Would not help. kllear, hear.) He might just instanc,o the trade With which he had to do, that of the manufacture of velveteens. Protection would not help him or the people in his employ, because they had no outside competition from abroad. So they would see that protection all round was utterly unworkable. He for his part was not' prepared to tax himself, or to tax the people who would have to suffer, that was, the work- ing classes, for the benefit of the landlord interest. (Loud applause.) Mr. JOSEi% HOWES, who was received with loud ap- plause, said he proposed that night to deal with that ex- traordinary meeting held a few nights ago in Warring- ton ; a meeting that was extraordinary because of the peculiar nature of the speeches delivered thereat. He thought he should be able to show them that the speeches at the meeting he referred to contained a great deal of rhetoric and very- little of fact, a great de.al of assertion but no proof, and that the speakers begged the very question they proposed to discuss. But before he called attention to those speeches, which were good speeches from their point of view, as they proved the strength of their position better than he could prove it, he wished to refer to the state of things. which existed in Warrington in reference to the Tory party. The last general election was fought on the question of Home Rule, and because there was a great deal of confusion in the public mind, and, as they thought, because of the want of information concerning the principle of the matter, and the facts in its support, the country for the time being went against them. Since then, however, they had been editcating the cenntr,v; and evei'y by-elec- tion since the - general election had gene in their favour without 'a single exception. (Applause.) Their Tory opponents knew that Home Rule would be a most difficult issue to face at the next general election in this town, and theref6re they came and talked to them about Fair Trade instead, (Hear, hear.) The Tory party dare not face the ques- tion of Home Rule owing to the peculiar nature of the constituency, so they wanted to turn the ques- tion on one , side, and to raise another issue by which they hope to maintain the seat at the next contest. He took it, however, that the electors of the constituency would insist on dealing with the ques- tion of Ireland at the next election. (Hear, hear, and applause.) The most important part of the Protection- ist meeting he had referred to was the reading of a let- ter b3fore any speaker was called upon. But although that letter was more important than all the speeches, the curious thing about it was that none of the speakers re- ferred to the letter. (Laughter.) This letter was writ- ten by Mr. J. C. Parr who wrote—" I think that Fair Trade to be fair trade must embrace all trades and in- dustries alike, and that to give protection to the artisan and manufacturers while fou deny it to the agricultural-, ist would be manifestly unfair?' That, continued Mr. Howes, was exactly their case. Protection was either good or bad. The principle of protection could not be both good and bad. If it was good everybody ought to have it; if it was good they ought to get as much of it as they could. If it was good everybody should be protected, and-not only one country protected against another country, but one town against another town. They -anted to protect us against America, but who were in America but their brothers, their cousins, and other relatives. If he was to be protected against his brother in Americas why should he not lao protected against his brother on this side of the Atlantic? (Hear, hear.) At the Protectionist meeting they said that if protection did make bread dearer the working-men Would have Moro money to buy it with, and one of the speakers said that the cheapest loaf was to be had in the workhouse, and yet none of them liked that loaf. But he (Mr. Howes) replied to that that if the loaf outside the workhouse began to be dearer there would be more applying for that inside. (Lan,gh- ter and applause.) They, however, never attempted to show how protection would cause a working-man to have a higher wage and he contended that instead of their wages increasing they would decrease, while all the time food was getting dearer. . He pointed out that the protection of agriculturists would simply lead to an increase in rents, as was the ease when corn used to sell at 90s a quarter. He should like to know whether their Tory protectionists would guarantee that the landlords would not increase their rents under protection, for in that case the farmers would in the end be no better off, (Heart hear.) Referring to the effects of protection in the case of other trades, Mr. Howes remarked that whenever they increased the price of an article they limited the demand for that article. It mattered not whether the article was a 41b. loaf or a locomotive en- gine. When locomotives were dearer railway porn- panies restricted their operations, but immediately mate- rial became cheaper they took advantage of that cheap- ness' to extend their operations. AM wherever they limited the demand for an article they threw working peeple out of employment. It was the interest of the wage-earning class that the bulk of trade should be in- creased as much as possible, but if they limited the de- mand for articles they reduced the bulk of trade, work- ing people were thrown out of work, and the wages of those who had work were reduced. (Hear, hear.) That was where protection all round led them to. (Hear, hear.) The chairman of the Tory meeting said th.g he was the only enrolled member of this National Fair i'recle League in Warrington. That spoke well for Warrington,

any longer. Coercion could not heal the breach ;it could not remove the wrong. Ireland was spoken of as the sister isle. The "sister isle" lay bleeding at the feet of England. A good Samaritan came by and poured oil into the wound, and bandaged it, but the terrible Tory Government tore off the bandages, and inflicted more wounds still. It was time that they lifted their sister up, it was time that they treated her as a sister. (Cheers.) Hold Ireland' to England as firmly as they liked, but let it be done with a bond of affection —a bond stronger far than coercion. (Cheers.) They were the real Unionists, and thosewhowished toperpetu- ate coercion were enemies to mankind, and not friends. Let them have unity, remove the strife, dismiss the Tory Government, call back their old physician, and he would treat the patient in a different manner, and with a different result. (Cheers). Councillor W. PIERPOINT said that he stood on that platform next to a man who had been designated not only an advanced Liberal, but a Radical, and he was proud to be able to say: after listening to the words of Mr. Howes, that he was ready to place himself in the same rank with Mr. Howes. (Cheers.) He would ad- vise all present to think calmly on this great Irish ques- tion, which must be settled according to the wishes of the Irish people. Then there would be a contented Irish nation, which would prove an element of strength to the Empire. He had great pleasure in proposing a vote of thanks to Mr. Howes for his lecture. Mr. E. PLINSTON seconded the proposition, which WES carried with applause. A vote of thanks having been accorded to the chair- man, on the proposition of Mr. HOWES, seconded by Dr. GORNALI., the meeting was brought to a conclusion.

WIDN73B v. BrAcxson.—Widneal had arranged to play Kendal at Widnes on Saturday, but in consequence of the policy of retrenchment, recently carried out by the Kendal club, the match was cancelled, and Widnes in consequence arranged with Blackrod, who turned up with only fourteen men and one or two second team Men amongst these. Widnes, however, had by no means their best team. Owing to an accident last week T. Hughes, their best forward, was unable to play, and Fogg and Howard were also unable to play. Notwith- standing these disadvantages, the home team, who are are now playing in splendid form, won by two goals, three tries, and two minors, to nil. The ground was hard owing to the recent frost, and made running rather more difficult than usual, but that did not mar the pleasure of either players or spectators to any considerable extent. Smith, the Widnes captain, kicked off down 's the slope, and the home players rushed the leather to the quarter, whence Barker ran into his opponents' fortress in splendid style, and secured a try near the touch line. Kiddie failed to improve. A few minutes later S. Bingham made a splendid drop at goal from Blackred half, and the leather hit the cross-bar and re- bounded into play. The attack, however, was kept pp, and Kiddie sucteeded in obtaining a try, from which Farrell placed a fine goal. Just before half-time Farrell secured a third try-, but the position was a difficult one, and Kiddie's kick again failed. During the second half Widnes again kept the ball continually on their opponents' line, and Barker and Hardman gained tries, Farrell placing the ball neatly over the bar on one occasion, and Widnes added two touchd)wns.* Barker made, a splendid drop at goal, the sphere missing by an ace. Throughout the home team had matters pretty much their own way, though the visitors played a very plucky and defensive game. Teams: Widnes—S. Bingham, back ; Plumpton, Parkin- son, and Barker, three-quarter backs; Farrell and Wil- kinson, half backs; Smith (captain), Kiddie, Hardman, Sampson, J. Bingham, Pennington, Gandy, Woods, and Barber, forwards. Blackrod—Dawber9 back; Mod- calf, Moran, and Foster, three-quarter backs; Grimshaw and Keeley, half backs • Hampson, Hough, Collier, Big- son, Cudden, Fenningtc:n, Ainscough, and Hargreaves, forwards.

div.head: WARRINGTON V. ASPTILL.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. ASPTILL.

This match was played at Warrington on Saturday, before a fair attendance of spectators. Considering the severe frost of the last few days, the ground was in splendid Condition and a good ,garne was anticipated. It 'will be remembered that the Aspull team opened the season of the local club, and suffered defeat by one goal, two tries, and two minors, to three minors, but on that ocasion they Were only weaklr represented, whilst the Warringtonians mustered their full strength. On Sat- urday each player on the Warrington side had a badge of crape on the arrn as a mark of respect to the late Captain Reynolds, who was a vice-president of the War- rington Football Club. The home tettin fell short of their usual men, Massey, Warren, and Rigby, being absentees; the Aspullites turning up in their full strength. At 345, Warrington having lost the toss, Frank Tur- ner started the game and a good return was made by Birchall, Ashton making his mark at centre. This took play to the visitors' quarter-flag, and from a subsequent scrimmage Speakman passed to Barnes, who handed Over to Daniels only to see that player well held by Morris. Seddon here relieved his lines by a timely kick in the Warrington twenty-five, and for a few minutes the home team were forced to act on the defen- sive. Antrobus, however, relieved his side brilliaAtly by a good run and pass to Barnes, who put in a huge kick to midfield, Dillon spoiling the return. An- trobus was again prominent with a neat run, but spoiled a chance by holding the leather too long. Morris trans- ferred the game again to the Warrington litfts, and from a grand return by Nevins, Seddon made his mark, but nothing came off it. Nevins was here applauded for an- other smart punt, and Speakman took play again to the Aspull twenty-five. The brothers Lindsay got away, but Jolley stopped their career at centre. Speakman, from a scrimmage formed here, passed neatly to Barnes, the latter making a good run and kick to Pilkington,. and, following up splendidly, again secured poS session close to the touchline, passing in midfield to his forwards only to see the ball mulled when there was a certain chance of scoring. Dillon almost got over, but the As- pullites relieved their lines, and by a grand rush trans- ferred the game to the Warrington territory,*Nevine only finding relief by touching doWn linlme returned the drop out, but Povey came through the pack with a neat dribble to midfield. Barnes had his kick charged down, and the visiting team again threatened danger, but Nev- ins was safe. Seddon next made a drop at goal, a minor only resulting. Franit Turner dropped- out, and from the return by Huline the Warringtonians were again forced to act on the defensive, and Jolley was compelled to concede a minor. After this succession of minorS the home team rallied. All their efforts,, however, were in vain, for the Aspull men played desperately hard for a

major point, Barnes kicking dead in the nick of time. I Exchange kicking by Morris and Nevin a ended in favour of the latter, and shortly afterwards Antrobus got away from the pack, only to, find himself in the arms of Cart- wright. Not to be denied, he again got away and trans- ferred to Fair. Turner, and that player to Jolley, who punted over the line, Pilkington saving. The lattet dropped out, only to see Barnes run the leather back to the Aspull line. He, however, had parted with the ()Val to Fair. Turner, who was just held on the line. Half- time was called with the game in dangerous proximity to the Aspull goal, the score reading—Warrington one minor to Aspull five minors. Lindsay re-started from the centre, and Barnes put in a dodgy run to neutral ground. Seddon made a useful kick to Nevins, who was collared before he could part with the ball, and play raged on he Warrington lines, Morris adding another minor to the Aspull score by a huge kick over the line. From a free kick awarded Aspull, Povey and Pavies ran the leather to midfield, and pretty exchange kicking by Jolley, Daniels, Pilkington, and Seddon ended in Barnes making his mark, but it gained little. The game raged at neutral ground, and by dint of hard work the Warrington forwards promin- ent amongst others being Littlewood and Frani. Turner, took the leather to the Aspull limes. A bad pass let in the cupholders, who relieved to the Warrington quarter Rag. The leather was soon after taken over the home team's line, Nevins saving. ,Give-and-take play fol- lowed from the drop out, and Jolley put in a strong run, but the Warrington team were again pressed, and anot.4er minor was added to the already long list. Daniels failed to get a kick of Seddon's away, but a splendid chance 'was spoiled by Frank Turner kicking in touch when all opposition had been passed. sßarnes next put in a neat run and pass to Jolley, but the tackling of the visitors was too safe. The home team captain next made his mark, and play continued in the Aspull quar- ters. Cartwright got away, but Barnes replied. Give- and-take play followed from now up to the call of time, and after seventy minutes' hard work, the game re- mained drawn, Aspull scoring eight minors to Warring- ton one minor.

The game was far from 'pleasant, being chiefly &nflned to the forwards. The pick of the Warrington team were undoubtedly. Barnes and Nevins, the latter having the bulk of the work. In the forwards, Povey, Dillon, and Fair. Turner were the most prominent. On the Aspull side, Seddon was the best of the backs, his kicking greatly assisting his side. The broth brs Lindsay and Hesketh also played well. The following were the teams 4—Warrington: Full back, Nevins; three-quarter backs, Jolley, Barnes (eap- tain), and Daniels ; half backs, Antrobus and Speakman; forwards, Ashton, Fair. Turner, Frank Turner, Davies, Littlewood, Povey, Haye:s, Craghan, and W. Dillon. Aspull : Full back, J. Pilkington ; three-quarter backs, E. Mona, J. Seddon, and W. Birchall ; half backs, D. Hulme and J. Cartwright (captain); forwards, T. Hee- keth, T. Monks, H. Bramwell, John Lindsay, James Lindsay, Catterall, G. Croston, G. Dempsey, and J. Grundy. Umpires, Messrs Gilbert and Seddon. Referee, Mr. Hall, Oldham F.C,

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
LAND AT ACTON GRANGE.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday,before Messrs. C. Reynolds and J. Handley, o. case of some importance was Mentioned. The facts of the case were that Mr.lhomas Ball holds a yearly tenancy of the Acton Grange Farm, under Sir Richard Brooke, and the Manchester Ship Canal Company re- quire a portion of land for the purpose of making the waterway. The company and Mr. Ball, being unable to agree as to terms, a summons was issued against the latter with a view to assessing the amount to be paid as compensation before the jus- tices. Considerable interest appeared to be mani- fested in the proceedings, Mr. Bradbury (instructed by Messrs Grundy, Kershaw, and Co.) appearing in support of the claim of the Ship Canal Company, and Mr. Pickford (instructed by Mr. T. J. Ridgway, of Warrington) for Mr. Ball. A lengthy consulta- tion took place, and Mr. Bradbury informed the ' Benph that it was decided to adjourn the case, as there were certain things that the Manchester Ship Canal Company had agreed to do that were absolutely in the hands of the contractor. If the contractor failed to carry these out the summons could be brought afresh. He merely asked for the summons to be adjourned, and not dismissed, as some arrangement might be arrived at in the mean- time.—The Chairman: Sine die?—Mr. Bradbury: Yes.—The hearing of the summons was then ad- journed sine die PREPARATIONS AT LATCHFORD.

Active preparations are now being made for a commencement with the work of construcing the Ship Canal in the neighbourhood of Warrington. During the present week a considerable Contingent of workingmen has been busily engaged unloading contractor's material at Latchford,Station. Amongst the machinery which has already been brought into the locality is a steam navvy, new from the hands of the makers, and evidently capable of doing effec- tive work. There is in addition a locomotive, a por- table engine, azi a travelling crane, also new, the whole plant being evidently worth some thousands of pounds. On Friday the portable engine was taken by road to Acton Grange, where it will, no doubt, soon be in active use. It is intended. we understand, to lay with as little delay as possible a siding from Latchford station to the canal 'which 'already belongs to the Ship Canal Company. The route of the siding will cross Wash-lane, and being mostly in the borough, no doubt the sanction of the Corporation will b 3 required. \ This siding will make it possible for all the machinery needed to carry out the works in this locality, to be lifted direct from the railway waggons on to barges by means of which it may, be , expeditiously conveyed either along the canal or the, river to the point where it is required. From what we can gather it is probable that active oper- ations, as far as the Warrington section is concerned, will be first begun in the neighbourhood of Moore or Acton Grange, and, we believe, Mr. Walker, the contractor who has undertaken the construction a the work, was in that district on Wednesday. Ex- tpnaive orders for implements and other material have, we are informed, been placed with various tradesmen in Warrington and neighbourhood, and the spade manufactory at Stockton Heath, which is in the possession of Mr. P. Caldwell. is to be ex- tended.

div.head: FIRST FATALITY.
div.p: THE FIRST FATALITY.

The Manchester Ship Canal Company have, as is well known, commenced operations at Eastham, where a very large number of men and avast quan- tity of plant are at present employed. Among the machinery brouglAt down by the Ship Canal Com- pany are fifty locOmotive engines, which are run OA far as Hooton on the lines, and then tra,ns- ferred to lurries built specially for their con- veyance and taken on to Eastham. In connec- tion with this branch of the work' an accident occurred on Wednesday, which resulted in the death of a foreman, or ganger, employed •by the Canal Company. This man, who was named Forbes, was assisting in the operation of lifting a locomo- tive from the railway lines on to one of the large lorries, and was directing the work from the level of the line. An engine was engaged in shunting a number of waggons to the siding, where the leco- motive was placed, and it being rather foggsmit the time, the driver, evidently unable to see any ob- struction on the rails, shunted a truck down the line in the directioy of Forbes. " The poor fellow was caught between the buffers of the truck and engine, and was terribly crushed about the lower part of the body. Dr. Bredin, a gentleman it one time resident surgeon at the Bootle Borough Hospital, but now engaged in practice at Sutton, was at once called to the injured man, whom lie conveyed to the Hooton Station Hotel. He rendered every 'assistance pos- sible, and staved with Forbes during the geater part ,of the night. ht all was unavailing, and he died on Thursday morning at nine o'clock. There is a feel- ing among the employees of the company that a hospital of some sort should be provided in the neighbourhood, for with nearly 4,900 men at work —as there will presently be—it is certain that a number of accidents will occur, to meet which there is at present no accommodation.

SIR WILLIAM HARCOURT AT LANCASTRII.—A conference of the representatives of the Liberal Associations in North Lancashire„ and the adjoining constituencies of Yorkshire and Westmoreland was held on Tuesday at Lancaster, undeit the presidency 'of Mr. Schnadhorst. Resolutions weie passed defining the attitude and work of the Liberal party, particularly with regard to Ireland. Sir William Harcourt, in the course of a speech support- ing the Nottingham prograrnine, said that the attempts to alienate Liberals from the cause of Mr. Gladstone were failing. In the evening a great meeting v,-as held in the Winter Gardens at Morecambe, under the presi- dency of Mr. Williamson, M.P. The principal speaker was Sir William Harcourt, who, in alluding to Mr. Gos- chen's recent speeches, said that since the election in 1886 I the history of the electorate in Lancashire was that it ! had been the battlefield of Liberal victory and the scene of Unionist defeat. Sir William drew an amusing pic- ture of the reception Lord Hartington would meet with in Dublin, and gave a forecast of the speech which, his lordship may be expected to deliver and in conclusion expressed himself confident of the ultimate victory of the great cause On which the great bulk of the English and Irish people had set their heart. "Sir Joshua Reynolds's, Discourses," is the issue for November in the Camelot series published by Mr. Walter Scott. There .is an introduction by Helen Zimmerli, which furnishes a brief but intensting account of tha great painter's career. It is a great compliment to Rey- nolds's power as a writer as shown in these discourses (which were delivered from year to'year to the studenta of the Royal Academy, of which he was the first presik dent) that it was thought by, some critics of the day that they were the work of either Samuel Johnson or Edmund Burke. Tilt: style, without being so ornate ani flowing as that of Johnson has much of the beauty anr dignity which characterised the writings of Burke. But, above all, the Discourses are weighted with thought a* the evidence of close observation. The general reat will find much in the volume tcrplease whil; the student of art it will always be a delight treasure. • th* " Diprose's Annual for 1888" is likely to keeP Init front rank of Christmas numbers—not so much teat ." rw early in the field, as that its stories and illustrations_a of a good quality. The cover is adorned with thi7; portraits of European Rulers—" thirteen Sovereigns a shilling," and there is, within, a brief sketch of the,tled of each of these monarchs. The first story is ~0. Mr. Dale has a special faculty for dealing e with events of the flesh-creeping kind; and it is feral_ s due to him to say that, unlike many writers of the senw-a. tional order, he so dove-tails incidents as t,o at all all times an air of reality. There is as much in eors, of these tales as would supply Mr. Word-Windy Iris"; " , material for a three-novel volume. There are lair stories, and their titles are--' • The cremated gheels'“ "A golden ring or a hempen cord," "At his owln,-- . quest," "The swimming ghost." "The ivy alid , oak," "Fanny's faith," and "Damon and Pythias." " Hood's Comic Annual" has now reached tl,l tweetieth year of its existence, and it is strong an e , brisk as over. It is published by Messrs. Dalziel Bro" thers, who are a hest in themselv,es. Mr. Go°,l4° -• ' Dalziel contributes some verse " The sea," and a chan, teristic sketch-" The wrong man," the latter I vigorously illustrated by Mr. ,Thomes Dalziel. There "g . a long and brilliant list of writers, whose contributnhee arefor the most part brilliant without being long. " lost author," by Mr. George R. Sims," is, like most his productions, exceedingly clever. It is a capital" tass'r off" of the style and general treatment of the asituYs of " She, and whoever has ,read that wild Story enjoy the fun of "The adventures of Mr. Horeenw- Guant." "How Tim Denby went's-courting " is a or. sant, lively story by Mr. George MenviLle Fenn ; but Annual is full of pleasant, lively things, in story, "re'-' and illustration. With regard to the latter, the revss7,a will be puzzled to understand how so much that is fr.-- • can be provided for a shilling. d • a Bow Dells Almanac, published by Mr. John Dicksets,s storehouse of useful information, and it is, sss, rePlel with some striking portraits of eminent persons, atn°nA whom may be mentioned those of Sir It. Haneon ( Jubilee Mayor of ,London), Lady Randolph Church' ' Right Hon. Arthur Balfour, Lord Harris, General langer, and Queen Kapiolani. div.head: Salthouse-lane, Hull,
div.p: Salthouse-lane, Hull,
March 14,

Dear Fred.—You will be surprised at receiving a letter from me, but, thank God, I am pleased to say I am getting better every say. I shall be so glad to breathe the fresh air again. It less seemed a dreadful long time to be in bed. You know I was taken to the hospital last April to be treated for Bright's Disease of the kidneys. Well, on July 31 they tapped me, and 'took away 304 ounces of water. The same thing. was +done again on September 18, and 408 ounces of water /obtained. On Oct. 9 I was discharged from the host pital as incurable. In January this year (the 20th) was again tapped at home,ttnd 360 ounces of water taken away. The St. Bartholomew's Hospital in London ,refused me admission as a hopeless case, and the Stt Bart holom e w's Hospital, Chatham, also refused me,' ae being the worst ease they had seen for years, and two local doctors gave me up as hopeless. When I came from the hospital it took three to put me to bed. My clothes had to be cut off. I was an object a misery and despair. After the hospitals had refused me, and doctors given roe up, my wife persuaded me to try HOP BITTERS, and from the commencement have Improved daily. I have only taken them seven weeks, and can now get,downstairs and walk about without even a stick. With the aid of a few more bottles of the Bitters shall be well again. The water has left my ibody and legs. The only trace left is in my feet. It is a wonderful medicine. I wish I had tried it sooner, as I have nearly ruined myself and family with doctors' bills and other expenses. I might have been well long ago. At the hospital rhad no appetite. whatever, but .since using the Bitters eat everything with a relish. The only difficulty is the expense, but must not mind tat so long as lam getting well. Am cheerful now that recovery is near, for every one had given me up as a bad job.—With best wishes
"Your affectionate brother,

IN THE STEERAGE ON BOARD THE • STEAM SHIP EGYPT. BY, H. VY HITHAM.

jI cannot exactly tell you exactly where we are just ati this moment of writing, but there is an opinion floating about that we are somewhere neat New- foundland. However that may be, I can assure you that my immediate surroundings are enough to shake nerves considerably stronger than mine. German Jews, Polish Jews, and every other sort of filthy lousy Jews, are either,calling on the Duke of Argyle, or jabbering so much as to make this most salubrious steerage a perfect bedlam. Two of ihy daughters are holding the lamp, and the deal board I am sat at rocks like—well not quite so bad as I have been rocked during the past 12 days. I should like to tell you of my experience in a ship's steer- age; but something else has impressed itself so , much on my mind that I must speak of it first. I have read many a sketch of voyages to New York, but I think I do not remember a sketch from the, steerage which contained so 'much eventful matter as has been crowded into so short a space of time. Leaving Liverpool on October 27th, it was late in the evening of the 28th when we reached Queenstown, in which splendid bay we rode until late on Saturday afternoon, when off we started into the boisterous Atlantic. Leaving Ireland's dreary and unhappy shores, we saw before us no welcome—no- thin.' but a threatening sea, find a sky that con- t,aine'd a power which before long we felt with a vengeance. I ata but a landlubber, Mr. Editor, but from the captain down to the ordinary "A. 8. there is lrit one opinion, and that is that 'for a number of years no stormier passage has been made across the Atlantie ocean. Scarcely had we left lax.d when we encountered what was called

div.head: WHITE SQUALL.
div.p: A WHITE SQUALL.

I thought it was a fearful black one. Sunday and Monday the sea was simply terrific, our yeas(' seemed to be engaged with all the powers of dark- ness at once; one constant struggle on the part of the engine to keep the Stern out of some horrid pit. What with the creaking of our bunks, in which we were cooped up, and the groaning of the engines and the rush to prayers of all the Jews on the ship, I should think there was matter enough for another " Inferno," were another Dante forthcoming. Well, thanks to a good ship, we pulled through until Tuesday at midnight, when both engine and storm came to terms, and both stopped. All Wednesday we drifted about, but out of our course. No one knew what was amiss, only that the engines had broken down. • So it was, and it was soon noised about that a petition to tl 4 Captain was afoot, but it was given up. Oh! what a dreary day, no on knowing what the next move was to be. Ultimately, we started again; so did the storm. No sooner did we get under weigh, and nicely, off, than the sea began to get lumpy. From lumps we got to , mountains, and until the storm culminated in blowing the wheel house and bridge away, I think few men's experience was more comprehensive of down-right misery than that of the few men, women, and children cooped up in this hole of a steerage den. My bunk was just under the wheel house, and -when it went, the sea rushed in in torrents. I certainly thought the end had come, and with my wife and the baby, I rushed to the ladder, knee deep, amidst screaming and noises from above enough to appal the stoutdst. We were met by the officers hurrying to pacify us, and tell us all , was right. Not very right, sir,‘ when serious consultation was held as to taking to the boats. There we sat, women in their night dresses ; such a sight! and I the only ,man out in it all. Well, the proverbial peace followed even this storm, but what a sight on deck next morning; plenty of work for carpenters;but still a stout ship. Slow she is witliout a doubt, but I think, and hope, sure. The peace, alas I Was accompanied with

ANOTHER BREAKDOWN, and I May here say that at this. date, November Bth, we have lost three days through breakdowns. Just previous to my sitting down, a White Star ship passed us like a greyhound, having left Liverpool some days after us. For the present I must leave the voyage; we have a thousand miles to run. Many a thing may happen, and you may not see this letter. I have it in my mind to say something of the ,

STEPER&OR CATERING. It is simply detestable. The wide difference between steerage and saloon is, of course, very striking. But there I will leave this subject, or I could fill columns of your paper. More than this, I protest against good honest Englishmen and women being closed in with these filthy Jews, creeping with lice, their eyes and fingers on everything you have. It is simply impossible to turn your back. If you do, something will be gone. I have all my life tried to nurse a Cosmopolitan feeling, but ugh! lam dead beat with these lousy sons of Abra- ham. Good night, Mr. Editor, and good night to all friends at home. I'll take hold of the pen again whett we see land.

div.head: LAND AT LAST.
div.p: LAND AT LAST.

Nov. 14.—Only thO;a7l;vic.f; have the tossing and know the weariness of a voyage extended to nearly a fortnight longer than calculated upon can understand the pleasure with which the ,cry of " land "is heard. During the past seven or eight days, splendid weather has helped us on our way. Once only have we had something excit- ing. A sudden squall: found us with all sail full set'; a squall not to. be forgotten; the very heavens seemed falling,,upon us.' The sea swept, the deck, the wind gathered in the sails, and for a few moments it was doubtful, even to the captain, which vf afl going prti- vail—the elements or . skill.. The ship was lifted right out of the sea, and dashed down in such a fashion, that sailors afterwards said we were within the possibility of foundering. Thanks to the slow old tub, we righted. It seems some of the cording or pulleys attached to the sails would not -svork, and so prevented the captain's orders from beingf carried out. Here let me say that Captain Summit. LS one of t ngland's best and cheeriest sailors, a man well behved by both crew and passengers, and one who has always a kind word for the humblest of those on board. In fact, the crew seem to be well selected for civility, and an anxious desire to minister to the comfort of all seems to prevail. And now .

A LAST WORD or two on the steerage, and its surroundings. It will be well understood that, when people arrange for a voyage of eight or nine days, and it is protracted to nearly three weeks, great disappointments must follow. Each party seems to carry with them a few luxuries. These all run out, and then the ship's stores are hunted out in every possible fashion, wise and btherwise. Any one coming out should lay in a store of apples and sweetbreads, tea, and sugar ; for what is provided is only eatable by a select few. Biscuits are a welcome addition to a bit of ' good cheese, and a few pickles, when, the first few days of sickness are over. Then it is that the steerage becomes sweeter, to obtain whiali desirable state of things no ;pains are spared. Each forenoon the whole tribe are bundled on deck, and a staff of scrubbers and swillers set to with a will, with soft soap and brushes, and under the superintendence of the chief steward soon make all as clean as possible. Of course, a voyage in November is a very different affair to one undertaken in the sum- mer months. Passengers during the latter months can lounge in sunny corners on deck. Baskitig in the sun, they can read, smoke, and chat, but in our case shelter from sleet, hail, and bitter winds could only be thought of—hot obtained. Fug nit IllVlfterage is a part of the.vessel boarded ott so as to make at oo- long space something like six yards wide by 12 yards long. Thisis divided into six cabins; each cabin is divided into 12 bunks. On One side are placed single women; on the other the married folks. Dressing and undressing are matters for much serious consideration, and only accomplished after a little manceuvring, con- sidering there are nearly 50 women and children yelling and bawling night and morning. But all things con- sidered, the troubles are surmounted very fairly. I do think the contrast between the saloon and the steerage is too great. What money can buy and what a want of it deprives people of is seen on board a ship, if anywhere. I and my family have not had anything to grumble at. So far as food went, we gave salt junk and butterine wide, very wide birth, and any friends coming over will do well to gain a little private knowledge ere starting, as it will be useful. During the voyage we have been passed by several of the fast' steamers, but the pilot, who is now with us, tells us that they have had much worse luck than ourselves, in one case several men having been swept overboard, and some killed. Our only personal casualties have been severe bruises, one broken arm, and one or twn black eyes, my wife having one lovely black eye, quite artistic in its way. Of course, as I have told you, the ship car- ries very good evidence of ,her past troubles, and from all I,hear she ought never to have left Liverpool in the statfi she was. Her shafts were not in first Tate sea- going order; nor yet is there a joint in the ship tip- top, unless in the butcher's And now farewell for a term to all my good friends. I want to go above, where a sea like glass meets the eye, studded all over With craft -Of various kinds. We are within a few hours of Castle Gardens, and then more trouble ; but never mind, "All's well that ends well." P.S.—I may say my companions on the voyage are well and hearty; in fact the twelve of us are all right for landing.
