PENNY DINNERS. 1 Sir,—Will you kindly allow me a little space in your \ valuable paper for a few facts 'about Penny Dinners? For the last three weeks these have been given regularly at Hamilton-street School, and have been much appreci- ated both by parents and children. The advantages of the plan are :-1. It does not pauperise, the recipient simply obtaining a fair return for his money. 2. It enables mothers who are obliged to go out charing, washing, &c., to provide their children with a good, hot, and wholesome meal, instead of putting them off with a piece of bread. 3. It enables children to ` obtain one really good meal in the day at a very low cost. More I could add, but I must not trespass too much upon your space. I believe this to be one of the best ways possible of helping the

poor. In the past three weeks we have provided over 1,000 dinners. The dinner is given at twelve o'clock each day, except Saturday and Sunday; the boys in the boys' school, and the girls in the girls' school. It consists of such dishes asslnsh stew, soup, pudding, bread and and cocoa, &c. Several ladies kindly take it in turns to wait upon the children, and any of your readers who would like to come and see for themselves what is going on will be very welcome. Scarcely a day passes without my finding some children who have not tasted food until they get their dinner, and it is worth all the trouble to see the relish with which it is eaten. , Now, sir, in the hope that some of your readers may be willing to help on this good work, let me state plainly how they can do so. (1) I want a few more helpers, either ladies or gentlemen. (2) I want donations to meet a small weekly deficit, which must occur until the numbers of the school and consequently of the dinners increase. (3) I shall be thankful for gifts in kind, e.g., anything that will make into soup, vegetables, apples, jam, bread, &c. (4) There are some children who have neither pence nor dinners. If any one will give me a , small sum for these I will undertake that it shall be be- stowed upon really deserving cases. Perhaps some of us as we sit down to our own comfortable dinners will as a grace put aside a few pence for these hungry little ones. I shall be happy to acknowledge and account for all sums, sent me.—l am, dear sir, faithfully yours, MORLEY STEVENSON. The Training College.

MR. PEERS AND THE PENKETH MUTUAL IM- PROVEMENT ASSOCIATION. Sir,—ln reference to the somewhat sarcastic letter on the above society which appeared in your last issue. I would in the first place desire to enter my protest against the habit of taking up space in public prints, and the public time and attention by childishly) ventilating fan- cied personal wrongs. Surely there are sufficient sub- jects of general interest with which to fill our newspapers that we can well spare the details of the disappointment sustained by Mr. Peers in attempting to carrya resolu- tion devoid both of point and sense in a villageimprove- ment society. This, however,. must not be interpreted into a hesitancy on my part to stand by all I have said or done in this matter. At the meeting this week I have already shown what Mr. Peers might have known, that, instead of desiring to smother what he calls" incon- venient facts and statements," I have been and still am desirous of hearing them. It was then decided on my motion that a special evening should be set aside fof the members to have an opportunity of further hearing Mr. Peers' views and his answer to the very vague question —"The text or its. expounders, which ?" Mt. Peers somewhat haughtily challenges me to show why the resolution, which appears for the first time in his letter, and which, of course, I had never before seen or heard of, should not be submitted to a Christian audience. He might as well challenge me to prove that the man in the moon, whom I have not seen, does not believe in the in- spiration of the Bible. It is as amusing as it is new for me to find myself re- presented as one who fears investigation into orthodox theology. I have in the past done so much in investiga- ting the beliefs and teachings of our religion, and so often differed from the generally accepted doctrines, that to find myself posed as a defender fearing attack is curi- ously strange. I would, however, remark that in the points wherein I have not agreed, I have always tried to state that disagreement ma clear and straightforward manner. I have never attempted by insinuation and resolution to get my opponents to take up an apparently innocent but false position that afterwards I might have the unworthy pleasure of knacking the platform to • which I invited them from beneath their feet. In conclusion, let Mr. Peers state his case and his be- lief in a definite, straightforward, and sincere manner, and I assure him that he will get perfect fair pray- from the meinberS of the above society, and from yours, kc tenketh, ...Tovember 25th, 1881,
C. E. PARSER.

THE NEW ARRANGEMENT AT THE LIBRARY. Sir,—l am afraid we must all come to the conclusion that Mr. F. Monks and Mr. T. Morris are ..not diploma- tists of the first order. This conclusion is forced upon us when we come to consider the regulations which the Museum and Library Committee have formulated in con- nection with the new arrangement for lending books out of the rate-supported library, the arrangement, that is to say, that Mr. Monks and Mr. MorrL, • of the other side, took upon themselves to negotiat on be- half of the agitating ratepayers. The grand feature of this arrangement was to be the perfect equality of the positions of those who took a penny for a book and those who pay quarterly or annual subscrip- tions. In fact, as was to be expected of an arrangement which met with theapproval of a gentleman whose popu- lar sympathies are well known, and of another gentle- man who always speaks with unfeigned reverence of the horny-handed," it was to be thoroughly democratic. But what do we find from the,regulations ? Simply that the distinction between the subscriber and the person who goes with a penny is to be remarkably suggestive of the distinction which exists between the man who pays his way and the man who seeks kublic charity. If 'a workman at Roney forge or at 'Monks, Hall, and Co.'s works, goes to the library for a book for which he is going to pay a penny, he must also take a voucher, signed by two persons, that he is respectable, or that, if he is not respectable, these two other persons will bear any loss his want of respect- ability may cause the library. That is to say, the man who goes to the library with a penny is a "suspect." The presumption is that he is not respectable, and the 'onus of proof that he is lies with himself; he must pro- duce evidence in the shape of two signatures of his re- speetability. That is the position which the man with a penny holds at the library under the new arrangement. Now what is the position that the subscriber holds? At the very moment that the man from Bewsey forge or Monks, Hall, and Co.'s works is producing his voucher of respectability at one colinte*, and the signatures on if are being critically scrned, there may be at another counter a scented" popinjay" having a book served out to him with obsequious alacrity without ever being re- quired to bring his voucher. At the same time it may be that the man from Bewsey or Bank Quay his lived and paid rates in the town for years, is reputed as a steady and industrious man among his neighbours, and has a house well stocked with furniture, while the indi- vidual at the other counter may have been in the town a few months only, may be dissipated and frivolous in char- acter, and carry his fortune on his hack, even if he do not merely carry a debt to his tailor. Where then is the equality in the positions of those two persons? Is it not clear that there is no equality in their positions, but a mean, unjust, and insulting distinction? It may be said that at the free libraries of other towns persons bor- rowing books have to produce vouchers. Yes, but in other towns books are lent out entirely free, and if we did in Warrington as they do in other towns the man from Bevvsey and the "popinjay" would be treated in every respect alike. For my own part, if I might pre- sume to advise others to do as I intend tu do myself, I should say "Have nothing to do with any such mean and contemptible arrangement, but endeavour to com- pel those who are seeking to ape the philanthropist in their dispensing of public money, to put the manage- ment of the library on a fair and honest basis."—l am. sir, Warrington, November 17,1887.
A RATEPAYER.

WHAT IRELAND IS, AND WHAT IT MIGHT YET BE. Sir,—lreland to my own knowledge, which extends over a period of half a century, has been in a chaos of misery, and of party and political strife; a scene of bloodshed and murder; the people coerced down at the point of the bayonet, so that the last state of the coun- try is worse than the first. The greatest curse of the country has been bad landlords and worse agents, they they neither built, drained, or reclaimed, nor did they plant, fence, or build manufactories, but they rack- rented their poor miserable tenants on their own im- provements, and spent the money in other countries. For want of manufactories everything has to be pur- chased in England, from the needle 'to the anchor, which causes a continual drain of money to go out of the coun- try. The Irish people feed cattle, sheep, and pigs, but they never can use any of them; as they require the money from what they have to sell off their little farms, to pay taxes and other demands. I think there is no people on earth worse fed and housed than the Irish. The rents to a great extent that are paid to the landlords never come out of the holdings, but are sent from other countries by the younger and streing,,er portion of the families that have had to emigrate; this accounts for the reduction in the population. The sons and daughters of these poor people who are toiling in servile labour in other countries, sending money to pay rents to keep a shelter over their parents' heads; but when from sickness or other cause their money does not come forward, then hundreds and thousands of police, and soldiers are sent by the Government to evict them from their houses. The very houses these people built are being levelled by the crowbar brigade ; every pound recovered in this manner is costing the country hundreds. I think it is high time the taxpayers of the country cried out against this unholy war of extermin- ation. You cannot force laws so unjust on a people against their will; if you do, you need not be surprised to see the laws disobeyed and ,disrespected. Respecting the tyranny of the National League that we hear so much about; it is all nonsense. I say with General Buller that it has been the salvation of the
• if

Irish people. It has kept land-grabbers and coward that had not courage enough to emigrate, from taking land that other poor people had been evicted from, not being able to pay an impossible rent. I say the League has assisted thousands that were thrown on the road- side by the landlords after working all their lives for stem. Some will say they will not let people pay that are able and willing. Well, there are some people will pay anything for peace's sake so long as they receive the rent from abroad; and this makes a bad impression on the landlords, who think all should be equally able to pay, whereas some tenants may not have a family able to earn money for them—a fact which the landlord, or his agent, does not take into account. The poor tenant has not the means to go into the Land Court and fight for his rights against a rich landlord, with the administrators of the law and squads of police and soldiers at his back. I say the tenant had nothing to look to but the League for support and sympathy. I have no doubt there are crawling creatures who tell the landlord or his agent of the tyranny of the League, but this is merely to gain favour, as there are informers and ruffians in all communities. . lam a Protestant of the North of Ireland, and I hate liged there for thirty years. I never knew in all my experiance during that time a landlord to make any im- provements for his tenants, or to assist them in any way, except to assist to take the money out of their pockets. Even this state of things exists among the contented and prosperous community of the North that we hear so much about. Anyone who has travelled through the highly cultivated country of England and then visited this prosperous community would not con- sider he had landed in the heaven represented. One half of the North of Ireland is lying as it was whet' Noah came out of the Ark • not a single tree or any other shrub has ever been planted on this mist-laden waste, no shelter for man or beast. The other half is producing about one-fourth what it would produce under proper cultivation. The land is lindrained, and unfenced, (at least what I would called unfenced; big clay mounds run zig-zag and taking up a lot of land with little if any Protection to crops) the ground not half manured, and full of weeds. I have heard it remarked, and believe with truth, that there are more weeds in one acre of land in Ireland than there are between Holyhead and London, a distance of 250 miles. IBesides there are no suitable buildings, gates, or water laid on; to my own knowledge it would take £5O per acre to bring even the cultivated part into the same con- dition in every respect as the agricultural land of Eng- land. The English labourer is better fed and better housed; his children better, clothed, and schooled, than the Irish farmer and his children. I have seen even the Presbyterian Clergymen? children going to school with- out any protection on their feet; what you cannot find amongst the children of the English labourers. When this is the state of things in that prosperous community, what is the state of the South of Ireland ? But more of this in my next.—Yonrs &c. JAMES McILWAINE. Knowsley, Lancashire.' •

THE LIBERTY OF THE PRESS, &c. Sir,—That great lawyer Erskine when defending' Cap- tain Bailie said:—" The liberty of the press, and the liberties of the country, must stand or fall together." I would venture to add tha right of public meetings, and perfect freedom must stand or fall together. The -privi- leges which we now enjoy were won after obstinate con- tention, and distressing strife between power and reason. We need a Fox or Erskine to-day to help to rescue the• most precious of our privileges from the insidious en- croachments of "black, tyrannous Toryism," and a Burke to speak and write in defence of the " lfberty which is the foundation of all other liberties." The bit- terest enemies of publicity are the malefactor who tries to escape the notice of the judge; and the tyrant who would stifle public opinion because he fears to hear its, voice. Unfortunately for the honour of England, we , are at present cursed with a tyrant in the person of Mr. A. .1. Balfour. He has not yet learned from history and experience the peril and utter fruitlessness of all attempts to curb the liberties of a people, or he would not pursue in Ireland a policy which is making Englishmen blush ' for their country's hoeotir. The future historian will be able to truthfully sy of A. J. Balfour what Macauley- said of Strafford: "that Than formed a deliberate scheme to subvert the fundamental Laws Of England." Mr. Bal- four may call his policy " the thorough maintenance of just authority," but it. is nevertheless "thorough ty- ranny." It is only right to bring forward evidence to support the charge! have brought against this pinchbeckStrafford. Leeus use our "mind's eve" and look on the evictions at Glenbeigh, Bodyke, Coolgreaney, Lisdoonvarna, and Woodford. Just look for a moment at Balfour's "lambs" called "emergency men "—pulling down the "mud cabins," from over the heads of poor old men and women, and young innocent children all that they could e 11 home; imitating to the very letter the malpractices of Rirke's lambs in Somersetshire in the time of Laud, Hyde, and Jefferies, whose names will for ever have the execration of civilised mankind. Let us not forget the death of young Kinsella, the murder ,at Youghal, the bloodshed of three innocent lives at Mitchelstown, the prosecution of Messrs Sullivan and OBrien for upholding the freedom of the press and the right of public meeting, andlast but notleast the treatment of Mr. and Mrs„ Blunt. All these atrocities are upheld by Balfour, Brownrigg, and blunder, bayonets, bludgeons, and blood. shed, and then we are told it is maintaining the "Integ- rity of the Empire." The time is close at hand when Englishmen of all creeds will say of this secondhand Strafford" never more be officer of ours." But what will posterity say of some of the defenders of this tyrannous government—of Mr. John Bright who told us that "force was no remedy," and vet pats on the back the apostles of fraud and force? Or of Mr. Joseph Chamberlain who said that England treated Ireland worse than Russia treated Poland. and yet appeals to the men of Derry to do what their ances- tors did hundreds of years ago? It will be said of him he was first of those statesmen whose profligacy has taught Governments to adopt the old maxim of the slaVe market, that it is cheaper to buy than to breed, to im- port defenders from an Opposition than to rear them in a minority. Let me ask, what fruits has this tree of persecution produced but evil fruits? Let us turn then with the homage of our whole hearts to liberty and justice. Let us take example and couragefrom the past. There was a time when men expiated political honesty at the scaf- fold and at the stake. That is over. Let us hope and trust then, that the time will soon pass also when it may still be punished by the long slow torture of social degradation, professional ruin, imprisonment, and a broken heart. There is another topic on which I should like to say a , word. I attended the Fair Trade meeting held in the , Public Hall, on Thursday night and was favourably im- pressed by the matter and manner of Mr. Edgecome, the editor of the Fair Trade organ. ,Ile repudiated the idea that the "Fair Traders" wished to put a tax on corn. But Mr. White, the chairman said that he would put al 10s. duty, per quarter on corn, and would be willing to use the money so raised for the purposes of Free Edu- cation. Mr. George Woods who claimed to be a great authority on finance and also as one svhohad enunciated the Fair Trade doctrine in Warrington, said that ha ) would not beat about the bush on the matter of placing a duty on corn; but would boldly say that he would go further than the chairman and put more than a 10s. per quarter duty on corn. Well, sir, I wish to ask Mr. White and Mr. Woods a few very simple questions on the matter. To do as these gentlemen suggest would be to at once raise the price of bread ld. per 4 lb. loaf. My family consume 20 loaves per week. That would reduce very much the purchasing power of the money I get per week. Will these great authorities of finance tell me how I shall be compensated for having to spend Is. Bd. more per week for bread than Ido now? Will they kindly point out to melchere and bolo I shall be benefited by the policy they propose? Again, in the old days of Protection were the wages and hours of labour Of the people, and the general condition of trade, as good as in our own day? Are those countries which still resort to Protection as prosperous as our own country? Whilst admitting that there has been and is a great depression in trade, can Mr. White say that England alone has suf- fered Mr. G. Woods also stated that modern scientific improvements such as steam navigation, electricity, chemistry. and improved machinery had altered the eco- nomic conditions of to-day, and that the arguments of Cobden and Bright were not applicable now. Have not other nations also benefited by the same scientificmeans? Why are the economic conditions different for us and not for other countries? An answer to these questions will much oblige a labouring man who at present can not see what the Fair Traders mean.—l am, your's res- pectfully. EDWIN WRIGHT. 10, Ellen-street, Warrington, Nov. 18th. 1887. •

The South Wilts Liberal Association, on Thursday, passed a resolution declaring that it could no longer support Sir Thomas Grove, the present member for the division, on account of his opposition to Home Role. THE COLLISION IN TILE CHANNEL.—A body wearing a lifebelt marked W. A. Seholten was picked up off Sand- gate on Thursday morning, the appearance of which leads to the conclusion that deceased was one of the Scholten's officers. _ _

THE LONDON DEMONSTRATIONS .—The demonstrations in London on Sunday passed off without any serious breach of the public peace. Not only had the Chief Com- missioner of Police issued a proclamation prohibiting any meetings in Trafalgar-square, but he had intimated to the members of the numerous Radical clubs and other political organisations throughout London that no pro- cession would be permitted to pass through the square on its road to the park, and in order to give effect to this prohibition heavy masses of police were drawn across every approach to the square. The proces.sionists, therefore, made their way by other routes to Hyde Park, where speeches were made and resolutions passed con- demning the imprisonment of Mr. O'Brien and the con- duct of the police in Trafalgar-square on the previous Sunday. On Tuesday Mr. Cunningham Graham, M.P., and Mr. John Burns appearedat Bow-street Police Court, charged with unlawfully assembling, and causing the riot in Trafalgar-squa-e, on Sunday, the 13th inst. Mr. Poland prosecuted. Police-superintendent Hunt, Super- intendent Giles, and some police-constables having given evidence as to the disorder that occurred in the square, the defendants were remanded till Tuesday next, their bail being renewed.

Mr. William O'Brien is a great power in Ireland. He is the editor of "United Ireland "—the official organ ot the Parnellite party—a weekly paper with a large circulation throughout Ireland. Mr. O'Brien, who is probably justly described as an Irreconcil- able, is physically a tall, slim, weakly built man, with an intellectual look; And he devotes an im- mense amr, ,nt of nervous energy to the service of his country s cause. He is one of the ablest and most active of Mr. Parnell's lieutenants. The bit- terness infused into personal relationships in Parlia- ment through the polity pursued by his puty can- not but be distasteful to such annul; but he accepts readily all the penalties of the position--which , often include social ostracism—in the belief that he ;is thereby best serving' the ir ,r. T. . fore Mr. 0' Brien was appointed e, Ireland," he was on the strff of the " .I.`zeei Journal." He was educated at tLe Dioct,s4:l lege, Cloyne, and the Queen's College, Cork. He is a Mallow man, and he sat in one Parliament for Mallow. Which he won in 11"33, after a contest which excited keen interest, the Solicitor-General Istanding against him. At the time of his candida- ture Mr. O'Brien was awaiting trial for a bitter libel on Lord Spencer; but the trial came to nought' through the disagreement of the jury. He is a graduate of that Irish `Parliamentary College, her Majesty's Prison, for he was imprisoned Tor six months under the Coercion Act. During this time he was permitted to leave the prison daily on parole. accompanied by a warder, to visit his mother, who was suffering from consumption in an advanced stage. The unfortunate lady died a day or two after her son was released. Mr. O'Brien, who was born in 1852, is a man who has come very rapidly into public notoriety, not less for his connection with "United heir d," of which he is proprietor as well as editor, than for his suc- cess as a Nationalist orator. His paper was only established in 1881, as the avowed organ of the Land League, at the time when that organization attained its eminence. The views to which it gives expression have always rendered it an object for Government suppression in carrying out successive Coercion Acts, but like many other threatened institutions, it has lived and flourished. Daring the first ycar of its establish- ment it was in difficulties with the Government, and its issue was seized on one occasion. But this has /by no means changed the vigour of its tone, and its editor has long been regarded as one who was graduating for the distinguished honour of being a political martyr. It was. Mr. O'Brien's jou-nal ' which published the present "plan of campaign" for Irish tenants to follow, and again the jounial was threatened with suppressicn. dir:O'Brien has sat in Parliament successively for Mellow (18K `:3), and South Tyrone (1,95), afterwards retiring for a time, but at a bye-election was elected for one of the divisions ofirork. Like his colleague, Mr. John Dillon, he is said to suffer from pulmonary affection, which will no doubt be aggravated by his present imprisonment. He is now lying in Tulla- more gaol, undergoing a sentence of three months' imprisonment, under the Crimes Act. He vowed he 'would not wear prison garb or associate with felons, and some aSallrance was given him when In was removed, through illness, to the gaol Infirmary that he would be allowed to contin as to wear his own. clothes. The authorities however, had the meanness to steal his clothes while he was lying in bed, leaving a prison suit in their stead. These Mr. O'Brien refused to put on, and remained, for a time in bed; but the latest news is that he and his friends have outwitted the officials. The gaolers were amazed on Saturday morning to find him dressed in a new suit of tweed. How the suit was smuggled was a mystery to the governor, and it is to be hoped it will ever remain a mystery. Mr. O'Brien has endeared himself to Englishmen as well as Irishmen for the great ability, courage, and patriotism which be has long displayed.

BRAVE WILLIAM O'BRIEN. BY THE EDITOR. Brave William O'Brien is lying in jail; But courage, my brothers —his heart will not fail. He lives for old Ireland, where'er he may be; They may load him with chains, but his soul is still free. Though they hound him to death with their tyrannous
They cannot, they shall not, e'er strangle the cause. Should he fall—his the glory, and theirs the disgrace, While a hundred Oliriens will step in his place. .

Let them send proclamations; the boy is not born Who would not tread on them, and laugh them to scdin. Sure the Castle is doomed; let it go! let it go! See! it sinks in the earth with its own weight of woe.
0 Erin, dear Erin! thy long night is past; We see the bright gleams of the daybreak at last. A new song shall be sung, and its burden shall be— Joy comes with the morning—our Erin is free!

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guar- dians was held at Whiston Workhouse on Thursday fore- noon, when there were present Mr. J. Fisher (chairman), Rev. Dean Finegan, Messrs. J. Leatherharrow, J. W. Wareing, J. Matthews, W. Middlehurst, J. Burchall, W. G. Ashton' W. Tyrer, C. B. Johnson, J. Musson, E. !Sy-der, J. Ranson, W. Swift, P. Longton, It. A. Graves, J., Kenwright, T. Eatock, H. Hulme, an S. H. Hartley

(clerk). INMATES.—The Workhouse Master reported there were 534 inmates of the house this week, 519 last week, and 458 in the corresponding week last year. TILE ELECTION OF GUARDIANS.—The Clerk read a com- munication from the Local Government Board acknow- ledging the receipt of a copy of the resolution, of the Guardians suggesting an amendment of the general order , with respect to the election of Guardians, and which should receive the consideration of the Board.

Resioxmoxs.--Louisa Appleton, one of the nurses, sent in her resignation, and asked the Guardians for a testimonial. The Board spoke highly of her services, and directed the clerk to give the testimonial and to adver- tise for a successor.—The Clerk reported that the porter and portere,ss (Mr. and Mrs. Williams) were applicants for similar positions at Fulham Workhouse, and wished to be favoured with a testimonial. The Board directed that the testimonial be given. Tire LATE MR. W. L. EVANS, J.P.—The Clerk read the following letter—" Fazakerley House, November 21st, 1887. Sir,—l in most gratefully to acknowledge the address of condolence which you have forwarded to me on behalf of the Guardians of the Prescot Union, and I must ask you to convey to them and to the officers of the Union, as well as to accept yourself, my heartfelt thanks for the tribute paid to my husband's character and labour, and also for the kind sympathy expressed towards me in my great sorrow.—l am, sir, yours faith- fully, E.G. EVANS.—Mr. Hartley." PreosEerrnoNs.—The Rev. Dean Finegan drew atten- tion to the prosecution of persons who viers in arrear with their payments of orders made upon them, and said he did not think such prosecutions should be made when the persons were out of work and altogether un- able to pay.—The Clerk remarked that the recommenda- tions of the Relief Committees were always adopted, and in many cases when prosecutions were ordered the men, in order to defy the authorities threw themselves out of work. _

At a meeting of the Building Committee on the 14th inst.' the Clerk submit- ted amended plans of the, proposed alterations at the Workhouse with explanatory notes from the architect. The plans were approved and ordered to be sent to the Local Government Board with a 'copy of the notes rti- ferred to.

THE OVERCROWDING OF THE WOTZEITOHSE.-At several committee meetings which had bean held it was reported that the Guardians' representatives had had an interview ith the county justices, and it transpired that im- becik•-• could not be received into the Asylum. except as ordir .ry lunatic*, and .that no variation in the weekly charge for mattitenanceCbould be made. The committee were unanimously-Cif opinion that it would nokbe advisable to:rcinove the imbeciles to the Asylum under the circumstances,•:and they were further of opinion that the Board-rodm and the of6ces should be utilised as bedrooms to relieve the overcrowding; and Messrs. Fisher, Tyrer, and the Clerk were appointed to inspect premises in Prescot and S. Helens, which could be used as temporary ofhceS and Board-room. At another meeting itwas moved and seconded that the premises of Mr. Dennett, at St. Helens; be hired for twelve months at £9O, as Board-room and offices, but the motion was lost by two votes to three. It was afterwards decided to leave the question of offices to the Board.—The minutes passed.—The question was afterwards discussed at some length, and it was admitted by several Guardians that something should be done to remedy the overcrowding. It was e'timal•Ay decided, on the motion of Mr. I eather- barrow, second:A by the Rev. Dean Finegan, that the Guardians form themselves into a committee for the revision of the list of the inmates of the house in order to ascertain who were in a position fit for their dis- charge. This concluded the business. • • WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

A special meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. P. H. Gossage presided, and there were present Dr. O'Keeffe. Messrs. T. Handley; D. Wright, J. Taylor, -F. Heyes. J. Mid- wood, Sadler, W. W. Gossage, S: Hoyle, (Assisfant Clerk). NEW Disratcr RATE.—On the proposition of Mr. T. Handley, seconded by Mr. D, Wright, the seal of be Board was affixed to a General District Rate of Is./ in

the £ for the half year ending 25th March next. TKE MERSKY CONSERVANCY AND MOSS BANK 'SEWER.— Mr. Hoyle read a letter from the Local Government ' Boand in reference to the Local Board's application for ! sanetien to an 'outfall sevfer which it was proposed to: construot in the river Mersey at that place: with the • letter was transmitted a communication which the Board of Trade had received from the Mersey Conservancy , Board respecting the proposed work, and the Local Gov, errtment Board Stated that if the Local Board undertook • to give effect to the recommendation of the Acting Con- seryator, and would favour them with a duplicate of the-plan forwarded in the Local Board's letter, the for- mal assent of the Board of Trade .would be inscribed on both plans—The letter of the Mersey Conservancy Board stated that the Acting Conservator found. upon examination of the plans and making local enquiry that (1) The Proposed sewer pipes will cross Widnes -Marsh at that place 960 feet broad and all below the level of a2l feat tide. (2) The pipes are to be. of stone- ware, except for the last hundred feet next the river, where iron pines rise to be. substituted. In the present state of the Rimer the pipes would be no obstruction to nnA Igation, hut in the event of the main channel working over to the Whines shore and scourine: away the edge of the Marsh, the end of the iron pipe would he laid bare and projeet beyond the edge to the probable injury of any flat striking against it. The Acting Con- servator vreuld therefore suggest that the whole of the Sewer tripes should be made of stoneware, which would break easily, and not be as likely to damage vessels com- ing in contact therewith as iron.. He understood that the Clerk and the Surveyor to the Local Board were willing to comply with this suggestion; subject to the alteration thus indicated. the Acting Conservator had no objection to offer. In. reply to the Chairman the Surveyor said there was no possible,objection to having stone pipes. and they would be cheaper. Dr. O'Keeffe ! moved, and Mr. Taylor seconded that stonepives be • substituted for ironpipes. The motion was carried un- aminouslv. TRE WASTE HP AP NUISANCE.—Mr. ITOVIC read a letter from the Local Government Tioar(l. 'with reference to the deposit of Alkali Waste in the Widnes Urban ,Sani- tan, district. It apieared to. the Local Government Board thaf the means which the Inspectors under the Al- kali ke. Works:Regulation Act:had caused to be Ilseri for preventing nuisance from the depositinv of Alkali waste, have had a very considerable effect in diminishing the nuisance arising therefrofn, but that some nuisance still arose during the process of deposit, for the pre- vention of which no practical means had been con- trived which it would be within the Inspector's power to enforce. This nuisance was never nartichlarly offensive in emsequenc.e.of the proximity ,of some of the places of doposit to habitations. The Board thought it was, to be regreted that deposits should!, be se. placed, but it does not appear to them that thereNvas any provision in the Alkali and Chemical Works Regulation Act, which would cause proceedings to be taken in respect of the. position of the deposit. Whether the Sanitary Author- ities under the nuisance clauses. of the Public Health Act, 1875, could successfully provide in respect of such deposits. was a question for their consideration... While the Chief Inspector. and Dr. Affiick, the local Inspector had done and were doing all that was in their power to prevent nuisance from these waste heaps, they would always be ready to consider any suggestion that the Sanitary Authority might make on the subject and it would be convenient that such swmections should be made in the first instance to Dr. Affiink. Mr. Haves denied that the nuisane,e Was caused through the prox- imity of the waste heaps to dwellircrs. At Appleton, two miles distant, the nuisance was abominable at tines.. He moved that the letter be referred to the Health Com- mittee. Mr. Wright seconded the motion, which was carried unaminously. Twit VACANCY ON rrt*• Botan.—With reference ,to the application of the Board for authority to postpone until April next, the tilling up of a vacancy which had or:- cured on the Board, Se that this might be done at the annual election, the Local Government Board wrote that it was the duty of the 'Local Board themselves to •fill casual vacancies in their number, the could not extend the time for filling such vacancies:7in order to permit of the vacancy being filled up at the annual election. The - writer was to add that if the vacancy was not filled lin within six weeks it must necessarily remain to be filled up at the annual election, in. the absence of an order of the Board., (Laughter.)—Mr. Taylor: I suppose that we shall let it stand. over. Mr. Chairman.—Tt, was re- solved without discussion that the letter be laid on the table./ There was no other business.

MURDER OF A ,POLICE SUPERINTENDENT.—PoIice-Super- ;-itendent Birkhill is reported to have been shot dead at Otley on Thursday morning, when apprehending a man who was alleged to have murdered his child. It appears that a gamekeeper named William Taylor, while quarrelling with his wife, fired a gun, the contents of which entered his child, aged ten months, killing it, and on the Superintendent going to apprehend him, he fired, killing him on the spot. Taylor w9s eventually arrested. THREE' CHILDREN BURNT To DFAT/I.—A fire, which was attended by most distressing and exciting circumstances, occurred at four o'clock on Wednesday afternoon at 71, Clarendon-street, London. The second floor front room was tenanted by "a Mrs. Stanley and her husbiftid, and it appears that the mother left her three children locked in the room while she attended a mothers' meeting. The firemen burst open the door, and discovered the children burnt to death, one being scalped and disembowelled, and the third charred in a dreadful manner. Their names are—Charles, aged 5; Richard, 2 : and Minnie Louise, 7 months.
orR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM OCR OWN CORRESPONDENT.]
23, Old Broad-street, E.C.

There has been movement but little progress in the Stock Exchange matters during the past week. The movement has been perpetual, prices altering fraction- ally nearly every hoer, the result of rumours often so wud that the wonder is that even the Stock Exchange could take arty notice of them. This has been due partly to continental rumours' which are proverbially noted as havrug their origiu for Stock Exchange purposes. Inter- national stocks have been very weak, with the exception ' of Russians, which have shown a rise ever since the visit of the Cmr of Russia; in fact, Russian stocks for the last day or two have been quite buoyant, and they have re.- turned to their normal price of 96, at which they stood before the recent panic—the result of the refusal of the Imperial Bank of Germany to advance loans on Russian securities. American railroad seeurities are still very uncertain and irregular and the exception is for any of these stocks to remain unaltered for a period of 24 hours. The steck which is up to-day is down to-morrow, and vice-versa. The chief feature of the week has been the budyancy of copper mines, copper having riscfn in price since tlie beginning of October, from £4O per ton until to-day it stands at 51 As a natural result the shares of copper mines have gone up in an equal ratio, the chief company being Rio Tinto's. When Rio Tinto's stood at 8 readers were advised to purchase. When they touched 104 as they did within a marvellously short time we ad- vised a sale upon which they receded to n, and we again advised a purchase. To-day they are over 13, and though they may go a point or two higher our advice is to take profits at once as we are firm believers in taking quick profits. The company promoter is just now making desperate effort through the Londen dailies to get in some money by hook or by crook. The London papers are not squeamish as to what advertisements they insert; one of the most astonishing is the prospectus of Armstrong and Co., with a capital of £lOO,OOO, The object is to take over another company established so recently as two years ago. They profess to be foreign bankers. Foreign bankers Who are doing a profitable business do not re- quire the aid of the public in dividing.their profits. The accountants' certificate accompanying the prospectus naively remarks that "more capital could be profitably employed in the business." This is a very safe assertion, as there ere very few businesses which are not in the same position. Our readers were last week cautioned against a company called the Kilkivem Mines, Limited, which was issuing a, prospectus marked for private circu- lation only. This private prospectus was sent to every known investor of any gold mines whose address could be ascertained. "he amount which the promoters were ,to receive ou's of this company was £90,000. Owing to the warnings which have appeared the promoters have wisely withdrawn the scheme, at any rate, for the pre- sent. It is quite-possible that the same scheme may come up under another name.

The nominations for Dulwich have been fixed for Tue- sday next, and the polling, for Thursday. Last night's " Gazette' publishes a considerable num- ber of promotions in the army for services in Burmah. Old Temple Bar is being removed from Farringdon- street to Theobald's Park, Cheshunt, where it will be - erected on Sir Henry Meux's estate. H.M.S. Ajax left her anchorage in the Clyde yesterday i morning for Lewis, to assist n suppressing the deer raid disturbances. She has nearly five hundred men on , board. A notice issued yesterday intimates that the City of London authorities intend calling out three thou- sand special constables in view of disturbances on Sun- y. d•aMiss Lingart-of Hoghton-street, Southport, who at- tined her one hundredth year last June, died on Friday morning. The deceased retained all her mental faculties up to the last. Her Majesty the Queen,with Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg, and the infant prince, the Princess Frede- rick of Hanover, and Princess Victoria of Battenberg, left Balmoral on Friday afternoon for the south. A CLERGYMAN SENT TO GAOL.—At the Old Bailey, on Friday, Her-y Valentine Pickering, a clergyman of the Church of England, was convicted of an assault upon John De Boer. He was sentenced to eighteen months' hard labour. THE Scwoursisi DISASTER.—The inquest on the twenty- one bodies of the victims of the Scholten disaster was resumed at the Town Hall, Dover, on Friday. Albert Goldsmith, manager of the Arundel Club, London, gave evidence identifying body No. 8 as that of his brother, Solomon Goldsmith, cigar dealer, at 71, Peter-street, Mile End-road, London, on his way to America. Cap- tain Webster, of the Rosa Mary, cross-examined, said he had two lights, one fore and another at the stern, although the regulation allowed only one. The jury found that the Scholden ran into the Rosa Mary, and that the latter was at anchor at the time. The verdict also praised the conduct of the Captain and crew of the Sun- derland steamer Ebro, through whom so many lives were saved. THE FRENCH CRISIS. • PARIS. FRIDAY.—M. Grevy informed M. Ribot yester- day evening that he had relinquished the task 04 at- tempting to form a new Cabinet. The President's mes- sage will, consequently, be communicated to the Cham- bers by M.
